entry.title: The Future is Bright: NICA Expands with Its First Western Regional Event in St. George, Utah
entry.content:
Last weekend, NICA (the National Interscholastic Cycling Association) hosted its first-ever Western Regional event in St. George, Utah. I was fortunate to be invited by NICA’s first non-endemic partner, Mazda, to take a road trip and attend the event in person. This allowed me to observe the NICA experience firsthand and see the level of participation, community, inclusivity, and love of cycling being fostered by the world’s largest youth mountain biking organization. 

Of course, I also got to see some of the top youth mountain bike racers from across NICA’s western leagues battle it out on course in the biggest race of the season. Let me tell ya, these kids are quick.

NICA Regional Events

Since it was founded in 2009, NICA has been growing steadily and has become the largest youth mountain bike racing association in the U.S. and the world. In its 17-year history, it has expanded across the U.S. (and recently to Australia) and has grown to 33 leagues nationwide, including over 1,000 teams, more than 26,000 youth athletes, and 16,000 adult coaches.

In recent years, NICA has expanded to include regional events across the U.S. to bring together and celebrate the NICA community with weekend-long festivals that include rides, races, expos, and other activities. The racing is open to male and female high-school-aged (grades 9-12) athletes in a tiered varsity system: JV3, JV2, JV1, and Varsity. The events also include several non-competitive activities, including adventure rides, GRiT, skill areas, and Teen Trail Corps (more on these below).

These events started with Eastern Regionals in 2023 and 2024, with NICA adding Central Regionals in 2025. In early 2026, NICA announced the addition of Western Regionals to its calendar, providing an opportunity for all of its leagues to participate in a Regional event. This week, NICA announced its 2027 Regional event schedule, which will include all three regions for the second year in a row. Additionally, as part of a new multi-year partnership, NICA’s 2027 Regional events are being presented by Mazda (more on this soon).

Inaugural Western Regionals

Taking place in St. George, Utah, this past weekend, the first Western Regionals drew participants from 10 western leagues representing the states of Arizona, California, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, and Utah. This included over 800 high-school-aged racers, more than 120 youth participants in non-competitive activities, and nearly 600 volunteer adult coaches.

Including families and spectators, well over 2,000 attendees came to the race venue in St. George to participate or support. They were greeted by 22 vendors in the expo area, including NICA’s lead partners like Trek, Mazda, RockShox, and SRAM, along with neutral support from Shimano and Canyon, and pit areas for all of the NICA leagues in attendance. Mountain bike races were nothing like this when I was a kid…

Beyond the expo and the sheer number of athletes, coaches, and spectators, I was immediately struck by the scale of the production, particularly the organization and professional setup of the venue. NICA, it seems, runs a very tight ship, and this was legitimately one of the best-organized events that I’ve seen in years. 

Purpose-Built Race Venue

As I was walking around and checking out the race course and venue, known as Renegade Ridge Trail Park, it struck me that it seemed oddly ideal for hosting mountain bike races. Not only was there ample parking and a large expo area, but the trail layout included a wide start area, feed zone, and a separate finish area. The trails were freshly cut and in pristine condition, and included rock-armored technical up and downhill sections. Frankly, it reminded me of a World Cup XC course.

After chatting with a few folks, I quickly learned that Renegade Ridge Trail Park was only completed a few months prior, in July, and was purpose-built to NICA race standards to host race events. Through a cooperative effort between Desert Color (resort), Washington County, and the Utah Trust Lands Administration, this new park was built to serve as both a competition venue and public trail network.  

Renegade Ridge Trail Park was first used for the Utah NICA State Championships in late October. With more than 7,000 student-athletes, Utah is NICA’s largest league, and its State Championships reportedly drew 2,400+ participants. Say what?

The Racing

NICA’s roots are in racing, and it is one of its core activities. According to NICA, their “inclusive racing format offers participants the opportunity to experience and learn discipline, success, failure, and graceful defeat,” while the “team environment helps student-athletes learn empathy, humility, flexibility, and resilience.” And as I observed over the weekend, it truly takes a village. Sure, bike racing is an individual sport, but these young athletes are supported by their coaches, teammates, friends, and family.

With over 800 racers competing across four categories (each with separate male and female races), there were a total of 8 races over the weekend. The four-tier varsity system — JV3, JV2, JV1, and Varsity — offers racing for athletes of varying experience and fitness levels, from entry-level up to those who might go pro in the coming years. 

On that note, NICA has become somewhat of a hotbed of up-and-coming athletes and a feeder system of sorts for top-level U.S. mountain biking. It has absolutely been instrumental in helping elevate the level of mountain bike racing in the U.S. and on the world stage. In fact, Brendan Quirk, the CEO of USA Cycling, was in attendance at NICA Western Regionals. He spoke briefly during a Q&A at the event, saying, “Our mountain bike program is as strong as it has ever been, and that is a direct result of NICA.” He pointed out that 100% of the top U.S. mountain bike racers are NICA alumni, and went on to say, “If you have aspirations to race professionally, this is where you want to be.” 

Familiar names including Kate Courtney, Gwendalyn Gibson, Savilia Blunk, Haley Batten, Madigan Munro, Christopher Blevins, Bjorn Riley, and Riley Amos all came up through NICA before making their way onto the world stage. Not to mention NICA alumni like Sepp Kuss and Neilson Powless, who went on to professional road racing careers. 

And it’s clear to see why. The level of racing is already incredibly high. On Sunday, the pace of the Varsity Male and Female races was very impressive. In the Varsity Female race, the top five were separated by just 15 seconds. Similarly, in the Varsity Male race, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th places were decided in an exciting 3-up sprint just 2 seconds behind the race winner — the top 15 all finished within 2 minutes of the leader. 

Of course, any of these racers and their fellow competitors could potentially go on to become professional racers. And with 26,000 NICA athletes and growing across the country, it certainly seems like U.S. mountain biking’s upward trajectory is bound to continue.

More Than Just Racing

NICA’s roots are in racing, and mountain bike racing is obviously still a major part of what the organization does. While those who wish to compete have ample opportunity, NICA’s mission and programs extend well beyond racing. Through its teams, trained coaches, and events, NICA aims to “help young people thrive both on and off the bike — building confidence, leadership, friendships, and making the world a better place.”

  • Our Mission: We build strong minds, bodies, character, and communities through cycling. 
  • Our Vision: Every youth is empowered to be a part of a thriving and engaged cycling community.
  • Our Values: Fun, inclusivity, equity, respect, and community.

Everyone Participates

While some NICA athletes might be all about the racing, non-competitive activities are a staple of NICA events. One of the non-competitive programs is NICA Adventure, where participants get outdoors, learn skills, and experience mountain biking outside of the race course. At Western Regionals, I watched as dozens, if not hundreds, of student athletes and families rode the adventure course at Renegade Ridge Trail Park. The skills zone was also getting plenty of use with a handful of features, including wooden ramps, rollovers, and a teeter-totter to test your bike skills.

Likewise, NICA’s GRiT (Girls Riding Together) is an effort to close the gender gap by bringing more girls and women into the community. NICA’s female participation is already impressive, but the goal is to increase female athlete and coach participation by 10% in the next 5 years. NICA’s Teen Trail Corps programs provide athletes the opportunity to get involved in their cycling community through advocacy activities, including trail building and maintenance. 

Community Building

At Western Regionals, I heard the word “community” probably close to 100 times, and I wasn’t even there the whole time. While it might have initially sounded a little cliché to a jaded old fart like me, it was abundantly clear that it wasn’t just a word in NICA’s mission statement, but it is, in fact, a very big part of the experience. There’s a lot more NICA than just showing up for a race. 

Every NICA team has athletes, coaches, and families involved, and they train and travel together, camp out, and support each other. As these teams go to league events or regionals, their communities and connections grow. I was honestly blown away by the number of student-athletes in attendance, but even more impressed by the number of coaches, family, and friends there to support them.  

And that’s what it’s all about. Success on the race course is great and all, but ultimately, it’s the campfires, dinners, friendships, and camaraderie that will likely leave a lasting impression on all those involved. And that translated directly to sportsmanship and respect on the race course. At the finish line, there was no shortage of high-fives and hugs between athletes, which is always great to see in such a competitive environment. 

My Takeaway

When I first arrived at NICA Western Regionals, I wandered into the expo area and ran into my friend Wayne Smith (aka Big Tall Wayne), a professional race mechanic for Canyon Bicycles, who was on hand providing neutral service for athletes. The weekend had only just started, and he said, “This is easily my favorite event of the year.” And this was coming from a man who has spent the past several years traveling to major professional races around the globe as Pete Stetina’s bike mechanic. 

And I think Big Tall Wayne’s sentiment was shared by many in attendance at Western Regionals. Everything from the venue, participation, organization, and even the weather was spot on. The racing was fast, and the vibes were high. And if there’s one thing I’m taking away, it’s that mountain biking is alive, well, and thriving, and the future of the sport, both on and off the race course, is as bright as it’s ever been. Keep up the good work, NICA.

To learn more about NICA or get involved, head to nationalmtb.org

entry.title: Is Tomac Bikes About to Make a Comeback?
entry.content:
John Tomac is one of the most legendary mountain bikers the sport has ever known. In a racing career spanning from the mid 1980’s to the early 2000s, “Johnny T” was renowned as one of the most well-rounded cycling athletes of his time. From professional road racing to top results in both XC and DH, John Tomac excelled at racing virtually anything with two wheels. Ultimately, he tried to leverage his notoriety and experience into a mountain bike brand.

In the late 1990s, Tomac partnered with Manitou’s founder Doug Bradbury and founded Tomac Bikes. In 1998, the brand debuted with three full-suspension models. After a few years, the name was licensed to American Bicycle Group and ultimately acquired by Joel Smith, who operated Tomac Bikes from 2006 to 2013. 

Now, 13 years later, a Tomac Bikes account on Instagram just appeared out of nowhere and is teasing what appears to be a comeback for the brand. The first post (above) is from October 29th, and says “THE LEGEND RETURNS. A new chapter begins.” The second post (below) is from yesterday, November 19th, and it includes a link to the Tomac Bikes website, which is simply a landing page where you can enter your email address to get on the mailing list. Whether John Tomac or his son, motocross superstar Eli Tomac, is involved remains to be seen.

So, whether you’re feeling nostalgic for the old days when John Tomac dominated nearly every cycling discipline, or you just want to know what Tomac Bikes is cooking up, you can click on the link below to sign up. We can’t wait to find out, and we’ll keep you posted when we know more.

tomacbikes.com

entry.title: HIRU Launches Cycling Shorts With a Menstrual Chamois Built for Women Who Ride, Period.
entry.content:
Chamois design has gotten pretty nerdy over the years. We’ve got multi-density foams, perforations, crazy shapes, and even the KuKu Penthouse from Assos. Somehow, though, the idea of building one for riding during your period has been left behind. Unfortunately, it’s not totally surprising in this industry. Thankfully, HIRU, Orbea’s cycling apparel brand, is stepping in with its first shorts that feature a menstrual chamois. Meet the HIRU Menstrual Chamois Shorts.

The new shorts are the result of two years of development. HIRU built multiple prototypes and tested them in the real world with female cyclists, aiming for a chamois suited to period days that still holds up to long-distance riding, training, and racing. As HIRU’s Product Director Óscar Pérez puts it, “If it’s that week, it’s still your week.”

But How Does it Work?

The big change is in the textile technology. The chamois uses targeted absorbent zones to capture fluid and keep the surface dry and comfortable. An integrated technical membrane acts as a barrier against leaks. All while still keeping the padded properties you need to sit on a saddle for hours on end. In HIRU’s development testing, the chamois absorbed up to 30 ml of fluid in one minute. The polyester surface also gets an anti-odour treatment.

The Chamois Tech

Under all that, the padding still gets the full chamois treatment. There are three foam layers, and each has a job: a 4 mm elastic memory foam, a 6 mm reticulated foam rated at 140 kPa, and a high-impact foam at 65 kPa. Together, they’re meant to dampen vibration and keep things comfortable late in a long day. HIRU says the result is a chamois that keeps the comfort and light weight it’s been known for.

HIRU Menstrual Chamois Shorts Retail & Detail

Retail: TBD

  • Absorbency: Up to 30 ml in one minute (HIRU’s development testing)
  • Absorption design: Targeted absorbent zones to capture fluid and keep the surface dry
  • Leak protection: Integrated technical membrane barrier
  • Odour control: Anti-odour treatment on the polyester surface
  • Foam layer 1: 4 mm elastic memory foam
  • Foam layer 2: 6 mm reticulated foam, 140 kPa
  • Foam layer 3: High-impact foam, 65 kPa
  • Intended use: Long-distance riding, training, and racing
  • Development: Two years, multiple prototypes, real-world testing with women cyclists
  • Versions: Short and long
  • Colors: Short in pink or black; long in burgundy or black

The shorts come in both short and long versions to cover different conditions and rider preferences. The short version comes in pink or black, and the long version in burgundy or black.

It’s a straightforward idea executed with the same foam-spec attention we’d expect from any high-end pad. We’ll be curious to hear how the absorbency and leak protection hold up over long days on the bike.

The shorts are on sale now through HIRU’s usual channels, including specialist retailers and the Orbea website. Hit the link below for more info.

Orbea.com

entry.title: Kona Remote 160 CR Review: Like a Process with Battery Options for Short & Long Rides
entry.content:
If the Kona Process is “the mountain biker’s mountain bike,” then that would make the Remote 160 CR the mountain biker’s ebike? The e-biker’s mountain bike? Whatever you want to call it, just know that if you like the ride of the Kona Process mountain bikes but want a little boost, you should love the new Remote 160 CR.

Built with a carbon frame, 160mm of travel front and rear, and 29″ wheels, the Remote 160 CR starts off pretty close to the Process 153 CR. That’s before you figure in the electric motor, of course. The Remote gets its extra go from a Bosch Performance Line SX motor with 60Nm of max torque and 600W of max motor power. That puts it at the higher end of what most would call the lightweight or SL ebike tier. It still provides noticeable power, but not ‘cut the tires loose while climbing at full speed’ kind of power.

Along with that relatively conservative torque and power number (especially when compared to recent bikes with up to 150Nm/1500W), the Remote gets a relatively small internal battery. This 400Wh battery is a big part of why a complete Remote 160 CR build comes in at 46.56lbs (21.11kg) with aluminum wheels, bars, stem, and meaty tires. Add the 3.29lb (1.49kg) PowerMore range extender, and you get 650Wh for a total weight of 49.85lbs (22.61kg).

The internal battery is not easily removable, but the included Bosch PowerMore 250 range extender is. We’ll get into this more below, but it’s a good thing this is included right off the bat.

Ebike things are controlled through the Bosch Mini Remote on the handlebar, or through the Kiox 400C integrated display, or through the Bosch Flow App on your phone.

The Kiox display has a bright color screen that is easy to see in bright sunlight, and there is actually a big benefit to it – in the event that your ebike has a problem, it will tell you the error code right on the screen and will even give you a QR code to scan to learn how to fix it. I needed to use this feature just once over the entire summer of testing (error code 510002), and it turned out to be as simple as turning off the motor and turning it back on again. Who needs an IT department?

The screen shows a number of other details like ride metrics, wattage of you and the bike, and assist levels. But its position on the top tube makes it hard to concentrate on while riding, so don’t expect to be watching your power output on the screen if you don’t want to power right into a tree. It’s a bit amusing that the Kiox and Bosch Flow app can do almost everything my cycling GPS computers can, but I still found myself mounting a GPS to the handlebar because it puts it out front where it’s easier to see at a glance with the trail whizzing by.

The Mini Remote is just about perfect. It’s easy to adjust to a comfortable position, and toggling up or down to different assist modes is second nature. Holding the lower button will engage walk mode, which is handy during tricky hike-a-bike sections, and if you have lights installed, the upper button can control those. There’s also a charging port built into the Kiox display for lights or computers, but don’t expect to have too much extra juice to spare.

The battery choice and build of the Remote 160 CR puts the bike in a unique position. Many lightweight ebikes are built to be lithe cross-country or trail racers. This is not that bike. Instead, the Remote 160 CR is most at home sending gnarly lines, hitting big jumps, and generally pushing the limits of your tires.

Built with satisfyingly grippy 29 x 2.5″ Schwalbe Radial tires with an Ultra Soft Magic Mary up front and Soft Albert out back, it’s clear that lightweight components came second to trail-worthy confidence. That extends across the build, with everything somewhat overbuilt in the typical Kona fashion. These bikes are built to ride (and probably crash).

That is all to say that battery life is not exceptional. But depending on what you plan to do with the bike, it may be ideal. Since the bike comes with the PowerMore range extender, it’s almost two bikes in one: a lightweight trail shredder built for shorter rides, or a heavier but still sub-50lb bike that can power you through longer trail missions with smart battery management.

With just the internal battery, I’ve been getting around 1.5hr ride times with something like 1,500′ of climbing on eMTB+ mode. For a lot of people, this will be plenty for a few laps after work, hitting up their smaller local trails, or for anyone who doesn’t need to be on a bike for 3 hours to have fun. Realistically, if you don’t need the extra battery range, you can save a lot of weight by not carrying it around on shorter rides.

For those who do want to ride longer, the PowerMore is the obvious option. With it, I’ve been able to extend ride time to 2-2.5hrs, with 2,500′ of climbing on eMTB+ mode. It’s still limited compared to full-power e-bikes with huge batteries, but it makes all but the longest rides I do on a normal basis possible.

The only catch is that the PowerMore takes the place of the only water bottle holder on the bike. Personally, there are plenty of longer rides that I do on a single bottle, so I’d prefer a bigger battery with a bottle cage, but it’s not a huge issue to have to carry a pack.

It’s worth pointing out that Bosch recommends you installing the PowerMore range extender before starting your ride, rather than adding it after your battery is already depleted. That’s due to the way that the Battery Management System balances power draw from the main battery and the PowerMore, with it switching back and forth between the two to discharge them evenly. This “protects the battery cells, minimizes electrical and thermal stress on the individual cell packs, and can help maximize the overall service life of both batteries.”

The PowerMore includes a clever quick-release mount that allows you to swap the range extender for their own bottle cage in an instant. Over time, the rails do get gunked up a bit, so I sprayed a bit of dry lubricant on them, and it seemed to help. When the PowerMore is installed, it uses a short cable to plug into the charging port of the bike. That makes it a little annoying when you need to charge, as you end up having to charge both the bike and the PowerMore separately. You can’t just plug into one place and charge both. But with the Bosch 4A charger, things are topped off quickly, and you can be back riding in a few hours if needed.

Being a Class 1 ebike, the Remote will cut out the assist as you approach 20mph/32kmh. It never has that OMG this thing is crazy kind of power, but it offers enough to easily get up the hill to hit that next jump line again and again.

The Build

In terms of the build, there were definite high spots, and only a few low spots. The Schwalbe Radial tires are certainly a bright spot. I have a similar setup on another full-power e-bike, and I’m left with the same impression – massive amounts of grip (you can hear it!), a casing that is so supple that you’ll likely need more air pressure than you typically run, and no punctures or issues to speak of.

The SRAM Maven Base brakes offer plenty of stopping power, which is exactly what you need on a bike like this. If I had my choice, it would be the new Maven B1s over the Base model for their slightly more progressive feel, but that’s splitting hairs.

Kona put a lot of thought behind each component in the spec, which is evident in their choice of dropper post lever. While the dropper itself is a TranzX model, the dropper lever is from SRAM. It was chosen because it offered excellent integration with the Maven MMX brake lever mount, and quite a bit of adjustment. I find that the ergonomics are acceptable, though not my favorite, and it also feels like it takes more effort to push than levers that run on cartridge bearings, like the Wolf Tooth ReMote Pro. However, it needs a very short push to activate the dropper, and it’s a better lever than you’ll find on most stock bikes.

The grips are fine, but I would prefer something with a little more cushion, especially with a very stiff 35mm aluminum handlebar beating up your hands.

The suspension duo with a RockShox Super Deluxe Ultimate 230×60 rear shock and a Lyrik Ultimate 160 fork does a lot to tame the trail. It took a while to dial in the settings, and I feel that the compression damping circuit in the fork may be a bit aggressive for my weight, but overall it performed quite well. Note that the bike does not include the integrated fender for the fork – I would buy one of these and install it immediately.

Spare Power

For drivetrain, you get a Shimano Deore Di2 1×11 system that’s powered directly by the ebike battery. The plus side of that wire connecting the derailleur is that you never have to worry about charging the battery for your drivetrain separately.

But what happens when you completely deplete the battery? Are you no longer able to shift or use your lights? Fortunately, the bike has a ‘Light Reserve Mode’ which keeps enough charge to allow you to shift and use your lights to get back to the trail head. This wasn’t set up on my early review sample, so I can’t speak to how it works but Kona assures me that all production bikes will have this setting.

Manual, Manual+, or Automatic Shifting

That connection of the derailleur to the motor also means you also get the eShift capabilities with either full Manual, Manual+, or Full Automatic shifting. Everything should be set up for this when you get your bike, but it’s a good idea to make sure both the bike and rear derailleur are updated first. After that, to access the different shift modes you press the small button on the top of the Shimano shifter.

You’ll see either an ‘M’, ‘M+’, or ‘A’ on the Kiox display for Manual, Manual+, and Automatic shifting modes. Manual works just as you’d expect with you controlling the only shifts. Manual+ makes it so only you can shift when you’re pedaling, but when you coast, the bike will shift into what it thinks will be the proper gear to start pedaling again based on your speed.

And full auto mode relies on a set cadence that you program either through the Kiox display or the Bosch Flow app. It will then shift automatically to keep it in that cadence range.

I used predominantly Manual shifting, but the other modes were fun to mess around with. Manual+ or Automatic could be very useful if you’re a new rider and focusing on just staying on your bike rather than when to shift. For advanced riders though, the ability of a human to know what’s coming on the trail and what gear they should be in before they get there is still superior to a reactionary machine… for now.

Elsewhere in the drivetrain, stubby little 155mm Prowheel carbon cranks are bolted to the motor along with a 34t ring from e13. Those propel a Shimano CUES LG500 chain, which drives a Shimano 11-50t 11-speed cassette. It’s all high-quality stuff that should last quite a while – and even better, it won’t cost a fortune to replace when you inevitably wear it out.

All stock bikes except the small come with 29/29″ wheels, where the small comes as an MX 29/27.5″ build. However, any frame can be built up with an MX wheelset thanks to the flip chip at the rear axle.

The stock wheels are decent, with WTB ST Tough i30 rims laced to Formula hubs in Boost spacing with an HG freehub. That freehub is fine, though it doesn’t have the quickest engagement. On the other end, the freehub on the motor seems to be rather loud and rattle-y when you’re coasting down the trail without any pressure on the pedals. This stands out because otherwise, this is a pretty quiet bike. The motor isn’t the most silent option, but its whines are fairly quiet and inoffensive.

Spread out on the frame, you’ll find smart details that hint toward how this bike is meant to be used. A custom OneUp chain guide is there to keep the chain in place when things get rough. There is a burly chainstay protector along with a skid plate for the motor and a shuttle guard on the downtube to protect against tailgate pad rub. You’ll also find a little mini fender to keep crud out of the main pivot, and a custom charging port with a swinging door to allow for easy use of the PowerMore. That last one doesn’t sound like much, but compared to flimsy rubber plugs on some other bikes, this is a very nice touch.

Retail & Detail

Offered in small, medium, large, and extra-large frames, the Remote 160 CR retails for $7,799. Not cheap, but considering everything you’re getting, it seems like a reasonable price – about $2,500 more than a Process 153 CR.

Riding Away

Riding the Remote 160 CR was enjoyable from the beginning, but it wasn’t until I took this bike to a local jump line that I had that lightbulb moment where I realized what this bike was really intended for. Along those lines, I was very happy to find that this bike didn’t suffer from the power cuts on hard g-outs that older Bosch ebikes experienced. You can pump, drop, and jib to your heart’s content and the motor will continue to propel you forward.

Without the PowerMore, the lighter-weight bike is more fun to throw around and jumps really well. This is the bike for people who complain about longer-travel e-bikes not being poppy and playful enough. The motor is there to help you get up the hill without leaving you gassed for the jumps on the way down. And it’s employed in a way that disappears when you want this to ride like a mountain bike, and not an ebike. As a result, this thing is a serious confidence booster on jumps you would normally shy away from.

On the flip side, if you want your ebike to ride like a worn-out sofa, enveloping everything in its path with never-ending softness, then this probably isn’t the bike for you. Even with the PowerMore installed, the Remote 160 CR still feels more like a Process than a heavy ebike. You can tell that this was a bike built by a team that lives and rides in the Pacific Northwest – in a very good way.

If you’re looking for a bike with the biggest battery and longest range, look elsewhere. But if you want a fun, lightweight bike that’s versatile enough for jump lines on the weekdays and bigger rides on the weekend, you might want to pick up the Remote.

konaworld.com

entry.title: In the Drops: New Shimano shoes and pedals, CeramicSpeed pulley wheels, Newmen’s wide wheels and an in-between Assos jacket
entry.content:
Cyclist
In the Drops: New Shimano shoes and pedals, CeramicSpeed pulley wheels, Newmen’s wide wheels and an in-between Assos jacket

As Microsoft has decided not to start its weekend early like it did last Friday, it’s back to business as usual for In the Drops in its Friday slot. As staff writer Ewan’s edition was the casualty of last week’s outage it was delayed to this Monday, so you get product round-ups to bookend your working week this week, you lucky lot.

I helped Ewan start the week off right with a complete history of Cannondale’s CAAD platform, then on Tuesday Ewan was back at the pumps reporting on Rapha’s return to the pro peloton with Red Bull-Bora-Handsgrohe.

We looked into where on earth once-touted wonder material graphene has gone in the bike industry on Wednesday, as well as published the first of eight mudguard reviews that have carried us through until today, with a brief pitstop to look into the rise of 32in gravel bikes.

Without further ado, let’s crack on with the second In the Drops of week 47.

Shimano S-Phyre RC910 shoes and Dura-Ace SPD-SLR pedals

The minty freshness of Shimano’s fifth generation S-Phyre shoes might catch the eye, and not without reason: Shimano claims they’re a few grams lighter and there’s a revised Boa cable path and carbon fibre heel cup to improve foot security. They also now use Shimano’s ‘Dynalast 2.0’ shape, which is wider at the toe and forefoot by 3mm and 2mm respectively, which the brand says helps the rider’s toes to splay more naturally, increasing comfort.

The real news here though is Shimano’s new pedal system, which sees its first major change in 23 years. SPD-SL moves to SPD-SLR, introducing several updates.

‘The pedal itself is stiffer and rotates more freely, but surfaces on both the cleat and pedal have also been altered to create a 2.3mm lower stack height. The rider’s foot is closer to the pedal axle, creating a more stable pedalling platform and improving power transfer,’ says Takao Harada, road and gravel product manager at Shimano Japan.

The pedal tip has a wider catch zone and the body is said to hang a slightly steeper angle (closer to vertical), both features that Harada says makes clipping in quicker and more natural. The cleat has been slimmed down and the necessary mounting hardware has been halved – this now no need for the washers between cleat and cleat bolt – reducing weight by 32g for a pair (142g versus 110g). This does mean fore-aft positioning is now limited to that which is baked into your shoe sole though (the new S-Phyres have increased adjustability in this area).

As Mathieu van der Poel will tell you as a result of his issues at Paris-Roubaix this year, the new system is not compatible with SPD-SL, though that will still be offered at 105 level, with Dura-Ace and Ultegra pedals moving to SPD-SLR.

CeramicSpeed Alpha pulley wheels

CeramicSpeed’s new Alpha PW upgrade kit looks to be a simple entry point to the Danish brand’s range of products, in that they can be a straight swap for a derailleur’s existing pulley wheels (CeramicSpeed’s complete OSPW cages generally require a new chain).

They are also half the price of OSPW systems, despite incorporating many of the same features: the ‘ADR’ debris-removing shape, a durable composite body that is claimed to last five times longer than stock and of course, the brand’s signature hybrid ceramic bearings.

The Alpha pulley wheels are said to lower bearing drag by 20% versus stock and come with a lifetime warranty. Along with the newly-released Alpha wheel bearings, this means that all of CeramicSpeed’s products are now backed as such.

Newmen Streem G.62 wheels

With its G.62 gravel race wheelset, German brand Newmen is doubling down on the theory that wider is better. The external width of the rims is a chunky 45mm, which Newmen claims produces aerodynamic results superior to rival wheels from Zipp and DT Swiss, so long as the right tyre is used.

‘You could use a tyre wider than 45mm, however the front wheel setup is fastest when the tyre is slightly narrower than the rim,’ says Bob Hoogerbrugge, Newmen’s brand manager. ‘Though the external dimension is wide, internally the wheels are more conventional at 27mm. The delta lets us make the bead hook portion of the rim walls very wide. They’re hollow though, so weight isn’t impacted, but the extra surface area goes a long way to prevent pinch punctures and improves rim durability against strikes.’

Newmen has also gone to the trouble of concealing the valves within the rim to eke out more speed – 0.5 watts according to Hoogerbrugge – and the rims are hooked, which sets them apart from many gravel wheelsets.

‘They are the safer solution as they do not require any special considerations of tyre compatibility,’ says Hoogerbrugge. ‘Hookless rims are primarily being offered because they are significantly easier to manufacture.’

Even with a hooked rim and a 62mm rim depth, the claimed weight is still competitive at 1,530g for the wheelset, thanks in part to carbon spokes, which Newmen says can produce the same level of stiffness as steel while using fewer spokes.

Assos Equipe Thermobooster P1 jacket

With a record-breaking summer almost still tingling the skin, Assos has reworked its jersey/jacket hybrid to reduce its weight.

‘We noticed riders on start lines wearing a spring jacket over their race suit to stay warm,’ says Luca Zanasca, senior manager of R&D Assos. ‘We wanted the Thermobooster to combine insulation with breathability without the bulk of a traditional recycled textile.’

Catering to the balmy autumn season – Assos says it works best between 12-21°C for rides that start cold and end warm – the updated Equipe Thermobooster P1 jacket combines the Sens Air Plus textile for the torso with a different sleeve material.

‘This Sens fabric is lightweight, non-brushed and highly elastic while also providing UPF 50+ protection,’ says Zanasca. ‘We think it’s not quite right that aero performance tends to be confined to summer outfits, so we’ve used our racing aero fit here too. On cooler days there’s still a need to be as fast as possible. The 575CX fabric on the sleeves has a 3D stripe structure and a second-skin fit, which makes it significantly more aero than a standard autumn jacket, plus we found that long sleeves are particularly fast between 35-45kmh.’

Ad feature

Get a Canyon Aeroad CF SL this Black Friday for just £2,899

This Black Friday you can treat yourself to a Canyon Aeroad CF SL (Stealth 1, 2, 3 and 4 available) for just £2,899.

This is a limited-edition bike using older frames and lower end modern groupsets (SRAM Rival AXS E1), all of which translates into great value for money.

You also get DT Swiss ARC wheels, Continental GrandPrix Clincher tyres and a Selle Italia saddle.

Keep an eye out for the November Canyon website sale, also coming soon.

Find out more

Ad feature ends

The post In the Drops: New Shimano shoes and pedals, CeramicSpeed pulley wheels, Newmen’s wide wheels and an in-between Assos jacket appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Le Col announces unmissable Black Friday deals
entry.content:
Cyclist
Le Col announces unmissable Black Friday deals

Not content with offering some of the world’s best performance-driven cycling apparel, Le Col is currently offering up to 60% off selected premium riding kit, with even bigger savings over the Black Friday weekend. Here, we’ve curated some of the best deals you can snap up between now and the final weekend of November.

And – as if you needed another reason to move quickly – the British-born performance brand is offering free UK delivery on orders of more than £130. Plus, on Cyber Monday (November 30), there’s a free gift with orders over £150 (see bottom for details). There really is no better time of the year to stock up on new kit, is there?

Also, by bagging a Le Col bargain, you’ll ensure every winter ride (whether rapid or easy) is warm, dry, comfortable and, just as importantly, performed in high-quality performance gear that’s developed with quality, style, and durability at its heart.

Men’s Pro Bib Shorts (grey/white): WAS £220 | NOW £90

If your rides are all about top speed and marginal gains, these are the shorts for you. They’re designed for maximum aero efficiency, and feature a compressive fit and top-end moisture wicking qualities. Everything about them is aimed at reducing bulk and boosting performance, right down to the all-new chamois – 6g lighter than previous incarnations, with antibacterial Silver Dry fabric (which also offers better breathability) and hydrophobic foam (which holds less moisture). Even the upper construction is improved, with enhanced ventilation.

Buy the Le Col Men’s Pro Bib Shorts

The ideal piece of kit for transitional days. Not cold enough for tights? Pull these on – they feature soft, thermal material to retain heat in your legs, a DWR treatment to deliver premium protection from showers and road spray, and a race fit to optimise aerodynamics. Not cold enough for tights, but too cold for just shorts? Pair these with a pair of leg warmers, and you have a versatile set-up to see you through late autumn and early spring.

Buy the Le Col Men’s Pro Thermal Bib Shorts

Men’s Pro Long Sleeve Thermology: WAS £170 | NOW £120

A no-compromise, aero performance jersey that not only looks stunning but also shields you from the elements. Developed with pro rider feedback and wind tunnel testing, it’s designed for high-tempo rides, and combines lightweight insulation (thanks to a brushed inner fabric) with exceptional wicking qualities. Its compressive stretch fabric moves naturally with the body, allowing an aggressive riding position without compromising on comfort. There are three rear pockets, plus a fourth, waterproof compartment.

Buy the Le Col Men’s Pro Long Sleeve Thermology

Men’s Pro Jacket: WAS £275 | NOW £110

True performance winter kit with speed at its heart, this race-fit jacket pairs breathability with weather protection, allowing you to pour everything into the ride in comfort, no matter what the weather. Polartec Power Shield fabric fights off wind and rain, and offers exceptional moisture wicking. A bonded front hem keeps the jacket anchored, scuba cuffs block cold air and spray, and a Vision Aquaguard zip further eliminates moisture ingress. Reflective details even add a dash of visibility for the darker months.

Buy the Le Col Men’s Pro Jacket

Women’s Hors Categorie Bib Tights: WAS £260 | NOW £145

These bib tights are engineered for long winter miles in less than favourable conditions, and are cut with a female-specific fit. Protection comes from a three-layer membrane to keep drizzle, spray and wind at bay. Insulation from a soft Italian Roubaix fleece lining is also bolstered by breathability. And the female-specific chamois takes comfort to new heights, with high-density foam construction for improved support, plus anti-bacterial Ionic+ tech for better moisture management.

Buy the Le Col Women’s Hors Category Bib Tights

Women’s Deep Winter Base Layer: WAS £80 | NOW £60

Perhaps the most essential weapon in the winter rider’s arsenal, this high-tech, lightweight, long-sleeved base layer not only insulates but also boasts remarkable temperature regulation, thanks to Polartec Alpha fabric at the core and upper back. Polartec Power Grid fabric on the lower back and arms uses a geometric structure to trap that heat in the first place, while also promoting airflow to wick away moisture. All in all, this base layer is a one-way ticket to training hard in comfort.

Buy the Le Col Women’s Deep Winter Base Layer

Women’s Pro Aqua Zero Long Sleeve Jersey: WAS £180 | NOW £75

The ultimate three-season jersey, designed to protect from the cold and rain while regulating your temperature, so all you need to focus on is your efforts. Thermal brushed fabric provides the insulation, and a tightly woven, stretch outer keeps the elements at bay, offering a water-repellent coating to shake off showers and spray. This is the piece of kit you’ll always reach for, whether your plan is autumn/winter base miles or spring tempo sessions.

It’s that time of year again. Most brands have already put out what will be their best deals. But a few brands are, for whatever reason, holding out until actual Black Friday for a short sale; for everyone else, everything below is what you’d expect.

The only wildcard here is if Uncle Amazon decides to randomly discount something without authorization from the company (great for us consumers!). That tends to happen for slightly older things, but sometimes even newer things. For example, the Garmin Fenix 9 sale you see below at nearly $100 off? That’s just Amazon doing Amazon. I wouldn’t expect much more than that though (based on years of history here). Instead, expect 2-3-year-old watches/etc. for Black Friday, where you’ll see some yolo pricing. Either way, if you see a deal you like, grab it now in case it disappears. You can always return/swap/whatever later (all the way till January in Amazon’s case).

entry.title: Readers’ Rides: Ihor’s 2006 Nagasawa Special
entry.content:
Maybe it’s all the recent Japan coverage, or maybe it’s the 20-year anniversary that has us nostalgic for track bikes over here. Putting that energy into the world resulted in Ihor sending in this stunning 2006 Nagasawa Special track bike, with a slick-as-shit build kit. Let’s check it out for this week’s Readers’ Rides!

I bought this frame in November 2023. I was just sitting at home, minding my own business, when I spotted this beautiful but broken Nagasawa frame on NJS Export for $150. It had a cracked seat tube near the bottom bracket. I bought it without a second thought.

It had belonged to a 2010 season champion and was originally welded in 2006. Shipping and customs fees cost twice as much as the frame itself. I already had a fork I’d bought in Japan earlier – possibly even the original one for this frame (I’m pretty sure it is).

It’s not that I needed another bike or had spare cash, but the purchase still stirred up a whirlwind of emotions. I fell instantly in love with that deep blue color. Like all glossy NJS frames, it’s hard to capture in photos – sometimes it feels like my photography skills just aren’t up to the task. Plus, the decals aren’t stickers – the lettering is stenciled on in white paint, something I hadn’t seen very often. It creates a striking contrast.

At that point, I was unemployed and had a broken frame, yet I had almost all the necessary parts at home – I was only missing a saddle and a headset. It was a situation that was both a blessing and a curse: I had everything, but I couldn’t actually build the bike. My idea was to build an NJS bike that looked like something from 2014 (I’m from Ukraine, where modern aluminum frames arrived a bit later).

I found a saddle on eBay for $30 (though shipping cost more, naturally) – brand new, in its original packaging from that era. I was absolutely thrilled because, for me, that specific saddle epitomized the bikes of 2014. Back then, my logic was simple: if you had a Fizik saddle, you were a serious road cyclist, but if you had a Zoncolan, you were just a street rider.

I bought the headset in Berlin in the summer of 2024. I just wanted to add some American-made components to the build of this Japanese bike.

I sourced all the other parts from the box where we keep our spare bike components (Yeah – I know you have a place like that). So, everything was ready – except for the frame. The seat tube needed replacing.

The moment I saw the frame, I knew exactly who I’d turn to for the repair – Dima from “Moskvich”. He handled the repair. I mailed the frame to him; he replaced the tube and sent it back.

It sounds simple enough. But in reality, Dima cut out the old tube and the old solder – while preserving the lugs – then inserted a new tube and silver-brazed it in place. NJS frame’s lugs were originally brass-brazed; they are easily repaired using silver, which has a lower melting point. When Dima finished, we saw the frame’s geometry for the first time – it turned out to have a slight sloping top tube, which pleased me even more. The journey of the frame from Dima to me took just over two months.

Just look at the quality of his work – it’s superb. The beauty and precision of his welds are amazing. As a gesture of appreciation for Dima, I also made a «МОЖНО КАТАТЬСЯ» sticker and applied it to the spot where the frame’s tubing material is usually indicated. Literally, the phrase means «Good to ride” –  Dima used to write it every time he posted on his Instagram Stories about a completed frame repair.

I had planned from the start to leave the tube and the heat-affected zones exactly as they were and simply clear-coat them. I had prepared the tube beforehand – it’s a heat-treated Kaisei tube sold by the guys from Rene Herse. Nagasawa seat tubes usually feature Italian and Japanese flag decals. I didn’t have any on hand, and without them, the “Nagasawa” lettering looked a bit lonely.

So, I photographed the logo from the down tube, scaled it up exactly twofold, and printed some stickers. The size of the lettering ended up matching the seat tube’s circumference almost perfectly – falling just two millimeters short. To me, those bold, oversized letters are a fundamental element of Japanese visual culture.

I didn’t want to go into too much detail, as that would spoil the bike’s simplicity. (If anyone is interested, I can send it via PM.) Overall, the bike is a simple build, as it’s meant for daily city riding. There’s nothing ultra-rare or collectible on it – except, perhaps, for the black SUGINO Super Zen chainring, which is nearly impossible to find these days.

But the bike is special to me because it incorporates some of my absolute favorite components that had otherwise been sitting unused. The old black pedals have faded in the sun, and their shade now matches the chainring perfectly. These are my very first Toshi double straps – they’ve been through it all with me since, I think, 2012.

For me, there is probably nothing worse than something built solely for the sake of building, without ever actually being used. After all, the true beauty of a mechanism lies in its operation. I finished this bike in February 2025. In a few months, I’ll have been riding it for two years, and it brings me joy every time I take it out. I really hope that feeling only grows stronger with each passing year.

The bike looks a bit different now – I’ve installed 25mm tires and a small basket. I might post a photo on my Instagram later. Thanks to everyone who read this article. Peace!

Build Spec:

  • Frame/Fork/ NAGASAWA SPECIAL 2006/NAGASAWA
  • Headset: Chris King GripNut
  • Crankset/Bottom Bracket: Dura-Ace 7600/ Sugino 75
  • Pedals/Straps: MKS Custom Nuevo / TOSHI double straps
  • Cog/Chainring/Chain: EuroAsia Gold 16T / Sugino Super ZEN 46t / DID
  • Handlebars/Stem/Bar Tape: Civia Emerson 46cm / Cinelli 1A 90mm / ENVE
  • Saddle/Seatpost: Selle San Marco Zoncolan / ENVE
  • Front Wheel/Hub/Tire: HED Belgium R / Dura-Ace / Continental Gatorskin 23mm
  • Rear Wheel/Hub/Tire: HED Belgium R / Dura-Ace / Continental  Gatorskin 23mm

entry.title: State Bicycle Co 6061 All-Road v2
entry.content:
Today, State Bicycle Co. launches the 6061 All-Road v2, its fastest and best-equipped gravel bike under $1,500…

The 6061 All-Road comes in three colorways at $1,499.99, two wheel sizes, and four frame sizes. Against v1, it is a generational change, not a refresh: new frame, new standards, new drivetrain, new brakes, new wheels. One fast drop-bar bike for mixed surfaces — pavement, fire road, gravel events — at a price where you normally cannot get modern frame standards. There are three colors: Liquid Emerald (green), Chrome Red, Metallic Smoke (graphite), four izes: X-Small 48cm, Small 51cm, Medium 54cm, Large 58cm, with two wheel options: 700c or 650b, same frame, same clearance, chosen at checkout.

6061 All-Road V2 Quick Hits:

  • Aero tubing. Double-butted 6061 shaped from the same aero profiles as our best-selling 6061 track frames. Profiled tubes plus fully hidden cables cut the drag a round-tube gravel frame gives away. The painted “anodized” finish is part of it — the aluminum shows through rather than sitting under paint.
  • Fully internal routing. An ID52 head tube takes the hoses from the bar through the headset and down the steerer. v1 ran a cable cradle on the outside of the fork.
  • T47 and UDH. T47 is threaded, so it cannot creak like a press-fit, and any shop can service it with normal tools. UDH is the bigger one: a SRAM Transmission derailleur bolts straight to the frame with no hanger. That upgrade path is rare under $1,500.
  • Tire clearance. The stock Continental is spec’d as a 29 x 2.0 — a two-inch tire on a gravel bike. Maximum clearance is 700c x 55mm or 650b x 55mm.
  • Wheels. 25mm internal width is the number to lead with: it is what lets a 50mm tire sit square instead of bulging. Add 30mm depth, 32 spokes, brass nipples. Tubeless ready out of the box — taped and valved, just add sealant.
  • Aero crankset. Solid narrow-wide 42T, 7075 ring on forged 6061 arms, 29mm spindle. The 49.7mm chainline sits outboard of a road crank, which helps the frame clear a 2.0in tire.
  • 12-speed, 11–46t. Range widens to 418%, with a low gear of 0.91:1, and because the 50mm tire is taller, the top end gains about 3% as well. Both ends open up. The derailleur is rated to 50T, so there is headroom for a mullet setup later.
  • Trail saddle. 150mm wide, for longer days on the bike.
  • Carbon levers, full hydraulic. A sealed hydraulic line from lever to caliper, so power and modulation hold up in the wet and at the bottom of a long descent. 160mm rotors front and rear.

Why it rides the way it does: 445mm chainstays and 73mm of BB drop make it planted at speed and on loose descents. A 50mm fork offset with a taller tire puts trail at roughly 73–78mm on the small sizes and about 68mm on Medium and Large — calmer without going vague. Head angles are size-specific: 70° on XS and S, 71.5° on M and L; most brands at this price run one angle across the range and let small riders deal with it.

Check out more info on the 6061 All-Road v2 at State Bicycle Co.

entry.title: Bike Camping With A Light Phone III – Mitchell Connell
entry.content:
Mitchell Connell chooses connection over connectivity, intention over integration, and looking around over looking down in this thought-provoking review of the Light Phone III. By the end of the review, he was even content to leave it at home. While you might not think a product’s goal is to go unused, that is not entirely the case with this one.

﻿

MapQuest Bike Camping

In June 2011, a small crew of my high school friends and I loaded our bicycles with miscellaneous camping-related things and headed southeast from our homes in Nashville, Tennessee. Our destination was Manchester, where some of our favorite bands were playing Bonnaroo, like Buffalo Springfield, My Morning Jacket, and Beirut. I carried my mother’s Canon AE-1 Program, and my brother carried turn-by-turn directions freshly printed from MapQuest.com.

When we made it emotionally halfway, we set up camp in a field by the road. Three of us slept on a large blue tarp from the local hardware store, and Lane lathered himself in homemade bug spray and strung a hammock between two trees along the property line. By morning, Lane was covered in ticks, while those of us who had slept on the ground couldn’t find a single one.

Sometime during college, bike camping began to change for me. Suddenly, my iPhone could chime whenever Ride with GPS thought I had wandered off-route. I could check my email from my sleeping bag. I could search for the next gas station along the following day’s route. All of this information made traveling much simpler (we had been lost for nearly the entire ride to Bonnaroo), but I began to wonder whether that simplicity came at a cost.

What had once been an exercise in uncertainty and improvisation was becoming another time to manage notifications, battery life, and data. Plus, I couldn’t help wondering what my high school heroes like Matt Segal or Grant Petersen would think of me checking my sleep score at camp or worrying that my iPhone might run out of data.

The Light Phone III

Fast-forward fifteen years and five iPhones. My friend Weston Poling showed me his Light Phone III, a simple cellphone that could text, make calls, manage a calendar, play music and podcasts, provide directions, and not do much else.

I was already familiar with Light Phone. I had owned a Light Phone II, but after one of its buttons broke, it was relegated to the drawer where my old charging cords go to die. Weston’s Light Phone III made me curious again. The screen was better, texting was easier, and the whole device felt like a night-and-day improvement over its predecessor.

I reached out to the folks at Light Phone and asked whether they would send me a loaner to use for a few weeks and take on a camping trip. A few days later, someone emailed me back with a simple response, “Why not?”

Planning the Trip

The premise was simple. A bike camping trip without a smartphone or bike computer. I planned an easy 30-mile round-trip route from downtown Chattanooga to a nearby swimming hole. I have never been particularly good at remembering road names or directions in general, so I kept the ride close to home.

I printed a small map of the full route, along with a zoomed-in map of one particularly tricky section, and laminated both. Just like in high school, I attached them to the stem of my bike with a binder clip.

Once the route was settled, I spent a somewhat significant amount of time typing out the trip details, then copied and pasted them into messages to about ten friends. Over the next few days, my phone chimed as people joined the trip or let me know they couldn’t make it. Before I knew it, the weekend had arrived.

Using the Phone on the Trip

The first thing I noticed while riding without a head unit or Strava was how slowly I was riding. I guess when I can’t see my speed, and I’m not tracking the ride to publish on the internet, I suddenly don’t care that I’m going eight miles per hour. Besides, the whole ride that day was fifteen miles. Who cares if it takes two hours?

The Light Phone III is also really fun to shoot video with. I wish I could press a single button and immediately open the video interface, but instead it takes about four taps to start recording. Still, the video quality is really nice. It reminds me of footage from point-and-shoot cameras made between 2005 and 2010. I found myself taking lots of short clips while riding and hanging around camp.

There isn’t an official campsite where we were headed, and there are several similar-looking pull-offs along the steady climb at the end of the route. It sounds kind of silly, but not knowing how much longer a climb will last feels very psychologically different. Instead of watching the distance tick down on a screen, I had to keep my head on a swivel and look for the graffiti that marked our pull-off. I was certainly paying more attention than I would have been if I were simply rolling along and waiting for my Wahoo to tell me when to stop.

We arrived just before dark and set up a humble camp on the sloped banks of the creek. I texted my wife to let her know we had made it, and then we headed to bed. The next morning we woke up early, and Thor headed off to fish. My friend Jon Jon had brought snorkeling gear, so after coffee we walked downstream to look for fish. Once we were all properly chilled by the cold water, we packed up our gear and headed back toward town.

The whole trip took less than twenty-four hours and barely carried us beyond the edge of the city, but it still felt like an adventure. It’s always nice to be reminded that bike camping doesn’t have to be ambitious or complicated. Sometimes all it takes is fifteen miles, a place to sleep, and a reason to leave your phone in your pocket.

Not Always Available: How the Light Phone Changed My Day-to-Day Life

The first change I noticed was my relationship with email. Suddenly, I couldn’t check every five minutes to see whether someone had gotten back to me. It felt strange for the first few days, but eventually I settled into it. Now, I have a much healthier relationship with work communication, and I genuinely believe I’ve gotten better at responding to people. Instead of checking constantly and replying sporadically, I sit down, focus, and deal with my inbox all at once.

The second change was directions. I’ve lived in Chattanooga for four years, so I know my way around pretty well. The Light Phone has a directions app that works well enough, but I’ve started carrying a small notebook and writing down directions whenever I’m headed somewhere unfamiliar, like picking up something from Facebook Marketplace. This has been absolutely lovely. It keeps me engaged while I’m on the road and has helped me discover and remember new pockets of the city.

My relationship with podcasts and music has changed too. The Light Phone has a great podcast app and a functional music app, but using them feels very different from having immediate access to an endless stream of music and commentary. For whatever reason, I’ve mostly stopped listening to anything while riding my bicycle or running. For me, that adds up to seven to nine hours each week that now feel entirely different. I notice where I am. Sometimes I’m just bored. It’s nice.

A Mini Light Phone Review

The Light Phone III is a beautiful object. It has a reassuring weight in your hand and feels extremely well built. Call quality is good, and the screen is bright and easy to read. Texting on the OLED screen is noticeably less accurate and responsive than typing on an iPhone’s buttery-smooth screen, but you get used to it. You will probably find yourself texting less and calling more, simply because calling is easier.

The calendar app syncs with the major calendar services, and the phone plays a pleasant chime when it reminds you that you need to be somewhere in half an hour. The hotspot works well too. When you genuinely need the internet, you can connect another device, like a laptop, and get online.

I also really like the camera. Rather than trying to compete with modern smartphones, Light Phone went in a different direction. The photos and videos remind me of a Canon PowerShot from the 2000s. The camera feels nostalgic without seeming like a gimmick, and I absolutely love the video quality.

The Light Phone III is not all roses, though. For one, it’s really expensive. The price recently increased to $899, which is a lot for my bike shop salary. I am thankful that Light Phone sent me a demo because I am not sure I could spend $899 while I still have an older iPhone that works perfectly well, even if I sometimes feel like it is slowly killing me.

The music app is also terrible. I know most people don’t use MP3s anymore, but I do! The app displays every song you have downloaded in one continuous list, arranged in the order you added them. There is no useful way to browse by artist or album. At the very least, the songs should be arranged alphabetically and organized into folders.

My other major concern is water resistance. The phone is designed to be repairable, but that comes at the expense of waterproofing. As someone who commutes by bicycle, I worry about carrying an $899 phone in my pocket when an unexpected rainstorm rolls in.

Final thoughts

Even with all of these complaints, I love the Light Phone III. Giving up my smartphone has been one of the most meaningful changes I’ve made in the last few years, and I highly recommend trying it for yourself.

Last weekend, I went on a canoe trip with my wife and brother. Worried that my phone might get wet, I left it at home. I spent two days on the river and never once wished I had brought a cellphone with me. Maybe the best review I can give the Light Phone is this: it helped turn my phone into something I’m happy to leave behind.

Pros

  • Intentionally designed to be used less often with greater intention
  • Stellar build quality
  • Camera has lots of character

Cons

  • Podcast and music playing function is underbaked
  • Waterproofing is questionable
  • Very expensive for what it is

See the Light Phone III.

The post Bike Camping With A Light Phone III appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Circles Builds: Sklar Bikes PBJ – John Watson
entry.content:
Last week, we looked at the Nagoya-based Circles bike shop in Japan. As supporting content, today we’re featuring a recent Sklar Bikes PBJ build that just rolled out of the shop for a customer…

Sklar Bikes PBJ

The PBJ makes a lot of sense as a multi-functioning mixed-terrain bicycle. Ten years ago, I commissioned Adam Sklar to build me a bike for desert touring. That custom titanium tourer started the Sklar Bikes PBJ lineage. Last year, in 2025, I reviewed Adam’s Taiwanese-produced PBJ model after riding it on a quick bike tour around Mount Tam in the Bay Area.

Here in New Mexico, I’ve taken my Desert Moose, the nickname the bike earned on one desert outing, on local overnighters as well as the Northern New Mexico CDT. It’s a true-to-form forever bike for me. Perfect for Canyon Country, the Mojave, and beyond. All this to say, I’m intimately familiar with the PBJ. If you’d like to learn more about the PBJ, read my review in the Radavist archives below.

The team at Circles have built up several PBJ frames over the past few years. Here are a few above, taken from the Ridealive Beautiful Bicycles gallery. The PBJ is best equipped with racks, since it has provisions for bolt-on cargo carriers, versus other bikes sans rack mounts that often rely on floppy bikepacking bags.

Circles Build

While I spent the afternoon prying into each shelf and display case at Circles, Makoto sat at his wheel-building station, zeroed in on a wheel build. First, he cut the spokes, then he prepped them before pulling a pair of Astral Serpentine rims from a box above the mechanics area in the small but organized Circles work area.

“Makoto!” I exclaimed, excited to see my friend again. “John-san!” he replied. We exchanged hugs and memories from our 2016 bike tour around Mount Fuji and on to Izu Oshima. After briefly catching up, he was back to work, lacing the spokes through the Chris King hub. Hours passed, and I’d finished documenting the Circles shop just as he was finishing the wheels.

The following day, I returned to Circles after documenting the Circles Tailored store, as well as a few custom builds to Makoto, putting the finishing touches on this silver Sklar PBJ; the home for those wheels. Every cable was perfectly routed, every t-crossed, and i-dotted. I asked if I could document the bike. Before I could roll it out of the shop, an employee came over with some cleaner and wiped down the handlebars.

Balleur Kit

Looking at this build, it exemplifies Circle’s Modus Operandi: supporting a mix of Japanese and Domestic US manufacturers, splurging on balleur parts, and hanging them on a comparatively approachable frameset. If this had been a custom Sklar bike, it’d be two or three times the price. Paul Component cranks, Boxcar stem, Klampers, Canti Levers, Taco Pedals, Sklar PBJ bars, a Shovel Research TC-1 top cap, and a friction Shimano Deore mech complement the Astral and Chris King build kit, making for one happy customer.

Circles and Circles Tailored roll builds like this out of small, well-organized workshops all days of the week, and this customer has to be stoked to be putting miles on it.

If you’re in Japan and would like a similar build, holler at Circles and let Makoto cook you up something delicious like this.

See the PBJ specs at Sklar Bikes.

The post Circles Builds: Sklar Bikes PBJ appeared first on The Radavist.
