entry.title: G32 SuperFast: Bike Ahead & Stoll Team Up Again for Ultralight 32″ Gravel Bike Project
entry.content:
Stoll & Bike Ahead announced a 10th anniversary collaboration that will see them turn this G32 Superfast prototype into an ultralight aero carbon production gravel bike on 32″ wheels early next year.

Describing it as “a purpose-developed 32-inch concept, born from Swiss bike engineering and German carbon expertise“, the G32 isn’t meant to replace the traditional 700c Superfast (which the Germans continue to refer to as 28″). Instead, the 32” bike will go a different direction, optimized for the speed and rolling efficiency of the bigger wheels, especially for gravel racing and ultra-distance riding.

Bike Ahead Composites + Stoll Bikes 32″ anniversary collaboration

We’ve known pretty much since we first saw 32″ wheels on race bikes that Stoll and Bike Ahead were going to be at the forefront. Bike Ahead’s XC Projekt 32 hardtail prototype was one of the first 32″ mountain bikes I saw in person. It was fitted with their own ultralight 6-spoke BiTurbo RS 32″ carbon wheels, which Bike Ahead’s Christian Gemperlein explained to me are even more of a benefit in the jump from 29″ to 32″, than they were going from 26″ to 29″

Then, Stoll’s P32 full-suspension prototype was the first time these even-bigger wheels were ridden to a race win on the elite level at this past spring’s Cape Epic.

Stoll + Bike Ahead G32 Superfast carbon gravel bike

The two ultra-premium carbon bike makers have already worked together for a decade, developing the original Superfast ultralight, aero gravel bike just last year. And in fact, Stoll frames are also manufactured in Bike Ahead parent All Ahead Composites’ factory in Würzburg, Germany. But to celebrate 10 years of working together, the G32 will officially be their first collaborative bike.

“Stoll Bikes contributes its extensive experience in the development of geometry, ride dynamics, and design. Bike Ahead complements the project with its expertise in composite engineering, carbon layup, and manufacturing.”

The two explain that the G32 project has been developed from scratch, taking into consideration the benefits of the larger wheelsize, like boosted speed, but also 32’s limitations.

The new G32 Superfast will feature all-new geometry optimized for the larger wheels. It doesn’t hurt that Bike Ahead customizable geometry cockpits help refine the fit for a wide rider size range.

And it features completely new frame shaping as well. This prototype shares a few angular tubing profiles with the 700c Superfast. But the frame layout is totally unique. It features an extended headtube and curved seattube more like Stoll’s 32″ mountain bike. Then, all-new dropped seatstays, tapering toptube, and aerofoil downtube more like many modern aero road bikes.

Tech details

  • ultralight aero carbon 32″ gravel race bike
  • two frame standard sizes M (170-184cm tall cyclists) and L (182-195cm riders)
  • custom cockpit sizing, tailor-made for each rider
  • optional 0.3L internal frame storage
  • optional mounting points for all types of adventure gear
  • 60mm (2.36″) max tire clearance (presumably not quite enough for 2.4″ MTB tires)

What’s next? G32 Availability in early 2027!

Officially, this is all still just a concept bike. But this is said to be a rideable prototype. And clearly the two are working on making this real.

Stoll & Bike Ahead say the start of production for the G32 Superfast will be March 2027, suggesting you might be able to ride one by the end of next spring. No word on pricing yet, but a limited number of bikes are available to pre-order now, from either Bike Ahead or Stoll.

Bike-Ahead-Composites.de & Stoll-bikes.com

entry.title: How cycling legends were born: Nicole Cooke claims gold for Britain
entry.content:
Cyclist
How cycling legends were born: Nicole Cooke claims gold for Britain

In early December 2007 Nicole Cooke was in China. Despite not being in a positive frame of mind, she had travelled to Beijing to research the 2008 Olympic Games Road Race circuit. A few months earlier Cooke had closed her season, losing her World Cup lead in the final round of the series before going straight into surgery in a bid to resolve a long-standing knee injury that had impacted the second half of the year. A period of rehab had followed but by November the knee pain had returned.

‘I was distraught,’ Cooke writes in her autobiography The Breakaway. ‘I couldn’t take it anymore; I wanted to stop and end my career there and then.’

Nevertheless Cooke had already booked flight tickets to Beijing. So she went, ignoring thoughts that maybe her career was effectively over, and inspected the course. Cooke rode the circuit’s main climb and bore the pain of sprinting on the uphill drag to the finish line, banking the details. Then she went home to try to get fit.

The start of 2008 proved as difficult for Cooke as the end of 2007 had been. Her season began late due to needing to recover from that knee injury – her first race coming at the end of March – and then came issues with her team.

Cooke had signed for a Halfords-sponsored outfit of British riders, run by British Cycling, in the belief their season would be structured around her Olympic ambitions. But her plans were hit when the team announced that they would not be riding in June’s Grande Boucle Féminine Internationale. It was a race that Cooke viewed as vital to her Olympic preparations and one where she was the two-time defending champion.

The team’s decision forced Cooke to look elsewhere, and she was able to secure a last-minute ride with the Swift team. Despite the disruption, she recorded a string of top five stage finishes at the Grand Boucle, including a strong ride in the Alps to claim second on the stage to Sestriere on her way to finishing third overall. A week later Cooke took her ninth British Road Race title. She was back on track. Now for the Olympics.

Fighting for Olympic Gold

Sixty-six riders started the women’s Olympic Road Race. Ahead lay a 126km route, including a run-in of 78km to two laps of a hilly 23km circuit that featured the final haul to the finish line Cooke had ridden eight months previously.

The British team comprised Cooke, Emma Pooley and Sharon Laws. Cooke writes that the final pre-race meeting was ‘far removed from a proper professional team meeting prior to a critical race’, with instructions being simply for Laws to cover moves in the approach to the circuit, Pooley to attack on the climb and ‘Nicole, be ready for the finish’.

The weather for the previous day’s men’s race had been hot and dry but the gloomy conditions that initially greeted the women soon turned to heavy rain. It made for treacherous conditions with riders losing control, crashing and landing heavily in the deep gutters that lined the roads.

As the bell sounded for the final lap, Russia’s Natalia Boyarskaya was leading the race. Pooley then launched her effort, soon joined by Italy’s Tatiana Guderzo. They caught Boyarskaya to form a trio of riders leading the race. Behind, Cooke sat tight until Germany’s Judith Arndt responded, then she followed her move.

With the three leaders caught, a flurry of moves and counter-moves went and came back, steadily reducing the main group of favourites in the process. As the finale neared, five riders remained in contention: Emma Johansson, Christine Soeder, Linda Villumsen, Guderzo and Cooke.

Reading through Cooke’s recollection of the final moments of this race reveals the extent of split-second tactical decisions that a rider undertakes in these highly dynamic situations. Where are the dangers? Who is riding on whose wheel? What does that tell me about how they are feeling? How should I use that information? How do they view what I am doing? If I hang back here, how will the others react? Will they attack or call my bluff? What is the next pinch point? Can I exploit that or is it too risky? All thoughts and decisions made instinctively and quickly through years of experience, all while on the point of exhaustion.

Cooke, worried about the possibility of getting caught in a crash in the wet conditions, chose to sit at the back of the leading group as the last technical bends were negotiated. She risked losing touch and had to launch her final effort earlier as a result.

‘It was going to be a very long sprint for me,’ Cooke writes. ‘I was catching them quickly and took the risk of taking the lead and the inside line around the last bend.’

With 200m to go, she hit the front.

‘My legs were already burning from the effort I had made to get into this position, but I wasn’t going to let the pain stop me. This was the moment I’d been dreaming of since I was 12, fighting for the Olympic gold medal.’

That final uphill sprint seemed to take an eternity as Cooke gritted her teeth. In the face of huge efforts from Johansson and Guderzo, Cooke clung on and crossed the line to claim gold, screaming in celebration. She had just become the first, and to date only, Briton to win the Olympic Road Race.

‘I just came over the line and there was so much in me,’ Cooke said afterwards. ‘So many emotions that all came out at once. I was not composed enough to take my hands off the bars, so much of it came out as noise because that’s just the person I am.’

On her return to Wales, Cooke’s home village of Wick, in the Vale of Glamorgan, threw a celebratory party featuring an open-topped bus tour, speeches, children’s bike races and the unveiling of a commemorative plaque.

‘It was the most perfect occasion,’ Cooke later reflected.

A little under seven weeks later, she was on the start line of the World Championships Road Race in Varese, Italy. She had been on three Worlds podiums before but had never stood on the top step. This time it would be different. After refusing to lead the pursuit of numerous attacks in the closing kilometres, Cooke briefly made her own effort, then sat up and watched Johansson make a move with the final kilometre approaching.

She resisted any temptation to follow, waiting for others to lead the chase. Into the final moments Johansson still led but the gap was now coming down fast. First Judith Arndt, then Cooke, then Marianne Vos blew past the Swedish rider. This was the podium, but in what order?

Arndt tired in the final 150m, leaving a two-up drag race to the line with Cooke taking the win ahead of Vos.

‘I was quite happy to see the race play out because so close to the finish I knew I wasn’t going to win if I chased Emma [Johansson],’ Cooke reflected. ‘[I thought] chasing her won’t help so I’m not going to… it was quite logical.’

With that win Cooke became the first rider in history to win both the Olympics Road Race and the rainbow jersey in the same year.

‘It was a dream come true in Beijing,’ Cooke said after her Worlds win, ‘and today as well. I don’t think I’ve realised it yet. I need some time to let it sink in.’

The post How cycling legends were born: Nicole Cooke claims gold for Britain appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Here’s the scoop on 32-inch gravel bikes
entry.content:
Cyclist
Here’s the scoop on 32-inch gravel bikes

32-inch wheels have become a hot ticket item, with many brands testing the new wheel size on prototype gravel and XC mountain bikes. As yet, not many have taken the plunge and actually sell 32in bikes, although that looks set to change, and fast.

In general, 32in gravel bikes are being sold by small volume producers, with titanium the favoured frame material, due to the ease of fabrication of a frame with novel geometry relative to carbon. The novelty of the new wheel size allows a frame to command a premium price over alloy as well.

The big wheels are already making their mark in gravel racing though, with Unbound XL won in 2026 by Robin Gemperle on a prototype Scott 32in gravel bike and Leon Kaiser winning the 109km Sea Otter Europe UCI Gravel World Series race in Girona riding a 32in Avona bike.   

So who is selling 32-inch gravel bikes or framesets? Here’s a non-exhaustive list, which is sure to be added to as more brands make 32-inch bikes and framesets available. Lower down, we have a rundown of the pros and cons of the new, larger wheel size.  

Brand selling 32in gravel bikes or framesets

Avona 

German brand Avona is somewhat unique in selling a carbon framed 32in bike, particularly a race-winning one. You can order the Callis 32 from its site in sizes M, L and XL as a frameset, rolling chassis or fitted with a SRAM XPLR AXS groupset. It reckons the bike will fit riders from 165cm up to 201cm and, unusually for a 32in bike, there’s a road-width 68mm BSA threaded bottom bracket shell rather than a wider MTB shell.

There’s a choice of its own Faserwerk 45mm wheels on two different DT Swiss hubsets or Newmen Streem G.62 wheels, fitted with Schwalbe G-One RS Pro 50mm tyres, with Maxxis Aspen ST tyres available from early 2027. It has Boost spacing and clearance for 55mm tyres and also comes in four colours. Claimed bike weights are from 7.78kg.

Baum

The standard Baum DBM is a 700c titanium frameset, but the Australian brand also offers a custom-built 32in upgrade. Baum says the DBM 32 is aimed at riders over 183cm tall. It too has Boost axle spacing, but also has an MTB-style 89.5mm width T47 bottom bracket shell.

Baum claims you can fit 2.6-inch MTB tyres and that Enve’s carbon MTB fork, which it specs, offers enough clearance for the larger wheel size. Baum has also built a bike fitted with a travel-limited Cannondale Lefty Ocho suspension fork.

Chiru Bikes

Chiru Bikes is a titanium specialist based in Hong Kong, but with French roots, with a history in MTB before branching out into gravel. The Chiru Veldt includes a 3D printed bottom bracket and a titanium fork and is available in two sizes: M/L and L/XL. 

The bottom bracket shell is an MTB-style 92mm T47 and it can handle tyres up to 2.25in, with Boost axle spacing. It showed off a striking bike equipped with Biturbo X 32 Safewing six spoke wheels from German brand Bike Ahead at Cycling World Düsseldorf in March 2026.

Mosaic Cycles

Colorado-based Mosaic Cycles’ GT-1 i55 32” is another hand-built, made to order titanium bike and offers 55mm tyre clearance, with Boost spacing and includes a carbon fork. There’s a T47 bottom bracket with gravel chainline. 

The bike features a 3D printed titanium bottom bracket yoke, which allows it to accommodate a 1x groupset with a chainring up to 46t in size and it says that its curved seat tube helps keep the wheelbase short and the ride lively. Mosaic quotes an eight week lead time, but expects to move the bike to its batch-built programme, which should make for faster turnaround.

Nordest

The Nordest Arisco Ti is also a 32-inch frameset made from titanium, in its case from Madrid, Spain. It can handle 2.4in tyres, with a steep seat tube, long reach and slack head tube claimed to make for efficiency climbing and allow fast descents. 

The frame is available in sizes ML and L, which should fit riders from 175cm to 193cm, as well as custom geometry. It has Boost spacing and a road/gravel width 68mm T47 bottom bracket. It’s designed to fit a 444mm length fork, which doesn’t form part of the build. 

Salsa Fargo 32

Salsa sells its Fargo 32 frameset in both steel and titanium, including a carbon fork. It’s unusual for 32in bikes in selling a small frame size, which it says is suitable for riders from 157cm in height. 

There’s 2.4-inch tyre clearance, it can accommodate an 80mm travel suspension fork and is Boost spaced with a 73mm BSA threaded bottom bracket shell. There’s room to fit a 36-tooth chainring.  

Singular Pterodactyl 

Singular’s 32-inch bike, the Pterodactyl, is also made of titanium. It’s sold in sizes L, XL and XXL and Singular says it will fit riders from 178cm in height. Sold as a rolling chassis with a Columbus carbon fork, it has a 73mm T47 bottom bracket and Super Boost rear axle spacing and can fit 2.5in tyres and a 34-tooth chainring.

In the UK, it’s sold with Maxxis Aspen ST 2.25in tyres on Willow AL rims with Hope hubs, in the US with Astral Jester rims on Approach hubs. 

32in gravel bikes: all you need to know

What are the claimed advantages of 32in wheels?

A major advantage claimed for larger wheels is better rollover of trail obstacles. It’s the same argument as when mountain bikes predominantly switched from 26-inch to 29-inch wheels.

The tyre has a shallower angle of attack when it hits a bump, so it’s not deflected upwards so sharply and will carry momentum better, as well as not translating forward motion into upward motion so violently. It’s a larger-scale version of the logic for wider tyres on road bikes.

There’s a larger contact patch with the ground too, due to the larger wheel radius, which also aids traction and control.

The wheel and tyre combined will, in general, be heavier than a comparable 700c wheel/tyre combination, which again helps preserve forward momentum over obstacles and also increases stability, as it’s harder to turn the larger, heavier wheel. 

Finally, 32-inch wheels may be a better choice for tall riders, helping to keep the frame in proportion – more on sizing below.

And what are the disadvantages?

Larger wheels mean more weight and inertia, so a 32in gravel bike, although it may maintain momentum better, may be slower to accelerate and climb than a 700c gravel bike. The stability we just mentioned can also result in a loss of agility to handle more technical ground.

As yet, there are relatively few components available for 32in bikes – again, we’ll dive into this more below.  

32-inch wheels would not be allowed by the UCI in road races under its current rules – and we all know how reluctant the UCI is to change those.

The wheel size first made its mark in XC mountain biking, and the UCI has indicated that it will not ban 32in wheels in MTB races. However, it’s rumoured to be considering a ban on the wheel size in gravel races it regulates, on the grounds that it puts smaller riders at a disadvantage. Most gravel races are outwith the UCI’s remit though, so it has less leverage than for road races.

Who are 32in gravel bikes for?

As mentioned, 32in bikes can appear more proportional for very taller riders and many of the available 32in framesets are sold in larger sizes only.

The larger wheel size makes it increasingly difficult to create a frame to fit smaller riders, due to issues of stack height and toe overlap.

Some brands have successfully sized 32in framesets for smaller riders though, notably Salsa, which sells the Fargo 32 frameset in size S, which it recommends for riders from 157cm to 170cm.

As for how they’re designed to be used, most brands highlight their potential for fast gravel riding and as gravel race bikes, although others highlight their stable handling as an advantage for bikepacking and configure their frames with a full set of mounts.

What other geometry considerations are there?

The bike needs a longer fork to accommodate the larger front wheel, which in turn requires a short head tube. Even so, the stack may be higher than for a 700c frameset, so the ride position may be more upright and less aero, which combines with the larger frontal area of the wheel to potentially increase drag. 

There’s also a need for a longer front centre to reduce the risk of toe overlap, which means a greater frame reach or a slacker head tube angle, or a combination of the two. 

There’s an equivalent lengthening needed for the chainstays to fit the larger rear wheel. Together they can lengthen the wheelbase, resulting in lazier handling than a gravel bike with a shorter wheelbase. Many 32in gravel bikes have a curved seat tube to help tuck the rear wheel under the saddle and reduce the overall wheelbase.

Almost all the 32in framesets above are specced with Boost wheel spacing, as the wider axle allows a wider bracing angle for spokes and so should result in a more rigid wheel; the Singular Pterodactyl has the even wider Super Boost at the rear. 

Some also adopt an MTB-width bottom bracket shell to maintain the chainline within groupset manufacturers’ guidelines. 

What is 32-inch component availability?

Another constraint is the availability of components to fit a 32in bike, although that’s changing fast.

With the wheel size also trendy for XC MTBs, there are already quite a few wheelset options and others in the works, both alloy and carbon. 

Newmen has launched a 32-inch variant of its ultra-deep G.62 gravel wheels and when it launched the 700c Streem G.48, it also said that a 32in variant of the wheels would be coming.

Other brands with 32in wheelsets available include Schmolke, Teravail and Bike Ahead, while other wheelmakers, including Boyd, have showcased prototype 32-inch gravel wheels.

Tyre availability is also increasing. Schwalbe has launched G.One RS Pro and RX Pro tyres in 32in size and 50mm and 55mm widths. Teravail also sells 32in gravel tyres, as well as carbon gravel rims. Other tyre brands including Maxxis, Silca, WTB and Vittoria also sell 32in tyres or have them in the works. 

As gravel bike tyre clearances increase, they’re heading into MTB territory, so 32in MTB tyres are also an option for some 32-inch gravel bikes.

There are a fair few 32in carbon forks on sale, as well as suspension forks for XC MTBs and, as Baum noted, some rigid MTB forks such as Enve’s have the clearance for 32in tyres.

The larger wheel size results in lower gearing being needed for equivalent metres of development, due to the increased tyre circumference, so a 32in bike typically needs to be fitted with a smaller chainring than a 700c gravel bike, which may mean fitting an out-of-series crankset. 

Who is testing the wheel size for gravel?

There are plenty of brands testing the 32in waters, showing off prototypes without committing to their production. Despite its success in Unbound in 2026, Scott labels its 32in gravel bike as ‘a prototype that will never go into production’. 

But other brands we know of with prototype or one-off 32in gravel bikes include Canyon, Ribble, Rose, Genesis, Raymon and Megamo. 

What’s the future for the 32-inch wheel size?

Many of the prototypes mentioned above are likely to come to market over the next few months, although others will be shelved. There will be more mainstream options and bikes are likely to be available at a greater range of prices. 

As the wheel size takes off, there will be more component choices as well, so there should be a greater choice of wheels and tyres to match.

As well as options for larger riders, 32in mullets may take off, with a 32in front and 700c rear wheel, offering the rollover advantage of the larger front wheel with shorter frame geometry and better fit for shorter riders. Despite the extra mass of the larger front wheel, a mullet is still likely to be lighter than a gravel bike with suspension provided by a fork. 

And if 32in gravel bikes turn out to be a bridge too far, 30.5in is also out there. Newmen says it will offer the Streem G.48 in the intermediate diameter in future, while Neuhaus Metalworks in California has built a prototype titanium gravel frameset to test the 30.5in size. Cube is also rumoured to be interested.

The post Here’s the scoop on 32-inch gravel bikes appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Defy the elements with Le Col
entry.content:
Cyclist
Defy the elements with Le Col

Winter: time to hibernate and hit the indoor trainer, right? Wrong. With the right kit for the job, Le Col’s autumn/winter 2026 range will have you relishing every ride in the great outdoors between now and the clocks going forward again in the spring.

Le Col has spent the past 15 years developing and refining the very best performance riding kit for all manner of cycling tribes, whether you’re a certified roadie or gravel rider. And, with the brand’s pro cycling experience informing everything it creates – not to mention boasting a community of almost one million cyclists – Le Col makes the strongest case for being the one-stop shop for all your performance gear needs.

This year’s seasonal collection is a shining example of the depth and breadth of the British-born company’s offering. Here are the highlights…

Need for speed

Le Col’s Pro Collection represents the pinnacle of its pursuit of performance gains. Every piece is designed with maximum speed and efficiency in mind, employing wind-tunnel tech and feedback from professional cycling teams to set new standards in race-ready apparel. This range is for anyone who wants the edge, even if you just want to bring the pain on a rapid training ride with mates!

New for 2026 is the aero-optimised Pro Jacket (RRP £275, now £165), a windproof and showerproof jacket with incredible breathability, thanks to Polartec Power Shield fabric – built for fast, high-tempo winter rides.

The Pro Aero Long Sleeve Jersey (RRP £210) is Le Col’s fastest jersey. It combines aerodynamic performance with a precision fit, so you get the most from your efforts. An advanced fabric on the inside reduces aerodynamic drag, while the jersey also boasts enhanced moisture wicking fabric to keep you comfortable when you’re pushing hard.

• Check out the Le Col Pro Collection here: men | women

In it for the long-haul

The timeless Hors Categorie Collection is designed for the rider who wants to go the distance, with no compromise made on luxurious fabrics, refined details and exemplary comfort.

The new Hors Categorie Long Sleeve Jersey (RRP £200, now £140) stands out for its comfort, light weight, insulation and fast-wicking construction. It’s knitted from a four-way stretch fabric with brushed inner, and is designed to shrug off cold weather.

Like the entire Hors Categorie range, this jersey has a premium look and feel, with top-quality sleeve grippers, comfortable neck taping, a large, zipped waterproof rear pocket (as well as the standard three other pockets) and reflective details for winter safety. In brief, it’s the ideal blend of performance and comfort for massive days in the saddle.

• Check out the Le Col Hors Categorie Collection here: men | women

Everyday heroes

The Le Col Sport Collection offers arguably the best of both worlds. Balancing performance and value, this range is aimed squarely at the rider who just wants to ride – but, whether a social spin or daily commute, to ride in comfort.

The Sport Long Sleeve Block Jersey (RRP £125, now £95 men’s/£75 women’s) is ideal for autumnal coffee rides, being lightweight, breathable and featuring a waterproof pocket for peace of mind (after all, nobody wants a waterlogged wallet).

The lightweight, windproof and packable Sport Gilet (RRP £95, now £55) will keep you warm on early mornings (or descents), and when not in use will stuff straight into a jersey pocket.

And, to keep your leg muscles warm, look no further than the Sport Cargo Bib Tights II (RRP £200, now £140). They combine soft-brushed thermal fabric, stretch-comfort, storage pockets on the legs, and a triple-layer, gel-insert chamois for optimum shock-absorbing comfort – whether it’s a century ride or a simple Sunday bimble.

• Check out the Le Col Sport Collection here: men | women

True grit

Le Col hasn’t forgotten those of us who love a bit of dirt, with the ARC Gravel Collection providing stacks of kit to help you perform at your best off the beaten track. This collection has been tested and developed with pro gravel racers, and, in Le Col’s own words, is ‘engineered with purpose’. Performance fabrics mix with premium Italian merino wool, the apparel is bristling with storage, and – most importantly – it’s designed with durability at the forefront.

The ARC Lightweight Rain Jacket (RRP £295, now £120) is the standout piece for winter adventures. Using Pertex Shield technology with fully taped seams and a waterproof two-way zip, it offers full waterproofing, yet weighs just 190g and packs down small. The hood fits over a helmet, the durable ripstop fabric is built to last (there’s even a repair patch included), and the relaxed fit makes it just as at home off the bike as on it.

• Check out the Le Col ARC Gravel Collection here: men | women

• Discover the full Le Col AW26 men’s collection here, and the women’s collection here and take advantage of the great savings currently on offer at lecol.cc

Exclusive until 1st December only:

Any new customers spending £150 with Le Col can add the Unisex Sleeveless Layer to their basket and enter code AFF-BFBLFREE at checkout to get it completely FREE! Offer applies to new customers only.

Click here to find out more

entry.title: Polygon Tambora Reshapes Lighter, Faster Gravel Race Bike with 55mm Tire Clearance
entry.content:
Polygon completely reshapes their all-rounder fast gravel bike with an all-new carbon Tambora that is lighter than ever, much more performance-focused, and sports big off-road-ready 2.2″ tire clearance. Plus, even as Polygon describes it as their “fastest gravel bike to date”, it also adds internal frame storage and smart accessory mounting for bigger adventure rides, too.

2026 Polygon Tambora affordable carbon fast gravel bike

The new Tambora is a ground-up redesign, as Polygon aims to reposition the bike for gravel racing and fast all-day adventures. But not without plenty of backcountry capability, thanks to room for up to a 55mm tire being one of the new bike’s core considerations, and long fork legs that build in potential gravel suspension compatibility.

While the previous generation of the Tambora was created as ‘one bike to do it all’, with so many mounts it was hard to count, plus an entry-level alloy frame option, now Polygon is working on another all-new gravel bike for more endurance adventure and bikepacking. That allowed their gravel bike designers to focus on speed for the Tambora.

What’s new?

Really, the new Tambora is a completely different bike.

Instead of the previous generation’s blocky & oversized sloping frame design, this all-new Tambora looks much more like a modern, semi-aero road bike. Smooth styling. A more open front triangle under a gently sloping toptube that will do better to fit any frame packs. Plus, a rear wheel cutout in the seattube, tall chainstays for drivetrain stiffness, dropped seatstays for comfort, and of course an upgrade to the UDH standard.

Additionally, Polygon has included the same PolyPocket internal frame storage in the downtube, adapted from their popular Collosus T mountain bike. And they put a recessed toptube bag mount just behind the headset. So you can securely bolt on a bag, or flush-mount a magnetic Fidlock adapter. Or stick with a smooth cover plate if you don’t want extra storage behind your stem.

New Gravel Race Geo, too

Geometry on the new Polygon Tambora also gets a big update.

First, there are now six sizes on offer (up from four) in the same overall rider height range to better fine-tune rider fit.

The new Tambora actually features shorter frame Reach figures than before, but much lower Stack numbers (down ~32mm) and a slightly slacker 70.5° head angle, which Polygon says improves stability and rider confidence, while also allowing for lower, more aero position on the bike. The new bike also gets longer chainstays to fit those big tires, paired with higher bottom brackets to balance agility and get rid of pedal strikes in chunky terrain.

Tech details

  • all-new lighter & stiffer ACX carbon frame and ACX carbon fork
  • 55mm max 700c tire clearance (29 x 2.2″)
  • extended fork legs (435mm axle-to-crown) compatible with 40mm travel gravel suspension forks
  • fully integrated internal cable routing
  • stealth dropper post compatible
  • compatible with 1x & 2x, electronic AND mechanical groupsets
  • PolyPocket internal frame storage, including neoprene spares bag
  • recessed toptube bag mount, optimized for a flush Fidlock mount
  • three sets of bottle cage mounts
  • T47 threaded bottom bracket
  • 27.2mm round seatpost, with wedge-expander clamp
  • FM160 flat mount brakes
  • 12mm thru-axles
  • UDH rear mount
  • removable braze-on style front derailleur mount
  • available in 6 sizes (XXS-XL)
  • 125kg (276lb) total system weight: rider+bike+gear
  • 1200g claimed frame weight (size M painted, with internal frame storage)
  • made in Sidoarjo, East Java, Indonesia

2026 Polygon Tambora gravel bike – Pricing, options & availability

Polygon offers the all-new Tambora in four complete bike builds and six sizes (XXS-XL), all sharing the same new lighter ACX carbon frame & fork.

Builds start at incredibly affordable pricing with the beige, black & bronze $1800 / 1900€ Tambora 4, thanks to a cost-effective Shimano Cues 2×10-speed mechanical groupset and alloy Novatec wheelset. Next up at $2500 / 2300€, the red & black Tambora 6 is still mechanical 2x Shimano, but upgraded to 2x12speed GRX for a more premium drivetrain feel. Then, at $3000 / 3500€, you get the seemingly 90s-themed white, blue & pink Tambora 7 that Polygon upgrades to a wireless electronic 1x GRX Di2 setup, a carbon seatpost, and G29 carbon wheels from Novatec.

Lastly, the top-spec orange & blue Polygon Tambora 9 AXS features, you guessed it, wireless SRAM Force Xplr AXS, the same carbon wheels, and a house-brand one-piece LINC integrated carbon cockpit.

All four models are available now from your local Polygon dealer.

PolygonBikes.com

entry.title: State’s 6061 All-Road V2 Goes Aero, Internal, and Transmission-Ready for $1,499.99
entry.content:
State Bicycle Co. built its name on affordable, good-looking fixies. Now, they’re known for an entire fleet of well-spec’d, affordable bicycles available in all disciplines. Lately, they’ve been knockin’ it outta the park with the insanely good deal on their new 4130 Trail bike. It’s not a big stretch to see the brand throw a T47 BB and UDH at a sub-$1,500 gravel bike. Meet the new All-Road V2.

The new 6061 All-Road V2 is available now through State’s website at $1,499.99. State says it’s the fastest and best-equipped gravel bike it has built for under $1,500, and that it’s a generational change over V1, not a refresh. New frame, new standards, new drivetrain, new brakes, new wheels. That’s a lot of “new” for a bike that still costs less than a high end set of carbon wheels.

Let’s go over the details, yeah?

Aero-ish & Hidden-Hoses

The new frame is double-butted 6061 aluminum, shaped using the same aero profiles as State’s best-selling 6061 track frames. State says the profiled tubes and fully hidden cables cut the drag. An ID52 head tube routes hoses from the bar through the headset and down the steerer. The finish is a painted “anodized” look, which is a fun bit of wordplay, but State says the aluminum shows through the paint, so take that for what it’s worth.

The Standards Stuff

There are two modern standards that come with the new All-Road frame. First, there’s the T47 threaded bottom bracket, which means no press-fit creaking and any shop can service it with normal tools. Second, there’s the UDH hanger.

The tire clearance maxes out at 55mm in either 700c or 650b. It comes with 29 x 2.0″ Continental tires. The wheels have a 25mm internal width, 30mm depth, 32 spokes, and brass nipples, and they ship tubeless-ready, taped and valved. Just add sealant.

Drivetrain & Brakes

The 12-speed drivetrain uses an 11-46t cassette. The derailleur is rated to 50T, though, so if you decide you want a mullet setup down the road, it is possible. The aero crank runs a solid narrow-wide 42T 7075 ring on forged 6061 arms with a 29mm spindle.

Stopping comes from carbon levers and a full hydraulic system with 160mm rotors front and rear.

All-Road V2 Geometry

The new All-Road V2’s chainstays are 445mm with 73mm of BB drop for stability at speed and on loose descents. State says the 50mm fork offset and taller tire put trail at roughly 73 to 78mm on the small sizes and about 68mm on Medium and Large.

Head angles are size-specific: 70° on XS and S and 71.5° on M and L, which is a nice touch when many brands, especially at this price, run one angle across the whole range.

Reach grew 5 to 10mm over V1, mostly on the bigger sizes, but State rebalanced stem lengths so fit stays close to V1. Crank arms and stems scale with size too, so smaller riders aren’t getting a shrunk-down big bike.

Wheel Upgrades

If the stock wheels aren’t enough, State offers two options: DT Swiss G1800 Spline for +$450 (650b or 700c), or Zipp 303 XPLR S carbon for +$1,000 (700c only, MSRP $1,500). Here’s a heads-up on the Zipp: it’s hookless, so it can run tubeless tires only.

State’s All-Road V2 Retail & Detail

Retail: $1,499

  • Colors: Liquid Emerald (green), Chrome Red, Metallic Smoke (graphite)
  • Sizes: XS 48cm, S 51cm, M 54cm, L 58cm
  • Wheel size: 700c or 650b, selected at checkout, same frame and clearance
  • Frame: Double-butted 6061 aluminum, aero-profiled tubes, painted “anodized” finish
  • Routing: Fully internal through ID52 head tube, down the steerer
  • Bottom bracket: T47 threaded
  • Rear end: UDH, direct-mount for SRAM Transmission derailleurs
  • Max tire clearance: 700c x 55mm or 650b x 55mm
  • Stock tires: Continental 29 x 2.0 (model unspecified)
  • Wheels: 25mm internal width, 30mm deep, 32 spokes, brass nipples, tubeless-ready (taped and valved, sealant not included)
  • Crankset: Aero, solid narrow-wide 42T 7075 ring, forged 6061 arms, 29mm spindle, 49.7mm chainline
  • Drivetrain: 12-speed, 11-46t cassette, derailleur rated to 50T
  • Gearing: 418% range, 0.91:1 low gear (State says)
  • Brakes: Full hydraulic, carbon levers, 160mm rotors front and rear
  • Saddle: 150mm trail saddle
  • Geometry: 445mm chainstays, 73mm BB drop, 50mm fork offset
  • Head angle: 70° (XS, S), 71.5° (M, L)
  • Trail: ~73-78mm (small sizes), ~68mm (M, L), per State
  • Fit changes vs. V1: Reach up 5-10mm, stems rebalanced, size-scaled cranks and stems
  • Wheel upgrades: DT Swiss G1800 Spline (+$450, 700c or 650b); Zipp 303 XPLR S carbon (+$1,000, 700c only, hookless, tubeless only, 50 psi max, approved tires only)

On paper, this looks to be a serious rethink of an entry-level gravel bike. The frame standards come in way above the price, and the size-specific geometry is the kind of detail usually saved for the pricier bikes. In my opinion, State just keeps doing things right, and you should probably take notice.

Hit the link below to find out more.

StateBicycle.com

entry.title: Stinner Launches Stoic Components with Three Carbon Wheelsets, Plus a Select 2.0 Refresh
entry.content:
Stinner Frameworks just dumped a pretty big fall/winter update on us. It includes a reworked Select lineup, a brand-new in-house component brand, and a titanium photo stick. It’s a lot of news for one press release, so let’s get into it.

Meet Stoic Components

We first got a glimpse of Stinner’s Stoic Components on the debut of the Romero at Sea Otter. Stinner’s house-brand component line comes to market with three carbon wheelsets: the R40 (all-road), G29 (gravel), and M34 (mountain/adventure).

Each wheelset starts at $1,499, and you can buy them standalone or spec them on any Stinner build. Stinner staff and ambassadors have apparently been riding prototypes for years, so this isn’t a “slap a logo on it and ship it” situation.

The story behind it is worth a moment. Stoic started nearly a decade ago as a partnership with Jones Wheels, and the brand honors the memory of John Jones.

Founder Aaron Stinner put it this way: “John and I planned to start a component brand together. We lost him to cancer in 2021, before we got the chance. Stoic Components is that brand. We’re starting where he would have: carbon wheels, each matched to a Stinner frame and laced to Stoic hubs. Built to stay true.”

That’s a fitting way to launch a wheel brand, and the “built to stay true” line works on more than one level. Nice.

Select 2.0 Upgrades

Ok, back to the bikes. Every drop bar Select now gets built using Columbus Life tubing. In comparison to the Zona tubes that were formerly used, Columbus Life uses higher-strength Omnicrom alloy for lighter, stiffer, oversized tubes across road, gravel, and MTB builds.

They will also get SRAM Rival AXS. So, drivetrain options now include Force XPLR or a Force/XO Mullet setup. You can also add the new Stoic carbon wheels, and there are new build options from Vision and Terravail.

Select 2.0 Details

  • Columbus Life tubing on all drop bar Select models
  • SRAM Rival AXS standard on all drop bar Selects
  • Optional Force XPLR or Force/XO Mullet drivetrains
  • Stoic carbon wheel upgrade available
  • New build options from Vision and Terravail

Photo Stick 2.0

Retail: $110

Finally, there’s the Stinner x MADE Photo Stick 2.0, because bikes are beautiful and should be photographed. It’s fabricated in-house from Grade 9 titanium at Stinner’s Santa Barbara factory, and the big change is a new 3D-printed yoke.

  • Grade 9 titanium, bead-blasted finish with black Stinner x MADE logo
  • New 3D-printed yoke
  • Packable design
  • Made in the USA at Stinner’s Santa Barbara factory

Stinner says that makes it stronger while cutting fabrication time. It’s packable for travel, finished in bead-blasted titanium with a black Stinner x MADE logo, and made in the USA. It’s $109.99, which is cheaper than most of the “stuff I definitely needed” in my shop. We’re fans of the Photo Stick for obvious reasons, but for version 3.0, we’d love to see a way to adjust the length to fit different bikes a little better.

Stoic Wheelsets Retail & Details

All Stoic wheelsets carry a flatness tolerance of 0.2 mm max, and a roundness 0.3mm max. Tubeless tape and valves included.

The Stoic R40 (All-Road)

Retail: From $1,499

  • Fits Gibraltar and Carrizo
  • Toray T700/T800 carbon, 700c, hooked and tubeless ready
  • 25mm internal / 32mm external / 40mm deep, asymmetric with 2.6mm offset
  • 24h front and rear, rim weight 420g
  • Max tire pressure 125 psi, max spoke tension 140 kgf, rider weight limit 120kg (265 lb)
  • Hubs: Stoic, made with Bitex (BX106F/R), 12×100/12x142mm thru-axle, Center Lock
  • 6-pawl freehub, 44 points of engagement
  • Freehub options: Shimano HG 11/12spd, SRAM XDR, Campagnolo N3W, Shimano Micro Spline (upgrade kit)
  • Sealed cartridge bearings
  • Pillar PSR Triple Butted spokes, Pillar brass nipples, J-bend
  • Hub weights: front ~126g, rear ~230-250g
  • Wheelset weight: 1,535g (taped, no valves)

Stoic G29 (Gravel)

Retail: From $1,499

  • Fits Refugio
  • Toray T700/T800 carbon, 29″/700c, hookless (3mm bead wall), tubeless only
  • 29mm internal / 35mm external / 25mm deep, asymmetric with 2.6mm or 3mm offset
  • 24h front and rear, rim weight 400g
  • Same Stoic/Bitex hubs, 6-pawl freehub, and freehub options as the R40
  • Pillar PSR Triple Butted spokes, Pillar brass nipples, J-bend
  • Wheelset weight: 1,450g (taped, no valves)

And the Stoic M34 (Mountain/Adventure)

Retail: From $1,499

  • Fits Romero and Tunnel
  • Toray T700/T800 carbon, 29″, hookless (3mm bead wall), tubeless only
  • 34mm internal / 40mm external / 25mm deep, asymmetric with 2.6mm or 3mm offset
  • 32h front and rear, rim weight 430g (AM) / 480g (DH)
  • Hubs: Stoic/Bitex BX212F/R, 15x110mm and 12x148mm Boost thru-axle, steel rear axle, Center Lock
  • 6-pawl freehub, 54 points of engagement
  • Freehub options: SRAM XD/XDR, Shimano Micro Spline 12spd, Shimano HG
  • Sealed cartridge bearings
  • Pillar PSR Triple Butted spokes, Pillar brass nipples, J-bend
  • Hub weights: front ~142g, rear ~270g

Hit the link below to learn more.
