entry.title: MKS Pedal in Tokorozawa, Japan: Value from Process – John Watson
entry.content:
Continuing our tour of heritage Japanese manufacturers, we visit the final bosses of pedals at MKS in Tokorozawa, Japan. When Cari and John walked away from this Shop Visit, they had one thing on their minds: value perceived from witnessing the process. Read on for another collaborative post between The Radavist and Slow Spin Society, presented by Sim Works…

Paul, Cari, and Masashi

Sim Works Road Trip: MKS

Kimura-san and I thousand-yard stared out the rainy windshield in his car, waiting at a red light after leaving the MKS facilities, about to embark on our drive to Zushi, Japan, for a day of downtime. His wipers were making a sound one might hear from a robot dog in an Akihabara toy shop. “Wow” is all I could say. Masashi laughed in his very astute Japanese way. “Yeah.” All of us in the car – Paul from Slow Spin, Cari, Masashi, and me – sat in silence, listening to the mew of the windshield wiper.

Value from process was swirling through my head. Being on the inside of bike media has allowed me certain privileges I’ve tried hard not to take for granted. One of which is being an observer of the manufacturing process around the globe. But nothing had prepared me for my perspective shift on pedals after visiting MKS in Tokorozawa, Japan.

MKS Pedals

Those 1983 Suntour XC pedals I have on my Steve Potts? Those loose ball pedals that still shine like rims in a Pall Wall music video? They were made here. In the thousands. With each set being touched by a dozen hands at this very factory. All those shiny 1984 Specialized Pista pedals that were the exact same as the MKS SVX Keirin pedals. Made here too. Many of the same workers who produced those pedals are still employed by MKS today.

The scars on my shins from BMX Foot Jaws pedals from my youth’s Mongoose BMX bike were tingling as I picked up a NOS pair, in blue, of course, to photograph from the MKS archives, nestled in a showroom with the most epic soft-box light.

BIKE

Yuba-san comes over, with a laugh, and shows me the brand’s first pedal model, aptly named “BIKE.” “I wonder how they came up with the name?” He said with a smile. The hefty pedals landed on the glass with a thunkkkk. We’d just finished burgers and coffee from Japan’s burger fast food chain, Mos. And Yuba was eager to get started on the factory tour but was being incredibly patient with Paul and me.

Moving throughout MKS’ facilities on that rainy day, Kenta Yubamoto (Yuba-san) stepped through the factory with a cool, collected demeanor, excited to showcase the factory he was working towards running, which is currently under the helm of his father-in-law and president, Toshiyuki Ogino. Ogino-san was recovering from a cold and couldn’t join us for our tour, but Yuba-san, representing the next generation in Japanese manufacturing, was doing a phenomenal job.

Knowing what we’d geek out at, he began the day with an exclamation: “We should go to the heat-treating facilities now. You’ll like it.”

We walked through giant celadon colored doors, a familiar hue in factories in Japan. My color theory classes during my architecture education bounced back into the forefront of my memory. This seafoam color was intentionally selected for factories in the 1940s. It helps reduce visual fatigue and improves worker safety and efficiency. And MKS was covered in it. Floor to ceiling.

Kenta Yubamoto and Toshiyuki Ogino. Ogino-san (right) showed up at the end of the workday and our tour for a photo…

Mikashima Industrial Company Limited

Before we continue, it’s important to reiterate what the word legacy means: an impact handed down from a person, predecessor, or historical period. Japan is no stranger to manufacturing. Nor to the bicycle. Your favorite component groupset, be it from Suntour or Shimano, arose from the east with the rising sun. And those pedals that just won’t quit, most likely were made behind these very walls.

MKS (Mikashima Industrial Company Limited) was not founded by a single individual; instead, it was established as a company managed and operated by the Ogino family. Toshiyuki Ogino is the current president, a classic Japanese businessman with an austere yet friendly demeanor. His son-in-law, Kenta Yubamoto, aka Yuba-san, acts as the vice president.

The factory in Tokorozawa was built in 1943 and was used to make airplane parts for the war. In the post-war Japanese manufacturing boom, the Ogino family bought it and immediately switched to manufacturing bicycle pedals in 1946 with its first model, the “BIKE.” Designed for mamachari bicycles, these hefty, 700+ gram pedals launched a brand that still stands today.

Unlike the Nitto factory, the MKS facilities look properly maintained and have been brought up to modern standards in terms of lighting, with a façade barely showing its age.

Fire, Fire!

Back to the tour Yuba-san was starting with us. In the heat treatment facility. A pilot flame spurts out of a giant steel vault-like machine. As a loud alarm sounds, a small trolley brings in racks of pedal spindles. Yuba takes a step back.

Please allow this brief aside from a gaijin, a foreigner, but Japan seemingly has no OSHA. Or if they do, it is more relaxed than the regulations I’m more accustomed to. Sure, there’s a line painted on the ground here, but no heat shield, and no one is wearing eye or ear protection, either. My innate self preservation instincts tells me I should step back a few feet.

The door to the heat treatment furnace opens, and flames bellow out as this beast of metal engulfs crates of freshly formed pedal parts. Hairs on my hands feel warm and lightly singe, dancing as I focus my lens on the inferno. Inside, these parts will endure 900 degrees Celsius for 2 hours and move through numerous phases. Quenching: after the fire, parts receive an oil bath at 55 Celsius, resulting in harder but more brittle parts. Annealing: this brings back material flexibility so it is not brittle anymore. This treatment would not work if the parts were oxidized, so the fire gets rid of all the oxygen in the chamber and creates a high carbon density layer to give the spindles strength.

After the heat treatment, we begin the normal tour, starting with a cold forge.

Coil Fed Cold Forging

Taking a step back, MKS has a series of cold forging machines: two smaller ones for things like cone washers, and a larger one, fed by a 100-meter-long coil of Japanese steel. This machine cuts the coiled steel into spindle lengths and then pounds them into shape over five cycles. This includes shaping the spindles and forming the 6 mm Hex key ends. The cold forge cranks out a spindle a second! With around 20,000 spindles made each day.

Again, very few safety measures, aside from a viewing window, are used here. My ex construction heeby jeebies were in full expression here, as the worker leans in to check the machine’s tolerances. Eeeeeee!

From the cold forge, the parts are very hot from the immense amount of friction they endure, so a cold oil bath cools them, where tolerances are checked. Then two machines: one for right- and left-handed threading presses in the threads with massive dies. One of these machines is run by a woman who’s been with MKS for 60 years, starting the day she graduated from high school!

In-House ISO Testing

From here, a couple of spindles from each batch of 2,000 will get ISO tested in-house, enduring up to 20 kilonewtons, or about 10x the ISO requirement, of force before shearing. Upon shearing, the spindle will be inspected under a microscope. Then there’s the rotation test, with 90 kg of weight pressing on a pedal spindle as it endures 1,000,000 cycles. The ISO requirement is 100,000. MKS only rotation ISO tests batches when a design changes.

Like Nitto, they’re also NJS certified, and NJS parts consume most of the factory’s energy.

Pedal Cages

MKS gets its pedal bodies die-cast in town at a local manufacturer, and from there, the various pieces are machined to attach cages and spindles. The cages, however, are die cut and pressed for embossing in-house. Elaborate designs like the Sim Works Taco Pedals require five steps to cut, stamp, perforate, and shape the pedal cages into their final form.

Assembly

From there, all the parts are loaded into crates: yellow for left-threaded, and green for right-threaded, and taken up to assembly. A machine will load the loose ball bearings, add grease, and set the initial preload on the pedals, while an employee torques them to spec before their final inspection.

The NJS pedals, however, use cartridge bearings and are fully assembled by an NJS-certified worker. He places a bearing drift into the spindle and whacks the bearing into place, listening carefully for the proper sound of a set cartridge. This worker checks each pedal multiple times before giving them a final spin in the bench vice. So much of this process is reliant on human hearing and feel. 20 years of working at MKS has made him more efficient than any machine, yet he can only assemble around 40 pairs of NJS Keirin pedals a day due to this painstaking process.

MKS Workforce

Like Nitto, MKS is grappling with an aging workforce, with 50 workers over 50 years of age. While the Japanese lifestyle has kept its national workforce young-looking, their bodies are slowing. Yuba-san explained that MKS is trying to reach a younger generation, enticing them to move to the area and work for the brand. It’s working, with the Tokyo College of Design providing some eager applicants, as well as people from Nepal and around the globe, eager to make a solid living working in industry. Currently, MKS employs 100 people, 20 of whom commute to work by bicycle.

There are many employees who have spent their entire lives working for MKS and are avid cyclists. Ito San, 65, rides a Rivendell Platypus into work every day. Her workstation is full of ephemera. Through a translation app, she smiled as she told Cari that she started riding a track bike at age 50 and was hooked on the feeling riding a bike gave her. She was assembling Keirin toe straps that day, including the buckles, and was keen to pause for a portrait.

Marketshare

Unlike Nitto, which only makes bicycle parts, around 60% of MKS production goes to the automotive industry. Japanese auto manufacturers will contract out things like seat brackets or headrests to MKS. This leaves around 40% of its output going wholly to MKS pedals. Over the past three years, the bicycle sector has grown, picking up a 10% dip in automotive work demand.

Shiny Parts from Greasy Machines

I used to think MKS pedals, like Nitto handlebars, were expensive, compared to others on the market. Yet, unlike those other pedals, they never died. If they got too loose, a simple box wrench would have them spinning like new again, and maybe a fresh repacking of grease every five years. The smell of machine oil and grease coated the machines, designed for creating some of the shiniest, prettiest pedals in the world. These acrid-smelling halls spawn perfection. Literal products of legacy from a brand that has perfected its craft over generations. I’ll never look at my MKS pedals the same again.

The Radavist x Slow Spin Society

As The Radavist celebrates its 20th anniversary of covering cycling communities, we wanted to partner with the next generation of cycling media on a lifelong dream trip of mine. We’ve featured Paul from Slow Spin Society on the website before. As a wearer of many hats – Paul also works for Sim Works as its Euro branch and was gracious enough to act as our Japanese translator during the trip – Paul is always balancing his job at Sim Works with Slow Spin. As we chatted about what a possible collaboration could look like, we landed on the idea of storytelling and interviews.

Paul wanted to focus on interviewing people at MKS, mostly the younger people, about how they got involved in working in manufacturing.

Roll on over to Slow Spin Society to read Paul’s interviews!

Fewer, Better Things

Throughout my life, I’ve strived to own fewer, better things, biting the bullet on products with an inherent value add, supporting makers and manufacturers who, against the late capitalist demands for 5% YOY growth, stayed the course and never relented. Never again will I look at a chromed spindle with black anodized cages and think: “those are too expensive.” Instead, I’ll rewrite my brain’s coding with “those pedals will outlive me.”

Pedals. They’re so simple and yet are desideratum to the functionality of the almighty bicycle. Incredulous commentators might not believe it when I say it, so it’s my job to showcase the process so that value might be perceived, no matter where the viewer may be.

I wanted to extend a special thanks to Yuba-san for showing us around and for bringing MKS into the Bespoked fold, supporting the world’s largest framebuilder showcase. I’d also like to personally thank Tanaka-san from Circles and Sim Works for believing in our work over here and supporting us through these stories. And to Paul from Slow Spin Society for his willingness and eagerness to collaborate. Miss you, friends!

The Radavist thanks Sim Works for supporting our independent Reportage here!

The post MKS Pedal in Tokorozawa, Japan: Value from Process appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: ‘I have this desire to be all-in and go all the way with it’: Kate Courtney interview
entry.content:
Cyclist
‘I have this desire to be all-in and go all the way with it’: Kate Courtney interview

Cyclist: You made your name in mountain biking. Why the switch to road?

Kate Courtney: It’s really about what excites me. I think there are certain goals in life that keep you up at night and speak to you, and for me right now that’s road.

How did the FDJ United-Suez link come about?

When I started considering the switch, things escalated very quickly. I don’t have an intermediate setting as a person, I’m a zero-to-100 girl, and this certainly followed that trend. I started to talk to everyone I knew involved in the sport who might have advice on what I would need to do to make the jump to the next level and where might be the right fit to make that jump. It came about really organically. It was clear from the beginning that the team would be a great fit.

Have you already moved from the US to Europe?

Not for this year. I’m currently based in California, just south of San Francisco, but next year I will certainly split my time between home and Europe with the team quite a bit. I’m looking at some potential spots to base myself – it’s likely going to be Spain like all the other American cyclists.

You went to Belgium recently for experience and ended up winning two races. What were you able to take away from that?

Kermesse racing is such a historic staple of the road development pathway in Europe, so I went to learn and pay homage to the origins of the sport and to these races. The biggest takeaway was learning to apply the skills I already have. The first day was honestly terrifying. I found myself in the back of a bar, signing up for what is essentially a crit race for over 100 girls. It was a mixture of all the things that I would say are weaknesses coming to the road, like bunch dynamics, wind, cobbles, cracks and the near certainty of a sprint finish.

I was actually pretty comfortable in the bunch and loved it. I used a lot of the skills that I have from mountain biking – bunny-hopping a rock, for example, is not that different from bunny-hopping a crack on the road in Belgium. The more I’m exposed to these types of opportunities that match my skill level the more I gain in confidence. That’s going to be the most important thing for stepping up to the next level and not just being there to participate but to really compete.

What kind of races do you see yourself targeting?

We’ll see, and that’s an exciting thing. This is an exploratory phase to see where I thrive on the road. The spring Classics and making a Grand Tour team next year would be big goals. Stephen [Delcourt, team manager] calls me his junior on the team and there’s something magical about that, feeling like you’re racing like a kid, just attacking constantly and seeing what happens. You don’t have this expectation – not from other people, but from yourself. There is magic in being a beginner and that’s a mindset I’m going to try to lean into for the next couple of years.

What motivates you?

I think of competitive sports as a way to push and discover what we’re capable of. Every athlete, every generation, takes the baton and runs as far as they can with it. For me, this era in my cycling career is all about seeing how far I can take that and truly give myself the chance to go all the way and discover what I’m capable of doing when I put my full body, mind and heart into the sport.

Is there a rider in the team or in the peloton that you find yourself wanting to pick the brain of?

It’s such a strong and deep team. We have an incredible leader in Demi [Vollering] both on and off the bike, and I’m excited to get to know her more, learn from her and support her as best I can. The special thing about being a beginner is how kind and generous everyone has been, helping me understand the ropes. Simple things like what time we go to the race, where to line up for signing on, all these things that aren’t a part of mountain biking.

You’re already a champion, but do you feel any nerves or apprehension about making this move to the road?

Absolutely! This has been an exhilarating and terrifying jump. One of the goals in making such an aggressive and quick transition was to push me outside of my comfort zone. I certainly have done that.

There’s a quote that really applies here from [American artist] Georgia O’Keeffe: ‘I’ve been absolutely terrified every moment of my life and I’ve never let it keep me from doing a single thing that I wanted to do.’

So much can be intimidating about road cycling. It’s a dangerous and aggressive sport that I think people really can’t appreciate on TV. But what makes life interesting is going after those goals that scare you a little bit.

We’re speaking at the Tour de France Femmes. You’re not racing, but are you soaking everything in?

It’s been incredible to support the team and see behind the scenes how hard everyone works, from the riders to the staff to every single person that’s involved. It’s an insane number of people. It’s very inspiring.

A key ambition of this race is inspiring younger people. Do you see yourself as a role model who younger people can look up to?

I hope to be. The ability to inspire the next generation to go further and dream bigger than we did is a huge part of the motivation to keep pushing and doing things that scare me.

What does a dream road career look like for you?

I don’t know that I can pinpoint it yet. Right now the goal is experience, and when that’s your goal, it makes it really fun to pursue something because you can learn from anything. Experiences of failure, of success, of overwhelm… I have this desire to be all-in and go all the way with it.

When I’m finished with my career I want to have given 100% of what I’m capable of, then having peace with that and taking that mentality into whatever I do next.

The post ‘I have this desire to be all-in and go all the way with it’: Kate Courtney interview appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Buena Onda Bikes: Taiwan Made Batch Built Titanium Hardtail Pre-Order
entry.content:
Buena Onda Bikes has been building bikes in the USA for nearly five years. Designing and refining the Buena alongside our manufacturing partner in Durango has allowed the small brand to iterate quickly and make sure the bike rides exactly as intended: capable on technical trails, loaded or unloaded, and ready for demanding riders. After refining that design through its US-built frames, the Durango-based company set out to make it more accessible. By producing frames in batches with our manufacturing partner in Taiwan, Buena Onda Bikes are able to bring the same proven geometry to more riders at a lower price point of $3,100 for a frame…

Buena Onda Bikes Quick Hits

  • Frame only: Starting at $3,100
  • Eagle 90 complete build: $6,250
  • AXS complete build: $8,400
  • Tubeset: Size-specific Double Butted Titanium Tubing
  • Optimal Fork Travel for Suspension Builds: 130mm
  • Rear Hub Spacing: 148 x 12
  • Bottom Bracket: T47 Threaded, 73 mm
  • Dropouts: Horizontal Sliding Dropouts with 16mm of fore/aft adjustment. Each frame ships standard with UDH-compatible dropouts and a removable derailleur hanger.
  • Seatpost: Straight seat tube, 31.6 mm ream, 34.9 collar
  • Cable Routing: Externally routed with M5 bolt securement. Internal routing through the seat tube for a dropper post.
  • Bottle Mounts: 2x bottle cages in frame, triple bottle cage mounting on downtube
  • Rack Mounts: Upper and lower hourglass-style rack eyelets standard on all frames
  • Headtube/Headset: 44 mm head tube / ZS44/28.6 EC44/40 Headset
  • Max tire clearance: 29 x 2.6

Made in Taiwan

Our Taiwanese manufacturer was selected for its advanced capabilities, experience working with titanium, and high level of craftsmanship. These batch-built frames begin with the same flagship geometry we have tested and refined in Durango, then are engineered for larger-scale production.

Intentionally selected butted titanium tubing provides a balance of durability, comfort, and ride quality.

Designed for the Colorado Trail, whether you are heading out for a day ride or tackling all 539 miles, the Buena is built to go the distance. Loaded or unloaded. Built around a 130mm fork, it balances comfort and capability with geometry grounded in function, not fads: a 66.5° head tube angle, 75.5° straight seat tube angle, room for racks and bottles, and space for a large frame bag.

MUSA Option

MUSA frames are still available on a custom basis. Each MUSA build is made in the good ol’ USA by our manufacturing partner in Durango, Colorado. The process begins with our proven geometry, then we tailor the sizing around the rider so you are not forced to choose between standard sizes.

From there, you select the components that best match how and where you ride for a truly custom bike.

Frame Details

Tubing: Size-specific, double-butted Grade 9 titanium, with thinner wall sections through the middle of the tube where we can save weight without giving up strength where it matters. Include headtube gussets.

Head Badge: Custom-designed and hand-fabricated by Revolution Jewelry.
Finish: Ceramic Bead Blast with Brushed Logo.

The frames are built by our partner manufacturer in Taiwan in small production runs, using the same proven geometry and spec we tested and refined on our US-built frames. Batch-built frames come with a headtube gusset and external routing. Small and Extra Small frames will be available in the second batch.

Geometry and Warranty

Based on a 2.6″ tire and 20% sagged numbers.

Every Buena Onda frame is built to be ridden hard, loaded up, depended on, and kept around for life. Our limited lifetime warranty covers manufacturer defects in materials and workmanship for the original owner, because if something is on us, we will make it right.

Bikes are also meant to be used, and sometimes that means crashes, mistakes, bad lines, roof racks, baggage handlers, and the occasional questionable decision. Those situations are not covered under warranty, but we will offer discounted crash replacement support whenever possible to help keep you on your Buena.

Ordering Process

Getting on a batch-built Buena is straightforward.

Place a Deposit. Put down a 50% deposit to reserve your spot in the production queue. Pre-sales open November 16th.

Confirmation. Batch-built lead times run roughly 4 months after the pre-order window closes.
Build and Delivery. When your frame exits production, we collect the remaining balance, complete the build, and ship your bike. Local Durango pickup is available. Bikes from this batch deliver in April.
As a thank you for supporting us early, riders in this first batch get introductory pricing on these initial runs.

See more at Buena Onda Bikes.

The post Buena Onda Bikes: Taiwan Made Batch Built Titanium Hardtail Pre-Order appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Sign-Ups Are Open for 2027 Rez Gravel
entry.content:
Rez Gravel is an Indigenous-led adventure ride that makes cycling accessible on the Gila River Indian Community. This supported ride goes through the Gila River Indian Community, home of the Akimel O’otham (Pima) and Pee-Posh (Maricopa) tribes. Registration is open for the 2027 event, which takes place January 9th and 10th. Sign-ups are now open.

This is a group adventure ride, not a race, and it will average around 10 miles per hour, so pack a lunch and expect an all-day adventure if you are riding the 60 Mile Big Rez Gravel Route on January 10th.

There are two fee options for each ride: Little Rez Gravel $25 or $50. The Big Rez Gravel is $50 or $100. Funds raised will help Rez Gravel continue the work of helping residents of the Gila River Indian Community learn how to do bicycle repair and maintenance. Funds raised will go towards purchasing tubes, chains, other parts, tools, and supplies as they are needed.

Check out registration at Bike Sign Up and see more at Rez Gravel. Also, check out our Reportage from the 2024 Rez Gravel event in our archives.

The post Sign-Ups Are Open for 2027 Rez Gravel appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Nobl Launches AR Series: Its Lightest Road Rims to Date
entry.content:
Nobl Wheels has launched the AR Series, its lightest road rims to date. Available in 40mm and 50mm depths, the AR40 and AR50 combine Nobl’s aerodynamic teardrop profiles, 25mm internal widths and fully hooked beads, with rim weights starting at just 350g.

Nobl AR Wheels Quick Hits

  • AR40
    • Rim Weight 350g
    • Wheelsets as light as 1124g
    • Depth 40mm
    • Internal Width 25mm
    • External Width 31.5mm
    • Widest Point 33.5mm
    • Hole Count 24h
    • Size 700c
    • Strength Rating 110J
    • Max Tire Pressure 80psi
    • Tire Size 28-45c
  • AR50
    • Rim Weight 380g
    • Wheelsets as light as 1184g
    • Depth 50mm
    • Internal Width  25mm
    • External Width  31.5mm
    • Widest Point  33.5mm
    • Hole Count 24h
    • Size 700c
    • Strength Rating 115J
    • Max Tire Pressure 80psi
    • Tire Size 28-45c

Nobl’s Take on All-Road

Road tires are getting wider. Riders want the grip and comfort of 30–32mm tires without giving up the speed and responsiveness of a dedicated road wheel. The AR Series was developed around that balance. Its 25mm internal width creates a supportive tire profile, while a fully hooked bead offers broad tire compatibility. The result is a lightweight platform built for everything from weekday training and local racing to long days on mixed surfaces. The AR Series carries forward Nobl’s aerodynamic teardrop rim profile, first introduced on the Far gravel race wheels. With a 33.5mm widest external point, the AR’s profile maintains an aerodynamic shape. It meets the rule of 105 with a 30c tire, which measures about 32mm on the AR’s 25mm internal width.

Lightweight, Strong, Versatile

By using T1000 carbon and advanced layup processes, AR Series rims are among the lightest and strongest 25mm internal road rims with a hooked bead. With complete wheelsets starting at just 1124 grams, you get the security of a hooked bead at the same weight or less than hookless rivals. The AR40 starts at just 350g. Despite its low weight, the rim has passed impact testing up to 110J. The deeper AR50 weighs 380g per rim and has a 115J impact rating. Both models feature a 25mm internal width and fully hooked beads, and are ready for tires from 28–45c at up to 80 psi.

Nobl AR Wheelset Options and Pricing

The AR Series is available through Nobl’s Core lineup & its fully custom wheel builder.

  • Nobl Core AR40 / AR50 Wheelset
    • $1,999.00 CAD | $1,599.00 USD
    • Wheelset Weight: 1307/1367g (Alpina Extralite Spokes, XDR Driver)
    • Rims: NOBL AR40 / AR50
    • Hubs: NOBL Core Road Hub, 36t Ratchet
    • Spokes: Alpina Extralite / Sapim CX-Ray
    • Nipples: Black
    • Brake Interface: Centerlock
    • Driver: XDR / MS Road / HG
    • Graphics: 4 Color Options
  • Nobl Custom AR40 / AR50 Wheelset
    • Starting at $2,279.00 CAD | $1,699.00 USD
    • Lightest Wheelset Weight: 1124/1184g (DT180 Hubs, Berd Polylight Spokes, XDR Driver)
    • Rims: NOBL AR40 / AR50
    • Hub Brands: DT Swiss / Chris King / Hope / Project 321 / Onyx / Industry Nine / SON
    • Spokes: Alpina Extralite / Sapim CX-Ray / Berd Polylight
    • Nipples: Black
    • Brake Interface: Centerlock
    • Driver: XDR / MS Road / HG
    • Graphics: 4 Color Options

See more at Nobl Wheels.

entry.title: Rapha to make WorldTour return with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe in 2027
entry.content:
Cyclist
Rapha to make WorldTour return with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe in 2027

After a year spent away from pro cycling’s top division, British brand Rapha is set to make its return to the pro peloton with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe next year.

The team, home to Remco Evenepoel, Jai Hindley and Florian Lipowitz, will become the third WorldTour squad to wear Rapha’s threads in the pro peloton, following in the footsteps of Team Sky and EF Education-EasyPost. This time, the brand hopes Red Bull will be able to ‘win with character’, having focused heavily on cutting-edge R&D alongside Red Bull’s aero expert Dan Bigham.

The brand believes the partnership will ‘put Rapha back where it belongs, right back at the front of races’. Red Bull’s team boss Ralph Denk sees the collaboration with ‘huge potential for growth’, as he eyes up a ‘homecoming’ for Rapha on British roads at next summer’s Tour de France.

Cyclist spoke to some of the key names behind Rapha’s latest WorldTour foray.

Rapha’s WorldTour comeback

Rapha bowed out of the WorldTour at the end of 2025 when the brand parted ways with EF Education-EasyPost. The news came with the announcement of a new deal with the US national team, with the LA 2028 Olympics seen to be the big goal. At the time, then-CEO Fran Millar said that Rapha aimed to get back to the ‘forefront of the sport’. That time appears to have come after just one season out of the loop.

‘While we were out of the sport, we had plenty of time to do some soul-searching and work out what we wanted to do next,’ Joel Natale, Chief Product Officer at Rapha, says. ‘We were able to partner with a hugely dominant team in Team Sky and then with EF, who tried to bring something different to the sport with content, personality, disruption.

‘Ultimately, we could only go back into the sport if we could do both of those things at the same time. It would only be worth it if we win, but win with character.’

Rapha told Cyclist that it was in discussions with other WorldTour teams, including Visma-Lease a Bike. Clearly, Rapha was eager to get back onto the top division, but what is different about this partnership in comparison to its previous WorldTour dabbles?

‘EF was an incredible partner for Rapha, but it was massively different,’ Natale tells us. ‘The responsibility was on us, and the desire wasn’t really there. We did one big aero project with them for 2022 to try and get Stefan Bissegger in yellow. Otherwise, it was down to us. But they’re at the other end of the ranking, and they’re doing something completely different in racing.

‘We came to terms with the idea that the [EF] story on its own isn’t enough. You need to win and tell the story. Even if we could have run a UAE deal, the story has already been told.

‘Everyone knows what Red Bull has done in every sport,’ Natale continues. ‘This is a storied team, and they were winning long before Red Bull was here. So we want to put Rapha back where I think we belong, right back at the front of races, on the podium.’

‘Bora have pushed us on timelines, in terms of how tight they wanted to be able to make changes, the volume of kit that they wanted and having everything on another level. This R&D challenge is really exciting for us. We wouldn’t get the chance to work with such talent within every team. We are ready at Rapha to reset our image for a new generation of cyclists.’

Achieving ‘cycling’s potential’

Rapha is pairing up with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, a squad that featured on the podiums of all three Grand Tours in 2026 and finished the season as the second-best team in the UCI rankings.

Its team boss Ralph Denk has been instrumental in the team’s growth over the past decade, including the Red Bull takeover in mid-2024. He believes having Rapha on board is a step toward transforming cycling’s audience.

‘When I was younger, cyclists looked like they were from the moon,’ Denk said at the launch of the partnership. ‘But now, cycling is a lifestyle, and for me, Rapha had a big part in making cycling bigger on a lifestyle level, not just a performance level.

‘The partnership is not just about performance, it’s about lifestyle. We were approached by several Italian brands. They make good cycling apparel, don’t get me wrong, but the combination of lifestyle and high performance, I see just one. Rapha.’

The London-based brand proved popular during its two previous WorldTour dabbles. With EF, Rapha attracted wide attention through switch-out kits in collaboration with streetwear brand Palace. During its time with Sky, then-CEO Simon Mottram told CityAM the brand ‘sold a lot of stuff’ on the back of the Team Sky deal. Denk is hoping for similar returns a decade on.

‘Cycling has huge potential in merchandising,’ Denk says. ‘In the Red Bull environment, we have all the numbers. What are the football teams, the Formula 1 teams’ revenue? For cycling, there is room to improve. I believe cycling has the same potential as Formula 1. Our mission is to make cycling bigger and we need different styles, both on bike and off bike.’

Team rider Callum Thornley has a more emotional connection to the new deal, stating that the partnership is a ‘big thing’ for a British rider like him.

‘I think my first pair of bib shorts were Rapha,’ the Scottish rider said. ‘It’s a full circle moment.’

‘It’s a scientific, knowledge-based arms race’

Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe’s Head of Engineering Dan Bigham has played a big role in the Rapha partnership. The aero boffin has been involved in the development of the kit since the spring, visiting wind-tunnels and creating a machine-learning system to chew the numbers. Two other aerodynamicists were taken on board as part of the Rapha-Red Bull deal – one a former McLaren’s F1 team employee, the other an expert in jellyfish movement.

‘There’s only so much knowledge published on cycling apparel out there right now,’ Bigham says. ‘The exciting bit is bringing that knowledge together with Rapha and being genuinely world-class at both so we understand the demands of the event and how we can influence that. We can execute that quicker than any other apparel manufacturer can.

‘We had full commitment when I told them [Rapha] everything we know and don’t know. That’s the frontier, and we want to push that forward. I was amazed by that because sometimes we pushed it a bit further than what’s sensible or reasonable.’

Bigham believes that riders could soon wear a different skinsuit each day, tailored to wind direction and racing ambitions. With Rapha, he’s building a database to support this.

‘[Aerodynamic] flow conditions change in every environment around the world, every rider where they’re riding in the bunch, whether you’re riding in a city, by a lake, whether it’s windy, raining. That changes the aerodynamic flow. It’s a complex optimisation problem, but with Rapha, we’re trying to find the true optimal flow solution for every rider.

‘We’re pulling it all together – mechanistic understanding of textiles through to measuring in the field. We’re building the full database we need, those causal links, so we can go to Rapha and say we need a sock for this exact condition, this exact race, this exact rider in the group. That’s the end goal, so we can do that quicker and more consistently than anyone else.

‘We’re closing in on this,’ Bigham says. ‘We’re probably only a few months away from at least having the bare-bones structure. It’s then a matter of feeding more data into that model and validating that model properly.

But does Bigham know Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe are a step ahead? He believes so.

‘There’s nothing in the literature, and there’s nothing that would explain why any other team or any other manufacturer has approached it with this methodology,’ he affirms. ‘From the things other teams say and what they do, it would imply that they probably are not [doing the same things as us].

‘It’s like throwing darts at a dartboard. Other teams would typically go to the wind-tunnel and do 20, 30, 40 fabrics and make two, three, four socks. They go to the wind-tunnel and test them on one or two riders. That’s quite logical, but we want to find the true nuance and have confidence to take it there. It’s multiple PhDs level of research. We don’t want to publish it. We want to contain that knowledge within Rapha Red Bull and beat everybody. It’s a scientific, knowledge-based arms race.

‘This R&D programme is not only unique, it’s absolutely game-changing. It’s quite scary how fast we’re moving.’

Details on the kit design are yet to be shared with the public, but we can expect the jersey to break cover once Red Bull host their team camp in Mallorca next month.

The post Rapha to make WorldTour return with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe in 2027 appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Suunto Run 2 In-Depth Review: Worth The Premium?
entry.content:
I’ve now been wearing the Suunto Run 2 for exactly one month straight, 24×7, for every workout from run to swim to ride to strength, and everything else in between. The Suunto Run 2 takes the existing Suunto Run 1 and elevates it a fair bit with offline mapping, a new brighter display, and a much improved optical heart rate sensor. They also increased GPS battery claims by about 30%, though smartwatch battery claims went down slightly.

Suunto seemed laser-focused on improving the things people rightfully complained about in the Run 1 and addressing those in the Run 2. Albeit, it now costs $100 more (and nobody complained about the price being too low last time). I suppose you can’t win them all.

The thing to understand about the Suunto Run series is that it’s hardly focused on just runners. In the same way that Garmin’s Forerunner series is hardly for just runners. Both these watches can just as easily be used for triathletes and any other sports that you can throw at it. And I’ve done just that.

With that, let’s get right into it.

What’s New:

The Suunto Run 2 takes the existing Suunto Run 1 from last year and turns it into something that’s more akin to a Suunto Race 2S. Except it’s still called the Suunto Run series, despite being just as capable a multisport watch as a running watch. While last year Suunto pitched the first Suunto Run as an inexpensive running watch, this second-generation model shouldn’t be viewed through that restricted lens.

Here’s what’s changed since the Suunto Run 1:

– Increased display brightness up to 2,000 nits (previous panel was ~1,000 nits)
– Same 1.32” display size as before
– Updated GPS chipset, though still multi-band/dual-frequency
– Notably new optical HR sensor that’s substantially better than before
– Increased GPS battery claims from 20hrs to 30hrs+ (depending on modes)
– Decreased daily smartwatch usage claim from 12 days to 10 days.
– Added offline map capability (download maps)
– Added EnergySense feature for run pacing
– Added HeatStrain Score
– Roughly the same weight as before (35g vs 36g on previous unit)
– Base price increased from $249 to $349USD (or from 249EUR to 349EUR
– Now offered in either 4GB or 64GB models ($349/$399)

In any case, keeping in mind the Suunto Run series still operates on a different operating system than the rest of Suunto’s watches, there remain some restrictions there (such as not supporting any apps in the Suunto App Store, and not supporting structured workouts from 3rd-party platforms). Further, it has fewer sport modes (~35) than the 95+ sport modes on the rest of the Suunto watches. But otherwise, it’s largely the same, minus a few little software quirks here and there that I discuss below.

The unit comes in three color options: Black, green, or white.

In The Box:

The design of the Suunto Run 2 box isn’t much different than other Suunto boxes from the last few years, but I’ve gotta say – every time I open one of the Suunto boxes, it’s one of the cleanest and best-done variants in the industry today. Of course, they took inspiration from Apple Watch boxes years ago, but the little touches on design/photography are well done.

In any case, once you extract all the pieces, here’s what you’ve got:

It’s really pretty straightforward:

– The watch pod
– The band/strap
– The charging cable
– A book you won’t read
– Some other pamphlets you also probably won’t read
– A few stickers you might use

And here’s a closer look at things:

As always, the unboxing section isn’t complicated, so let’s get right into using the watch.

The Basics:

For this first bit, I’m going to dive into all the basic features of the watch, things like activity tracking, daily usage, sleep tracking, and so on. Plus some bits from the Suunto App in those categories. In the next section I’ll cover all the sport-related aspects (including navigation).

The Suunto Run 2 mirrors the also-recent Suunto Race 3S in terms of the Suunto 3-button layout. This means there are two main buttons on the right side, plus a Digital Crown (that also acts as a button). The upper right button goes straight to accessing the most recent sport profile, the middle accesses your ‘Today’s Plan’ and the rest of the sport modes, and the bottom button acts as an escape. The Digital Crown also allows you to access the widgets. On top of that, you’ve got the touchscreen display.

If you’re familiar with other Suunto watches, the Suunto Run 2 might cause you to stumble a little bit with the user interface. While it is similar to other Suunto watches, the Suunto Run 1 & Run 2 run a slightly different operating system than all other Suunto watches. The differences are minor, but enough that muscle-memory tasks (like tapping the upper-right button to select a different sport mode) will cause some stumbles until you re-map that to the middle button instead. It’s no biggie if coming from any other brand watch, and after nearly a month of wearing it, I’ve mostly gotten used to it.

In any case, as for the display, the Suunto Run 2 uses a 2,000-nit display. It’s been perfectly fine in all my outside testing here in the Mediterranean over the last month, even on the sunniest of days. That said, as I noted in my Suunto Race 3S review, launching with a 2,000-nit display in 2026 at this price point is a bit dicey. Companies like Amazfit are putting in 3,000-nit displays in the Balance 3 at the same price point. Again, the display is perfectly fine, but if Suunto is pitching this as a premium budget watch (as weird as that sounds), then it should contain premium parts.

In any case, scrolling down from the watch face, you’ve got the widgets, which include things like steps, training volume/metrics, the weather, and more. It’s funny to see again the differences here from the other Suunto watches, for things like a lack of a specific HRV widget for example (which is on the Suunto Race 3S and other watches), and instead rolling that into the “Recovery” widget.

Nonetheless, all the things are still there, just the deck chairs in slightly different places. And as you’d expect, you can tap into any of these items to see an expanded view of them, such as steps, weather, sleep, etc.

In terms of things like sleep tracking, I haven’t had any accuracy issues here. It’s been basically spot-on with all my other wearables in this realm, and of course, the actual times I went to sleep and woke up. Note that I don’t compare sleep phases/stages, because doing so is peak faux-science. The best-case reference devices you can use to do so are only about 80% accurate, which isn’t all that great (and again, that’s a best-case scenario in perfect lab conditions). Thus, we’d never compare a heart rate sensor to a chest strap that was wrong 20% of the time. Therefore, I’m not gonna do it here either.

Of course, all of this data is mostly driven by looking at your heart rate and other movement sensor data. The Run 2 features a new heart rate sensor on the back (same as the also-new Suunto Race 3S). This sensor is a big step up from the previous Suunto sensors, which didn’t have a history of being super awesome.

In terms of a few other odds and ends, the unit is sold in two variants in terms of storage. One option is at 4GB, and the other at 64GB. This allows for more maps, but most notably also offline music that you’re never going to put on the unit. Sure, it can technically support putting MP3 files via USB cable. But there’s no support for streaming services (e.g., Spotify/etc), because those walled gardens went up years ago, and Suunto was left out in the cold (and that’s not gonna change anytime soon). Still, the option technically exists to stick MP3 files and use Bluetooth headphones to play back the music.

For everyone else, you’ll just use the Media Controls option, which controls music/podcasts/etc on your phone from the watch. Though, I often find that quite finicky. As of this very moment, I’m playing music on my phone, and the watch doesn’t show anything in Media Controls.

Sigh. But when it does, here’s what it looks like (in this case, a few seconds later it decided to enumerate for its photo shoot):

As for smartphone notifications, that too can be finicky as to whether or not they show up. But when they do, here’s what they look like:

Note that there is no flashlight built into this watch. I’m not sure if Suunto got spooked with their current lawsuit fiasco (TLDR: They picked a fight with Garmin, and Garmin fought back against Suunto’s Vertical 2 flashlight). Either way, there isn’t a physical LED flashlight here, but there is a display-based one. I’ve used it a few times for some random under-the-bed type tasks, and it’s OK enough, but it’s no real flashlight either.

When it comes to daily battery life, I’ve been using the always-on mode this entire time. And with roughly 1-3 hours of GPS time per day, I’m getting roughly 4-5 days of battery life between charges. I’m OK with that, though, as I’ll cover in the GPS battery section, that battery life seems to be falling notably short of expectations.

In terms of charging, it uses the same charger as the rest of the recent Suunto watches, which is a magnetic charger that works perfectly fine. It even has a nice braided cable, something that Garmin only offers on their $3,000+ MARQ watches.

Finally, I do want to mention briefly that I’m not in love with the strap/band. Specifically, the tiny little doohickey at the end that keeps the band from flapping around. This doohickey portion that goes through the band is simply not big enough, perhaps 1mm too small (maybe 0.5mm too small), and thus it’s constantly popping off.

I know this sounds trivial, and sure I could go buy another band, but equally, it’s just as if nobody actually wore this thing.

In fact, one day while out gravel riding, I paused for a second to grab some stuff out of my hydration pack, and when I did so, it caught the strap of my watch and actually removed the whole thing and flung it out into the bushes (because it undoes so easily). Not a huge deal, as I was able to go find it, but frankly, I’ve never had that happen in my life before. Let alone the strap unhinging on a multiple-times-a-day basis.

Ok, with that, let’s get into the sports bits.

Sports & Navigation:

The Suunto Run 2 is definitely not just a watch for runners. It’s a true and fully capable multisport watch that can be used for running, cycling, swimming, and a gazillion other sports (including triathlon). And in fact, I pretty evenly spread my time out among those sports and more during my testing.

To start a workout, you’ll tap the middle left button. This then shows anything in our ‘Today’s Plan’ section, which can be structured workouts you’ve saved. Below that are your sport modes:

The Suunto Run 2 has 35 sport profiles on it, which are as follows:

Running, Indoor Cycling, Cycling, Trail Running, Pool Swimming, Openwater Swimming, Track Running, marathon, Treadmill, Vertical Running, Walking, Hiking, Trekking, Mountaineering, Climbing, Triathlon, Orienteering, Cross Training, Mountain Biking, Jump Rope, Indoor Rowing, Crosstrainer, Aerobics, Weight Training, Circuit Training, Stretching, Boxing, Yoga/Pilates, Cross-country Skiing, Alpine Skiing, Snowboarding, Tennis, Badminton, Outdoor Training, Indoor Training

Once you choose a given sport profile, you can then select to enable different features for it, such as following a structured workout, navigating a route/point of interest/bearing, as well as enabling certain targets, like a distance/calorie/pace/duration target.

It’ll also show you how much battery is remaining for that particular battery mode/configuration. Meaning if you get ready to start a workout and you realize you only have 2 hours of battery remaining, but need 4 hours, you can change to other battery modes, including performance, endurance, and power saving. These toggle various features on/off to eke out a bit more battery. I’ve generally found that the Suunto Run 2 overestimates how much battery it has. More on that in a second.

Anyway, in my case, I’ll pick a course for today: This straightforward trail run I did the other day that goes up a mountain and comes back down again:

I do wish I could see more details about the route before (or even after) I select it, such as rendering the actual map below it, rendering the elevation profile, etc. I create routes all the time for trail runs, and while I usually just know it’s the most recent one, it’d be handy to see exactly where this is – rather than just on an empty black screen.

In any case, we’ll head out and start running. You’ll see your normal data on the screen as you’ve configured in the settings.

You’ll also see your navigation and map fields as well. In my case you can see the upcoming route shown on the map, as well as distance remaining.

Then, you’ll also see an elevation profile of the route and where you stand in that situation:

If you go off-route, you’ll get a buzz that you’re off-route, and you can check the map page to see how you managed to screw up. There’s no automatic re-routing; you’ll just want to get yourself back to the course/route itself.

There’s also the new Energy Sense feature, which tells you how much juice it thinks you have left in the tank at that given intensity level, in distance. Suunto bills it to be used in a race-like situation, though there’s no need to do that. You could use it in everyday training as well.

In many ways, it’s got similarities to Garmin’s Stamina feature that’s been around for a number of years (and recently expanded to include both pace and heart rate stamina zones). Now, to be clear, I don’t really ever consult Garmin’s Stamina feature, as I don’t find it super useful.

That said, once you start using a Suunto and a Garmin side-by-side, you quickly realize the fatal flaw in Suunto’s implementation: It has nothing to do with energy (per the name EnergySense), but instead, Pace. It should be renamed “PaceSense”. That’s because the Suunto watch only looks at your pace, not your heart rate.

The easiest way to see this is to simply go down a hill (like above, showing a reduced 55%, when seconds before it was in the 90s). This isn’t because my heart rate is high (it’s not, it’s just 152bpm). But instead, because I’m going faster down a hill (4:06/km, or about 6:50/mi). Yet, when I’m going up a hill at a harder intensity like below (161bpm at 5:18/km or 8:32/mi), now I have somehow more Endurance (88%).

Again, I don’t really understand the point of calling this EnergySense, when it doesn’t look at energy at all (e.g., heart rate, or even calories). Instead, it’s purely looking at pacing, and even if you have a perfectly flat course, when looking at a longer event, like a marathon, how you pace energy-wise is just as much a function of heart rate as it is of pace. And further, to that extent, your ‘Endurance’ isn’t going to be a result of your pace, but of how hard your body is working to maintain that pace. I’m honestly baffled that this is as shortsighted as it is, even being marketed as a beta feature. Did nobody run with this anywhere with hills?

In any case, speaking of the data fields you’ve set up, these are configurable in the Suunto App, and you can customize them on a per-sport profile basis. I still wish I could just tweak existing core sport profiles, rather than having to create duplicates – but that’s just the way Suunto’s been for years.

Oh, speaking of things in the app, this is where you can download maps to the Suunto Run 2. As noted earlier, there is a 4GB and a 64GB model. The thing is, Suunto’s maps are divided up into very small regions, so you can pretty easily get away with just the 4GB model. Especially if you don’t do a ton of traveling. Realistically, I think Suunto could have just gotten away with a single 8GB or 16GB model and called it done. For example, while all of France would be 7GB, the region around Paris would only be 200MB (0.2GB).

In any event, once your workout is completed, you’ll see the details on the watch or in the Suunto App. For example, here on the Suunto App:

Beyond singular workouts, Suunto is also tracking your overall training load and recovery stats. Starting with training load, it’ll track that a few different ways, the first being TSS (Training Stress Score), in a widget you can see on the watch and the app.

It’ll show a bit of a breakdown of your sports:

Next, there’s CTL (Chronic Training Load), showing how this compares to recent history:

Within that, you’ll see your estimated VO2Max, as well as estimated 5K/10K/etc times. These all seemed a bit low to me (as in, both VO2Max was estimated low, and my current 5KM time seems about 1-2 mins slower than reality).

Then there’s TSB (Training Stress Balance), and it’s recommendation for me and my recent training load:

And then finally, there’s Recovery Time, looking at how you’re recovering from recent workouts. I do find the contrast between my TSB noted above and my recovery state noted below…well…notable. In theory, I should see some correlation here.

Meanwhile, within the Recovery area is where you’ll see your HRV values:

And all of this is also visible within the Suunto App as well:

Lastly, let’s quickly chat about battery during workouts. In my experience, this is falling short of my expectations. And seemingly, short of Suunto’s claims. Or more specifically, the watch’s own ability to predict battery life. In every case where I was under 20-25% battery, and the watch claimed one thing (e.g., 5-7 hours of battery remaining), the watch would run out of battery mid-activity, well below/before its own estimates.

Here’s the actual battery claims from Suunto’s site:

Here’s a simple battery example during a ride:

Start: 86%
End: 70%
Duration: 3 hours
Estimate: 5.45%/hour or 18.35hrs capacity
No navigation or external sensors enabled, multiband configuration AOD.

In this configuration, it got the 18 hours it’s rated for, but equally, every single time the estimates on the watch itself would be incorrect for what it actually burned. Meaning, I quickly came to not trust those estimates. If it said 5 hours remaining, you had at best 2-3 hours remaining.

But at least it did hit the estimates on their site. They just need to tweak whatever logic they’re using in the watch to correctly figure out battery burn.

Accuracy (GPS & Heart Rate):

In this section I’ll look at the accuracy of the new optical heart rate sensor, the upgraded GPS/GNSS chipset, as well as an occasional glance at the elevation profile, especially for mountain runs. These are compared to both a chest strap and other watch/band optical HR sensors.

First up we’ve got this mostly steady-state run, including an initial downhill portion for a few kilometers. Zero issues here, it looks good:

Next, we’ve got an interval run. This one got off to a rough start for whatever reason. But after that warm-up, things simmered down and it nailed all the intervals without issue.

Next, a trail run up/down a mountain. This had some variability in it, running with others (meaning, sometimes a bit lower HR’s). Still, overall this is pretty good. At some walking intensities, it was slightly mixed, but when actually running, it was mostly good enough.

Next, an indoor trainer ride. Here we can see it’s a bit wobbly in the first few minutes, but it gets the general trend right. After that it’s perfectly fine.

Whereas heading outside, looking at one of (many) outdoor rides, this one with lots of up and downs into the mountains, things are…shall we say, rough. Sure, it’s right for a good chunk at a time, but it’s wrong an awful lot – especially when I’m descending or at slightly lower intensities.

Switching over to the GPS side of things, starting off with a relatively straightforward run. Some occasional buildings and such, but nothing too complicated to begin:

Still, when I zoomed in, the Suunto was consistently the ‘odd duck,’ being just slightly offset from the others, even in basically open sky conditions:

Or here, where both COROS and Suunto are off in the road, playing in traffic. The Fenix 9 Pro has me properly on the sidewalk:

Next, a trail run into the mountains. Pretty straightforward up and down, but with lots of switchbacks:

Most of the trails were pretty good. Occasionally, a few quirks from different units being off a couple of meters, but nothing I was super concerned about.

Looking at the elevation profile, some slight disagreement there on the offset, but they all largely trended together. I don’t know the precise elevation of the ‘summit’ here since it’s sorta a forest service style road that just meanders along the mountains. Note: this was at/through sunset (over the course of two hours), so temps were shifting.

Next, looking at an outdoor road ride up into the mountains, from a GPS standpoint, things look perfectly fine at a high level:

And when I zoom in during some of the climbs, things are good here too:

That said, as I descend for some of these switchbacks at higher speeds, it’s a bit more Mario Kart than I’d like. I don’t tend to see this amount of variability here (into the bushes, wrong side of road, etc.), as I am from the Suunto Run 2.

Meanwhile, the elevation profile here is all good. No problems at all:

Finally, I’ve got GPS tracks from an openwater swim. Suffice to say, this was going well…till it wasn’t. No idea why it decided to slam through the side of a mountain when I didn’t. But maybe it just wanted some pool time instead. As for the swim buoy track, well…the watch fell into the water (flipped over on the strap). But you can pretty clearly see when it was above water and when it was under. Either way, the Suunto Run 2 was a hot mess here. MARQ was spot on.

Overall, I’d say that the GPS is probably perfectly acceptable for most land-based activities, but if you’re a bit nitpicky, you might not love some of the imperfections that I didn’t see on the higher-end Suunto Race 3S, or other competitive watches.

Meanwhile, for heart rate, this is a massive step up from the Suunto Run 1. While this sensor appears to struggle with outdoor cycling, for all other scenarios it’s been perfectly fine.

(Note: All of the charts in these accuracy portions were created using the DCR Analyzer tool. It allows you to compare power meters/trainers, heart rate, cadence, speed/pace, running power, GPS tracks, and plenty more. You can use it as well for your own gadget comparisons; more details here.)

Wrap-Up:

The Suunto Run 2 brings with it a lot of improvements that make it a compelling upgrade over the original Suunto Run 1. While that original watch was aimed at the budget end of the spectrum, with the jump to $349, Suunto is focusing a bit more on the premium end of that budget running watch realm. For those that want a much better display, offline maps, and a better optical heart rate sensor, it’ll probably be worth that $100 jump in price.

Where Suunto gets themselves into a little bit of a pickle is they’re essentially giving up the budget end of the spectrum to COROS (with the Pace 4 and Pace Pro) and Amazfit (and even Garmin with the Forerunner 70/Vivoactive 6, sans-maps). While I think Suunto can largely justify the $349 price point with premium materials/looks, I worry that, long term, not having any current-gen Suunto watch model below this price point takes Suunto out of the running for a portion of the population. Time will tell, though; I feel like time and history already told us how this ends about 4-5 years ago, the last time Suunto tried this pricing shift and had to retreat. Adding to the complication is that the Suunto Run 2 doesn’t run the same operating system as the rest of Suunto’s watches, making it less likely to get as many new feature updates (again, as history clearly told us with the Run 1).

Nonetheless, if you view the Suunto Run 2 through the lens of what it has today, especially around the looks/materials, it’s a good option that gets the job done. Said differently, if what you see in this review, feature-wise, makes you happy…go forth!

With that, thanks for reading!
