entry.title: Nitto in Fukushima, Japan: Multi-Generational Mingei 民芸 – John Watson
entry.content:
Visiting Nitto in Fukushima, Japan was a dream Shop Visit for John. After Bespoked Osaka and before the Circles Ridealive weekend, Cari and John, along with Paul from Slow Spin Society, embarked on a week-long road trip to visit Japan’s most iconic cycling manufacturers. Partnering with Sim Works, today The Radavist and Slow Spin Society are telling the tale of Nitto, with its multi-generational operations, stemming from the Japanese philosophy of Mingei…

Visiting Japanese Manufacturers

Over the next three days, we’ll be looking behind the scenes at Japanese manufacturing, focusing on three legendary component manufacturers: Nitto, MKS, and Honjo. These posts will be a collaborative effort between The Radavist and Slow Spin Society with me writing about the manufacturing process and Paul interviewing people from each company.

Going into this road trip, fresh off of my Bespoked Osaka coverage, I was already thinking of an angle for this series looking at my iPhone calendar app. We were visiting Nitto on Monday, Honjo the following day, and MKS on the third day. This has been a lifelong dream of mine but, like everything, I was nervous about both the brands’ expectations and my own.

Chatting with Sim Works brand director, Masashi Kimura, about Japanese manufacturing in a post-Bespoked conversation that lasted for hours, he said something that resonated with me. As someone who is an observer of manufacturing, there is a distinct approach present in Japan that differs from Western manufacturing, but I hadn’t put my finger on it quite yet.

Starting at Cost, Not Margin

Masashi summed it up beautifully, stating, “The uniqueness of Japanese manufacturing starts at the cost, not the margin.” He continued, “In the States and Europe, they start at the margin; say 33% for product, 33% for distributor, 33% for the shop.” The 30/30/30 split works, but it can put pressure on the manufacturer to come in at a certain number and cut corners in doing so. When you’re beholden to a 30% margin, your focus is misaligned.

“Japanese manufacturers start at cost. We add a reasonable margin to the cost total for the wholesale pricing. And we’re making more numbers in production, so it works out. Then, a dealer adds 30%, and that’s the final MSRP. In doing so, we know that a higher cost is going to equate to a better product. Toyota, another Japanese manufacturer, also does this. Products from brands like Nitto, MKS, and Honjo last for decades, just like Toyota. They live longer in the market.” Kimura-san explained.

Cost-based manufacturing allows for easy adjustment for material or labor costs, and when you’re making thousands of units, it guarantees a reasonable profit margin for the company and 30% for the dealer. Cost of steel on the rise? Just bake it into the cost. Luckily, Japanese steel production and costs have been fairly stable.

Money, however, isn’t the sole motivator for makers in Japan. Along with the concept of ikigai, 生きがい, or a “reason for being,” manufacturers are a part of a bigger picture concept known as mingei.

Mingei 民芸

In the mid-1920s, Yanagi Sōetsu conceptualized the philosophy of mingei in Japan together with ceramic artists. Mingei (民芸) roughly translates to “craft of the people” in English, and it was a conscious attempt to distinguish functional utensils from “higher” forms of fine art.

There’s a certain aspect of anonymity to the philosophy. Whereas fine art shines a light on the artist as much as the artwork, mingei focuses on the utensils’ anonymity, being crafted by a group of people. This philosophy embodies the craft of Nitto, the 103-year-old component manufacturer.

Nitto 日東 History

Founded on February 11, 1923, by Masae Yoshikawa, this historic Japanese manufacturer of high-end bicycle cockpit and utility components began in the Arakawa Ward, Tokyo, Japan. The name “Nitto” (日東) comes from “日” (sun) and “東” (east), reflecting Masae Yoshikawa’s wish for the company to always rise like the sun.

While Nitto rose in 1923, it shifted to manufacturing bicycle handlebars in 1925, and future products rolled out of the factory over the following decades. In 1973, the brand moved to a brand new factory located in Nihonmatsu, Fukushima Prefecture, where it still operates today.

Masae Yoshikawa’s grandchild, Akira Yoshikawa, currently serves as president, with Akira’s son, Takahisa Yoshikawa, acting as the managing director.

Rajio Taisō ラジオ体操

For almost 100 years, the Japanese government has run a morning radio program called Rajio Taisō every morning. Directed at the health of its citizens and workforce, most companies begin their day with the calisthenics program. Upon our arrival at the Fukushima factory, we were greeted with a display of Nitto workers stretching in unison that I’ll not soon forget.

As soon as the program ended, the workers took to their stations and began production. Akira and Takahisa introduced themselves, and we convened in a back office where one of its seatposts was undergoing ISO testing. Akira began explaining how in-house testing helps keep the brand on top of quality control, while informing future design decisions.

In-House ISO Testing

He pointed to the Nitto post, in some sort of pneumatic medieval torture device, noting that most seat posts use M6 hex screws but will almost always fail on this machine, which tests at an MTB level of certification. So they use M7 instead for more strength on their “all terrain” posts. A standard post undergoes 100,000 cycles, but Nitto runs this twice.

Outside the office, a similar device housed a 1980s steel mountain bike frame with Nitto racks. Weight is loaded in the panniers and on the rack surface itself. Running at 600 cycles per minute with a 5 kilo load, the racks jostled aboard the bike frame. This will run for 100,000 times, again, twice what the standard ISO testing requires. Nitto will run its ISO testing on handlebars often 4x the required cycles, just to see where they will break.

Remarking on how old the frame was, Akira noted: “That frame has been in the machine for 30 years.” An employee added, “We tried to use a modern frame, but it broke after a week, pointing to the split steerer tube and cracked chainstay on a frame from a popular steel bike manufacturer.” Everyone in our small group grimaced.

NJS 競輪 Manufacturer

While other bicycle component manufacturers often rely on military products to keep the lights on, Nitto is proud that it “has never made machines or tools for killing people” and instead is largely supported by its manufacturing contract of NJS-approved components for Keirin, or 競輪 racing.

Keirin is Japan’s national track bike racing circuit, supported by the Japanese government and bet on like horse racing by the Japanese people. The demands of Keirin are extreme, and manufacturing products with the coveted NJS stamp of approval requires thorough testing through the Nihon Jitensha Shinkōkai certification process.

Currently, Nitto manufactures stems, handlebars, and seatposts for Keirin, with its steel B123 handlebars owning 100% market dominance. It also does all of its own ISO testing in-house to ensure its products meet the demands of Keirin. Needless to say, NJS production keeps Nitto’s production busy.

Aging Facilities

My time at Nitto was a dream come true. As a lifelong bike geek and a fan of documenting makers, I’ve owned several of its products, so seeing where and how they were made, while being able to document them, scratched both sides of my creative brain. After a few hours of photographing the space, I couldn’t help but acknowledge something: Nitto’s facilities and its workforce had aged and were in need of rejuvenation.

The factory was built in 1973 and shows its age in what one might call, politely, a patina of oxidation. On our visit, it was raining, and various buckets were catching water as it leaked from the roof. Its steel façade was pitted and rusted, and in some areas the factory’s dark and moody demeanor wasn’t intentional; the light bulbs are too difficult to replace for the workers.

Aging Workforce

But the most apparent sign of age is the brand’s workforce, with 25% of the workforce being over 70 years of age. Nitto’s factory has 42 employees and 8 work in its Tokyo-based offices. The move to Fukushima in the early 70s was decided after a failed relocation attempt higher in the mountains outside of Tokyo due to too much snow and a desire from local farmers interested in factory work. 50 years later, hiring younger people has been very difficult.

Akira explained the difficulties Nitto faces when hiring young workers. “Young people don’t want to live in the countryside; they want to live in the city,” he noted, while pointing out that “countryside living is cheaper. You’ll have a better quality of life – you’ll be closer to nature, too.”

Currently, Nitto relies on graduates from the Tokyo College of Cycle Design, where it landed its newest framebuilder, Jamin, who is eager to modernize Nitto’s offerings. “Nitto’s biggest challenge right now is making frames,” Akira noted as we talked about manufacturing hurdles. Looking over the perfect welds, Jamin leaned in to say, “They are not perfect; these are samples.” They looked perfect to me.

Mountain Biking

When I asked Akira what his proudest moment was, he promptly replied with “Developing the Slingshot stem for mountain bikers in the US market.” The Slingshot proved to be a challenge for Nitto, who, after meeting with Tom Ritchey and Gary Fisher, knew the mountain bike market was going to explode.

“Meeting Tom Ritchey and Gary Fisher led to Nitto making MTB components, and still to this day, it was our biggest challenge at Nitto. Everything was new to us. We had to start from scratch, from the materials to the designs; we’d never done anything like this before.”

When Tom visited Nitto in the late 1980s, he taught this woman, Mrs. Noriko Yabashi, to braze. She uses half as much filler as the other brazers on staff and holds her torch the same way Tom does.

Tom Ritchey’s Bullmoose design was time-intensive, and he was always looking for ways to offload intense workflows like building Bullmoose bars. After a handlebar slipped while Tom was racing Repack in 1978, he designed the Bullmoose. And by late 1980, Nitto was already manufacturing fillet-brazed Bullmoose bars for Ritchey.

In 1983, the Nitto-designed and built Slingshot stem debuted on Specialized mountain bikes. The same year Shimano launched its Deore “Deer Head,” the brand’s first MTB groupset.

Lifelong Legacy

Spending the day with Akira and Takahisa, the father and son represent a modern trope: an experienced elder running the business while an enthusiastic younger person waits to take over the reins. Akira speaks of Nitto’s founder, his grandmother Masae Yoshikawa, with great honor, and you can feel his pride in the company.

Akira has designed, engineered, and marketed a number of legacy products during his time running the company. When I asked who designed and engineered Nitto’s new products, he replied simply, “I do it all.” At 78 years old, he’s still got a pep in his step and was constantly tapping on his watch during our tour as we pried into the various stages of manufacturing with our cameras.

Takahisa, 46, is still learning under his father, and he has big shoes to fill. He hopes to take the company into the future and cut down on backorders and long lead times. Currently, Nitto’s manufacturing is months out, and that’s Takahisa’s number one priority. On top of Nitto’s own line, they also make components for a dozen other third-party companies, including Sim Works.

Shige, in 2016, at the SimWorks offices in Nagoya

Sim Works

Tanaka-san from Circles launched Sim Works in 2009, as an attempt to inject fresh designs into Nitto’s catalog. Currently, the best-selling bar in Nitto history remains its B123 bar, the professional Keirin racing, NJS-approved handlebar. Sim Works’ first collaboration handlebar with Nitto was the John B Bar, which was the B123 shape, updated for a 31.8 clamp.

Sim Works took the legacy of Nitto’s bars and updated them with new specs, rolling out seven of its own handlebar models. Nitto also makes Sim Works stems, spacers, racks, and Sim Drops bar ends.

The Radavist x Slow Spin Society

As The Radavist celebrates its 20th anniversary of covering cycling communities, we wanted to partner with the next generation of cycling media on a lifelong dream trip of mine. We’ve featured Paul from Slow Spin Society on the website before. As a wearer of many hats – Paul also works for Sim Works as its Euro branch and was gracious enough to act as our Japanese translator during the trip – Paul is always balancing his job at Sim Works with Slow Spin. As we were chatting about what a possible collaboration would look like, we landed on the concept of storytelling and interviews.

Paul wanted to focus on interviewing people at Nitto, mostly the younger people, about how they got involved in working in manufacturing at Nitto. Fukushima, where Nitto is based, is very rural and about a three-hour drive north from Tokyo in the mountains. Being a young person usually means you want to be in a city, experiencing all the excitement of an urban environment, so what drove these young people to give up the city life for rural work in manufacturing?

Roll on over to Slow Spin Society to find out!

The Radavist x Sim Works x Nitto

We’ve got a bunch of fun products on the way, collaborating with various makers within The Radavist brand ecosystem. Here’s a teaser of what we cooked up with our friends at Sim Works and Nitto!

The Radavist thanks Sim Works for supporting our independent Reportage here!

The post Nitto in Fukushima, Japan: Multi-Generational Mingei 民芸 appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: Scottish Mixtape Pt. 2 // Cairngorm Traverse
entry.content:
A self-supported mission to link 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks in Scotland.

In partnership with Arc’teryx, Moots Cycles, Tailfin, and Skratch Labs.

Words by KYLE RICHARDSON · Photos by THOMAS WOODSON, KYLE RICHARDSON

TRACK 2:  Cairngorm Traverse

Thomas and I wake to the pitter-patter of rain against the metal roof of the Ben Nevis luxury inn. We are happy to get a good night's rest and sleep inside, but the rain outside challenges our mood and stokes. I like to prescribe to coffee and then take on the day. No use formulating outcomes or stressors on the day till you're fully awake and alert. We are treated downstairs to a classic Scottish breakfast fare and some striking characters. Thomas and I don’t say much to each other this morning. Our crown jewel for this project — Tower Ridge on Ben Nevis stands mysteriously in the clouds, and the rain is picking up.

In these moments, I always wonder what good it does to check in with the weather. It is what it is, right? On this day, the weather gods were against us. Torrential rain, 40- 50 mph winds, and sub-freezing temps. I think we were both wondering if heading up into the cirque was even possible on a day like this, not to mention all the riding we needed to do. Thomas was also starting to show some signs of the previous wet and cold days, developing a minor cold. Still, we don’t speak about the obvious objective and weather challenge.

Dressed and ready for the day, we head down to the hotel's bike storage and start assembling and tinkering with our rigs for the day. There is a door to the outside there that is slightly cracked. I can hear the rain smashing against the door in waves, and gusts of wind occasionally breach this door and rush in. It’s at this point that we start to look at a more detailed forecast. Grim. At this point, it just seems a bit foolish and dumb to force this technical ridge in these conditions. Could we hike up the standard hikers route and summit Ben Nevis? Yes, for sure. That being said, our inspiration lacked for this alternative. So as the rain continued to fall, we biked away from Fort William with no peak.

On trips like this, the timeline doesn’t allow for you to wait on good weather or hunker down. The rest of the mixtape was waiting. I have a love-hate relationship with cruxes on a trip like this. You need to make a decision and get on with it. No point in sulking or being bummed about your current state. I told Thomas we would be back for it someday, and I’m sure he was grateful to focus on the bike for today and his body preservation. Certainly, going up into the Ben with those temperatures and winds would have only sent his body plummeting (and start my downfall too!). Which is totally fair; we have to compromise and make the best of our current situation. As you will find out in the coming paragraphs, we had a wonderful day as we started our traverse of the Cairngorms.

Leaving Fort William on Day 4, the rain only continues. This helps validate our decision. As every day prior, we are quickly into the rough stuff and off-piste trails. As we leave the highlands and start heading East, we assume that maybe today's riding will be slightly less vert-intensive. Only time will tell. An hour into the ride, the skies really open up. The torrential rain meets us a mile or so outside of the tiny village of Spean Bridge. The type of rain you can’t really ride in. Feels proper sketchy. Your first reaction under these conditions is to find shelter. We spot the first cafe and pull in. The sound of rush-hour traffic plowing through pooled-up water on the road keeps us alert. Inside the cafe, we see fellow cyclists and motorists looking soggy and dreary. This is all just part of the unexpected adventure. Going with the twists and turns of the day is what makes an outing rich and rewarding. We both order a big stack of pancakes and tea. Calories usually help keep the good vibes going. Plus, Thomas and I keep a healthy banter going that usually keeps the good times flowing.

Leaving Spean Bridge, we were treated to a brief moment of truly blue skies and sunshine, a first of the trip. As we transitioned from the Highlands and started riding East, we began to ride favorable winds, and the terrain started to shift. As we traversed many a farm field, we began to get a taste of the sneaky gnarly tracks that lie in the rolling hills between the big mountains. The riding here was lush and interesting. We chased sheep around corners and swooped down into grassy fields. To me, this style of riding is quintessential Scotland. Some low country, hard-to-read and faint tracks that really keep you guessing where you are going. We rode by some ancient ruins and crossed a few technical creeks. The riding here is playful and slow. Our bikes are filthy and covered in muck, yet Thomas and I forget about our morning sorrow and worries. We climb beautiful singletrack through a purple haze of heather and twist our way into new zones.

The rain and swirling clouds pick up as we climb towards Lochan na h-Earba. The exposure and grandeur of this place set in. The clouds shift to a darker tone, and Thomas and I space out. We are sandwiched between some peaks, but the atmosphere feels desolate and isolated. No trees or anything for shelter. The rain worsens. I start smashing pedals in hopes of crossing the few miles of this loch to a set of woods on the other side. The double-track here is lined with unavoidable mud and puddles. Franz Ferdinand jamming in my ears, the pedals turn over, and the legs feel good. I look back behind me for the flash of Thomas’s sinewave beacon, letting me know he is on his way. We both reach the safety of the woods in a bit of a blur. The cold has really set in, and Thomas and I comment on how things are getting quite serious. Both soaked to the bone, we know this isn’t a place we can really hang out.

After the wave of storms rolled through, we were rewarded with tailwinds and sunshine. Crossing castles and more lochs, our sights were set on the village of Kingussie. It felt good to stomp out some tarmac and make decent time to our final stop for the day. My classic memory of this day is rolling up on a pair of Highland coos. I will never forget their eyes slowly closing and their hair blowing in the wind. Symbolic of the day we had. Thomas and I were ready for our usual fish n chips entree and then sleep.

Day 5, our routine is starting to find its Scottish rhythm. Having ridden here in 2022, I can confidently say that the riding around Cairngorm National Park is world-class. The network of trails and gravel roads between the River Spey and CNP is amazing. You could spend a couple of weeks exploring and setting a home base in Kingussie or Aviemore. Definitely something I would consider doing sometime in the future. Diving bombing single track and pine needle tracks through quaint neighborhoods had Thomas and me stoked for this new shift in terrain and topography. Skies also looked calm and mostly favorable all day, a real Scottish treat! We stopped to admire ancient castles and babbling brooks. Our chatter flowing and bike cranks spinning.

Rolling into Glenmore National Nature Preserve at the bottom of Cairngorm National Park feels distinctly different than the Highlands. This side of the country feels more arid and dry. There are clusters of woods and trees that make this area feel more like Colorado. We can see the peaks forming above us, their alpine tundra looking distinctly beige and purple. On this day, we were going to be meeting up with a local friend and professional photographer, Johnny Cook. Thomas and I met Johnny at the Kendal Mountain film festival in 2021. We instantly hit it off with Johnny, and we both had just made a friend for life. It was extra special to reunite with him on this trip and have him show us our second ridge of the trip: Fiacaill Ridge.

From Glenmore, it was a roughly 1,000ft climb up to the Cairngorm Mountain and ski hill, our staging zone to start running. I reveled in the 1k tarmac climb, reminiscent of an alpine switchbacked road that we are both familiar with back home. The sun was shining brightly; I took my shirt off for the first time all trip. With the energy from the sun and our excitement to start running, we smashed our way up this climb. The juxtaposition of going from more isolated terrain to a more touristy spot is always a shock, but I have grown used to this dynamic over the many trips in my career. I just embrace the adventure and enjoy the side banter with random folks. We are on our own quest, and it's best not to get overwhelmed by much and stay rock steady.

As Thomas and I were transitioning from cycling shoes to running shoes, our friend Johnny appeared. Our morale was great, but when you see a friend after a long hiatus, our mood and vibe totally skyrocketed. Thomas and I were eager to catch up with Johnny and have him show us one of his local alpine romps. As we started to run, the wind said hello. Okay, maybe it was more of a raging hello! The wind couldn’t dampen our spirits as we started to travel cross-country towards Fiacaill ridge. From far away, this ridge looked unassuming and chill. Up close, the ridge became uniquely geometric and blocky. The granite scrambling here was super unique, and the positioning above the corries (bowl- or amphitheater-shaped hollows carved into the side of mountains by glacial erosion during past ice ages) was dramatic and exposed. The wind tried to blow us off the ridge, but it just added an alpine feeling to it all. Fall colors were beginning to show in the tundra, and the views were panoramic and otherworldly. Johnny does a lot of skiing and works in the ski industry, and he was pointing out all the couloirs and interesting lines. As we ran back down into the corrie, we spotted climbers on more vertical terrain. A subtle reminder for me to come back and do more exploring here. It's always inspiring to get out with a local and really absorb the flavor of a zone.

Back on the bikes, it was another transition and then a mach speed rip back down Cairngorm mountain road to Glenmore. On our way down, we could see the devastation from wildfires that have consumed and burned a lot of the hills surrounding where we were running. From my research online, “The blaze burned approximately 25 square kilometres (around 3,500 football pitches or 2,500 hectares) of rare Caledonian forest, Scots pine, and moorland on July 24th, 2026, prompting the evacuation of over 700 people from areas including Glenmore and Nethy Bridge. Over 500 firefighters, helicopters, and partner agencies fought the blaze.” From what I recall, the embers seep deep into the soil and burn for a while, making it super hard to control and mitigate. Seeing the burned hillsides is sobering and also reminds us of the very similar fire reality we live with back home. Okay, time to keep rolling.

Back down in Glenmore, Thomas and I are ready for some calories. Johnny meets us at the Pine Martin, a ski après-style bar for our post-run hang. We sat there and chatted for a while, eating some delicious curry, enjoying a pint of something light and refreshing. Thomas and I didn’t look at the clock or feel rushed. This was part of our adventure, and our agenda was being created in real time. Soaking up the good times together, not knowing when our paths would cross with Johnny again. When it was time to part ways, Johnny gave us a celebratory sip of a really nice whiskey. As we wet our palates with something way too nice and expensive for Thomas and I ever to own, the sweetness of orchard fruits, baking spices, and smoke dance on our tongues. We say farewell to our Scottish friend and hop back onto the bikes.

Due to the fires I mentioned above, our original plan to go up and over Ryvoan Pass is thwarted by wildfire closures. Moments like this always happen on bikepacking trips, so it's best to just stay calm and not stress about a potential detour or going a new way. In all honesty, I was excited to ride something new; I had done Ryvoan Pass before in 2022. It's really, really cool, but what we ended up doing was equally cool and unique. It was getting to be late afternoon, and Thomas and I were strategizing how far we could make it that evening. As we shredded down some loamy forested tracks, we set our sights on the village of Nethy Bridge; from there we would make our dinner plans and riding goal for the rest of the evening. I always really enjoy getting back on the bike after running. Feels like you end up covering so much ground when using multiple modes of transportation.

In Nethy Bridge, we were coming up on 5 pm. We dashed into a quaint convenience store in an otherwise tiny and quiet town. Inside, it was the usual grab for something salty and sweet. A sip of sugar and chips... oh wait, they call these things crisps. After the pitstop, we got back on track, linking our tracks to the fire detour. The afternoon and early evening were unfolding in good fortune, and hopping between villages kept us psyched and spontaneous. As the purple sky began to meet the purple heather-lined two-track, our stopping point for the evening came into focus: Tomintoul. The segment from Nethy to Tomintoul was a wonderful all-terrain delight. Premier Cairngorm cycling, a bit of an adventure navigating a twisting river, and a dash of hiking. An hour of sunset spinning brought us to a tarmac climb up to our final destination of the day.

Tomintoul felt a bit mysterious and quaint. Less than 800 people call this place home, and only a few spots of sustenance are available. The one place with lights on was the local hotel and Indian food joint. Well, I know what we are having for dinner. What seemed maybe slightly suspect ended up turning into a fine evening of calories. Maybe slightly chaotic for our tired bodies, but it was our only option. After dinner, it was a few-minute spin towards the park above town to find a spot to camp. Thomas and I set up our tarp, donned the midge nets, flicked our red lights on, and tucked into our bivy. A solid day out traversing one of Scotland’s wonderful landscapes!

Stay tuned for Track 3: the Pictish Trail.

In partnership with Arc’teryx, Moots, Tailfin, & Skratch Labs

entry.title: Scottish Mixtape Pt. 1
entry.content:
A self-supported mission to link 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks in Scotland.

In partnership with Arc’teryx, Moots Cycles, Tailfin, and Skratch Labs.

Words by KYLE RICHARDSON · Photos by THOMAS WOODSON, KYLE RICHARDSON


Exploring a place by bicycle works its way deep into your soul. Once you’ve traveled this way, it becomes your beacon and north star for how you want to explore the world. Taking in the landscape pedal stroke by pedal stroke, you start to learn the fabric of a place. Feeling the weather and terrain isn’t just one aspect of the outing; it becomes your identity and sole purpose for moving. The reward for moving your body all day through a place is knowledge and wisdom, things you can apply towards future trips and life in general.

Scotland is world-renowned for its rugged and beautiful landscape. Its people are hardened by the weather, but their desire for exploration and adventure in the hills is very much alive. There is a deep mystery about this place that is intriguing to me. The craggy tracks and alpine roads cutting through magnificent mountains planted a seed of curiosity. What would it be like to travel through this place simply? On bike and on foot, carving our way through this ancient country. Thus the Scottish Mixtape was born — a fully self-supported mission to link up 3 classic cycling routes and 3 peaks. From Scotland’s capital, Edinburgh, we traveled over the famous highlands, traversed the Cairngorms, and then down the Pictish trail, creating a big, diverse loop.

For the purposes of organization and to showcase this route, I will break the mixtape into 3 separate tracks, each corresponding to the 3 cycling routes we explored.

Filmmaker and photographer Thomas Woodson was alongside me for this Scottish adventure. This wouldn’t be a bike blog without digging into the bikes, and I will touch on setups a bit throughout. Thomas was riding his Moots MXC, and I was on the new Moots Womble, both bikes equipped with front forks and dropper posts for maximum shredding and efficiency. As always, feel free to drop a comment or email if you have more specific questions about setups, and I will include full bike check photos at the bottom. Sit back, grab a tea or a pint, and listen to the play-by-play from the Scottish Mixtape.

   

Track 1: Into the Highlands

Our bodies are stiﬀ and creaky. It’s really 3 am Colorado time as we depart our flight into Scotland's capital, Edinburgh. I think the biggest stressor for a trip like this surrounds traveling with a bike. This topic alone deserves its own blog and write-up. Needless to say, our bikes made it, and soon enough we were building our extremely capable mountain rigs in the crowded airport arrival terminal. Thomas must have snuck some coﬀee in somewhere, because by the time I was getting organized, he was ready to roll. Dang, time to get with it! I was distracted by the bright lights and stream of people passing by.

Handlebars, wheels — straighten it up - wait, tinker again, fix. Okay, is this right? Thomas! “I need help!” Good thing we make a great team. I have been adventuring with Thomas for a decade now. We have traveled to many countries together and mesh super well. Finding a partner that complements you and brings out your best self is a wonderful thing. Outside of being strong in the mountains and competent on technical terrain, Thomas is a logistical wizard and has an everlasting attitude to get things done no matter the circumstances. These are instrumental attributes on a trip with so much uncertainty and the unknown. We have a tight timeline. We need to be back in Edinburgh in 8 days to then catch our flight back to Colorado the following day. Okay, enough of this, time to hit the road!

Moots all built up at Edinburgh International Airport

In classic Scottish style, as we roll away from the hustle and bustle of the airport, the skies open up. The wind picks up in a fury, and we put on our rain gear. This would be the first of a long trip- a long process of navigating and handling the weather. Under my hood and amidst the rain, I crack a smile and let out a giddy laugh. This is why we are here. To experience the full spectrum of conditions and emotions of traveling through a new place. Our first day of riding would almost exclusively be on canal and bike paths; what a treat! One of my goals for this trip was to get oﬀ the main roads and into the magic of a place. And by magic, I mean all the sneaky little roads that take you to the heart of place rather than around it. As we worked our way towards Callander, we got to experience the canal boats and farm lifestyle that make up this part of the country. Riding through tunnels and lush forest, we sneak glances at quaint villages and ancient cobblestone paths. At one point during another wave of rain, we pass by a school. It was clearly lunch break, and all the teens were out walking towards their favorite hangouts. In the pouring rain, we noticed that no one was wearing raincoats. Huh. Are we doing this wrong? Rain and being wet is a way of life in Scotland; not much fuss about the weather. Go do your thing and get on with it!

By this point in the day, we had linked into the famous GBDURO (Great Britain Divide), a cycling route that covers the entire length of Great Britain. We would use this route to help carry us North. We traversed our first fields of Scottish livestock and enjoyed varied riding on all types of surfaces. Our bodies still on Colorado time, we visualized and dreamed about our first proper. Bopping and weaving around more farms, we could see our first stopping point of the night in Callander. A beautiful little village right on the edge of the highlands. We had booked a night at the Crown Inn, knowing that a real night's sleep in a bed would help set us up for a successful trip. Thomas and I love to play games, but when it comes to bikepacking, we generally adhere to a few basic rules and let the rest go with the flow. We see what the land and weather give us. This trip wasn’t about how hard and brutal can we make things; it's about the full-body and mind immersion into a landscape. We have our notepads out and want to learn and grow from this place. Students of the world traveling by bike.

One of the beautiful things about Scotland is how popular and welcoming the people are to bikes. People tour here on bikes, and it's not a new thing. You won’t get any strange or random looks. You will get chirps of encouragement and curiosity. The hotel staﬀ and BnB hosts will welcome your dirty bikes and bike shoes and have a safe place to store that stuﬀ, either in your room or a dedicated indoor bike shelter. I think this way of life helps cut the tension and edge that one can have while traveling in a new place, especially when your body is depleted after a hard day of pedaling. After sorting ourselves in our lodging, we slipped on our running shoes and headed out to the streets of Callander for some fish and chips. Thomas and I exchanged stories from the day as the native language and tongue echoed through the dining hall. Mates bantered about golf and what pint to drink next; we quietly observed our surroundings as our new reality for the next week set in. With our bellies full, we enjoyed some sunset light while strolling down the River Teith. It was a hectic and full-on first day in Scotland. Time to dry out our clothes and get some rest.

Moots arriving in Callander Day 1


Alarms chirping at 5:45 am, the hot water kettle starts bubbling, and we tear open our instant craft coﬀee from Idle Hands Roasting. The little morning treat that brought us energy and psyche every day. Thanks to Peter Jones for the full trip supply! Skies were grey and overcast, with mild temps. After hunting down some classic Scottish pastries and goodies down the street, it was time to set oﬀ. Our day would start oﬀ following the GBDURO to the small town of Killin, before branching oﬀ towards the mega-classic West Highland Way — (Scotland’s premier long-distance walking route, stretching 96 miles (154 km) from Milngavie (just north of Glasgow) to Fort William in the Scottish Highlands).

A misty collection of clouds started to form as we made our way north along bike paths, contouring lochs and villages. It felt special and unique to be on such fantastic bike infrastructure, tucked away in the woods. After a couple of hours of spinning, we reached a tiny pass, and the skies started to open up. As we stopped, we came to our first interaction with the famous Scottish midges. Tiny microscopic flies, coordinating in unison and buzzing towards their next victim. I could feel their wrath as we stopped to put on our rain jackets and pants. Maybe it's better if it's raining? At least then the midges subside. More to come on that later. As we buzzed down to the town of Killin, we had our first proper feeling of being completely saturated with water. My giddy smile and laugh from the day before started to flatten.

Thomas Woodson on film above Loch Lyon


In the town of Killin, we rushed towards the first cafe in sight. Was this a storm that would pass, or something that was hugging the mountains and would be around all day? Only time would tell. No use looking a weather app or forecast, it was unreliable and inaccurate. In classic Scottish style, we ordered a few breakfast teas and some toasties (basically a grilled cheese with a sweet chutney). Thomas and I slipped out of our wet cycling shoes and air-dried our feet discreetly under our table. As we were eating, a pair of cyclists showed up in similar fashion. Good reminder that this is totally normal and what we were doing wasn’t anything extraordinary. They were from Poland on a similar grand adventure (albeit on gravel bikes) out taking in the wonderful countryside.

For us, it is always encouraging and enjoyable to chat with folks along the way and feed oﬀ the energy of a place. Our new Polish cyclist friends seemed to have a determined edge, and we ended up sharing a similar route for a few miles. As we hit some steep grades, I think they started to grow jealous of our mountain bikes and gearing. As we soft-pedaled up our first real mountain pass, I was grateful for our setups and the terrain we were about to encounter. While never truly quitting, the rain turned more into a soft mist, which is far more favorable than a straight downpour. Our views were limited at the top of this pass, but I could tell we were on the cusp of getting into the good stuﬀ. Remote, wild, and properly in the highlands.

As we traveled around the south side of Loch Lyon, we rode premier double track. The kind of tracks I dreamed about, my inspiration for putting this whole trip together. Riding the right bikes, with the right person, everything was falling into place. Steep grassy hillsides, sheep, Highland Coos, countless river crossings- this section really had it all. Quintessential Scottish riding. Beams of sun would occasionally pop out and highlight a magnificent hillside. My giddy smile and laugh returned. Thomas was on the same page, and we hooted and hollered around each bend. Finally able to let loose and ride our mountain rigs with some flair. Being out in the wild, tucked in the mountains, felt like being home in Colorado. This is where Thomas and I thrive. At the end of this double track segment, we started a long downhill towards Kinglass Cottage and the West Highland Way. It was pretty obvious once we were on the WHW, as we immediately started passing thru-hikers. As we traversed the hillside, we set our sights on our next pitstop: Bridge of Orchy.

In classic logistical Thomas style, he had found a semi-secret stop for dinner, just a ways past Bridge of Orchy. He had made a call during lunch to set up a dinner reservation. We planned to stop in Orchy, grab a pint, then roll down the road for dinner plans. After dinner, we would continue on the WHW and find camp somewhere. I think trips like this require you to act fast and think on your toes. No one decision is ever that hyper critical, but make a decision and then go with it. I think having a good partner helps this process. Sometimes it's easy to get lured into a resupply or waste time. Finding the balance between riding the flow and making calculated decisions is the game. On this Day 2, we played our cards right and were rewarded with a fantastic day of quality and diverse riding. At dinner, we enjoyed one of our best meals. Sometimes best on a trip like this equals quantity, but at this fine establishment, we were treated with massive portions and delicious food. We even had a first tasting of some local whiskey. Felt rude not to sample!

Throughout the day, we had heard rumbles of evening and overnight torrential rain. Let me skip to the chase. Yup, that happened. We ended up riding maybe 3 miles to one of the few clusters of dense trees in the area. All of the Highlands is barren due to centuries of deforestation. Which means finding a good bivy site that is protected is tough. I think most locals would have laughed at our sleep setup, but I think I still stand behind it. Between us, we shared a flat tarp and ground sheet. Individually, we each had sleeping pads, bags, and bug nets. It appeared most people camped out in the open with proper enclosed tents. Hmmm. So we were oﬀ into the dense woods and mossy floor for a tucked-away bivy. I like feeling cozy even if it has its downsides. An exposed tent out in the open just feels wrong, especially on a night forecasting torrential rain and high winds.

Sleep was on and oﬀ. Out of the whole trip, this was one of the harder moments. The rain was persistent and loud against the Dyneema tarp. I also don’t want to gloss over the fact that just a couple of hours earlier, I was being eaten alive by midges. It was the Scottish gods (and maybe Thomas) seeking sweet revenge on my trip and idea. Making sure you never walk away unscathed, gathering a few lessons to learn along the way. In some aspects, the heavy rain eased my tension and pain. As we would come to find out later on Day 3, which proved to be one of the grandest and hardest day yet. Despite the rough night, we still had the energy and stoke to keep pushing. Waking up in the mist, Thomas and I remarked back and forth how intense that was.

morning wakeup ritual with Idle Hands Instant coﬀee


Moots on the West Highland Way


Awake and caﬀeinated by morning cold brew in a running soft flask, a few bites of something go into the body (not to mention the bites I was nursing on my body). We pack our wet bikes and gear inside fully waterproof Tailfin bike bags, proving their weight in gold. For me, I think it was seeing the sun that morning. It provided me the internal stoke and confidence to complete this trip. The light and scenery were otherworldly and magical. Entering the Glencoe valley was what dreams are made of. Giant peaks and ridges in all directions. We stopped for breakfast at one of the few ski resorts in Scotland, the famous Glencoe Hill. Full Scottish breakfast and coﬀee for me, please. The midge welts on my face and arms burned and itched. This felt like a warm trap to stay here all day, and I’m glad we were both motivated and stoked to keep the pace up.

Back on the bikes, feeling small. Coming around the corner, seeing Buachaille Etive Mòr (Stob Dearg) is a top 3 moment of the trip for me. This perfect pyramid, erupting out of the earth, was visually too perfect. How could something like this even exist? It was full steam ahead to our next objective, our first scramble of the trip, Curved Ridge. I first heard about this route when I saw an iconic photo of Kilian Jornet Burgada scrambling up Curved Ridge during his 2017 win at Glen Coe Skyline. Ever since then, it’s been on my tick list. One of the anchors of this project was to link 3 technically interesting running and scrambling routes in Scotland. Curved Ridge proved to be indeed a mega classic. As Thomas and I approached this massive pyramid of a peak, we could see a series of twisting ridges jutting up towards the summit. Clouds were swirling and rays of sun stabbed through the sky. It was now or never. As we approached the trailhead, the scale of this mountain started to introduce itself. We stashed our bikes against a climbing school hut, switched into our running kit, and set oﬀ. I’m always full of stoke and excitement when switching to running oﬀ the bike. The legs feel wonderful with a new motion, fresh to carry us up the peak.

Starting up the iconic Curved Ridge


Curved Ridge was everything you could ask for. Exposed, steep, airy, with wonderfully solid rock. As we ascended higher and higher into the clouds, the moves got more interesting. Culminating in a steep crux with plentiful holds and jams, Thomas and I motored our way up this aesthetic feature as a light mist set in. The view of the valley floor as we climbed up seemed mystically low and far away. As we reached the summit, the perspective we were rewarded with was hard to describe. That sweet satisfaction after biking for 2.5 days and lots of hills; the trip and vision were all coming together. After a few summit photos, the clouds swallowed us up, and the wind said hello. Okay, time to get oﬀ this thing! Running back down was a techy treat, practicing some quick footwork to navigate many a slippery rock and chunky talus. When it was all said and done, despite feeling like a full day's adventure, we were back at the bikes in 2 hours. Plenty more time for adventure and progression in the day.

Back into bike shoes, we grabbed our rigs and crossed the road. Next up was the most infamous section of the West Highland Way: Devils Staircase. From the summit of Stob Dearg, we could see the Staircase. Coming from Colorado, Thomas and I are accustomed to hike-a-bike (HAB). Some of our favorite local rides include HAB. I’m on record saying multiple times that all good adventure rides need to have some HAB. Despite the hype, Devils Staircase made us feel at home. No big deal really, maybe 30 minutes of pushing at the most? Come on! That is light work for us, even after a 2-hour run. The thing that challenged us really in this section was the weather. It was raining pretty hard for the rest of our day. Towards the bottom of the Staircase, Thomas had a rear tire slash while riding over one of the many water bars that line this climb. If my memory is correct, this was the only bike mechanical issue we encountered all trip. One of the benefits of doing a trip like this with a partner is that bike mechanicals and problems are so much easier to solve as a team, especially when the weather is bad. Couple plugs, add some air, back on the trail!

We made fun work of that climb, hiking with our heavy rigs past many thru-hikers. Showing them who is boss. At the top of the pass, we then proceeded to encounter our gnarliest true MTB terrain of the whole trip. Rowdy riding and chunky terrain. It was a brake-squealing, arm-pumping descent down to Kinlochleven. We were reminded once again that our bike choice was 10/10. I was thinking to myself that if I had been on my fully rigid ESC, I would have walked that entire descent. The trip would have been nearly impossible and stupid on that bike. Hardtail mountain bikes for the win!

In Kinlochleven, Thomas and I hit the local grocery store for some orange soda and a bag of chips. Something on the lighter side to fuel us over the next pass to Fort William. In some ways, I think we both thought our day was close to ending; little did we know we had some brutal climbing and weather to contest with. Oh, and some really rough and muddy tracks. The day was starting to add up. Waking up in our wet bivy spot just some hours earlier felt like a lifetime ago. Eventually we made our way up a steep mixed-surface climb and started a long gradual service road to a small pass that gave way towards Fort William. The riding here was tough and tedious. Our progress slowed, and our motivation waned. As we battled into a headwind, we eventually hit our last steep climb before ripping down to Fort William. Town was a bit of a blur for both of us. I remember stopping at a bike shop, and Thomas pleaded for a hose. Our bikes were filthy and covered in all types of mud and manure. The rain started and stopped. Thomas had booked us luxurious accommodations down the road that included a full sauna/steam situation. Felt like we had earned that, and with how the weather was acting and our current location, sleeping inside felt like a no-brainer. When I think back to planning and dreaming up this trip, it was a day like this that really lit the spark. Interesting riding, run/scramble up an incredible peak, get back on the bike and do it all again. It was only the night of Day 3; Thomas and I were getting our full value experience I was grateful for how it was panning out.

Stay tuned for Track 2: Cairngorm Traverse

Moots Womble (Kyle)


Moots MXC (Thomas)

entry.title: The complete history of the Cannondale CAAD
entry.content:
Cyclist
The complete history of the Cannondale CAAD

There aren’t many bikes that can lay equal claim to the titles ‘race bike’, ‘dream bike’ and ‘first bike’, but Cannondale’s CAAD is one. Perhaps not all of those titles all of the time, but when you can trace a design’s roots back over 40 years, it’s unsurprising that the model has gone on quite a journey.

The innovation started even before CAAD was CAAD. Back in 1983 Cannondale’s head of R&D asked his team how they could make bike frames faster.

‘Traditional frame manufacturing techniques required a lot of fixturing and tooling,’ says Chris Dodman, Cannondale’s advanced projects engineer. ‘So the guys figured that if they could get rid of the need for custom tooling, we could develop and iterate much faster.’

Todd Patterson, one of Cannondale’s first and most influential employees, was tasked with providing a solution.

‘Todd is incredible, a true polymath,’ says Dodman. ‘He came back with a method involving lasers and computer software, which was pretty wild back then. Computer aided design, or CAD, created trajectories for lasers to cut the tubes. This meant that all it took to swap between geometries was a change in programming. We could produce the tubeset for an XS mountain bike and then a 66cm custom geometry road frame one after the other on the same workstation, with maybe about a two-minute changeover. We called it tab and slot manufacturing. It was a huge investment but so revolutionary that we patented Todd’s invention and it drove our aluminium bike production all the way up to CAAD 9 in 2007.’

But we’re getting ahead of ourselves.

Back to the beginning

The first aluminium frame that the manufacturer made using the CAAD blueprint was the ST500 in 1983.

‘Compared to steel bikes at the time, the ST500’s tubes were comically oversized,’ says Dodman of a bike that was designed for road touring rather than racing. ‘But we knew oversized aluminium was stiffer and lighter than steel and titanium at the time.’

The formula proved a successful one and the diversification began. The road performance category really kicked off in 1986 when Cannondale produced the 3.0 Series, so named because the frames weighed 3lb (about 1,300g), which was uniquely light at the time.

‘In 1991 we introduced the 2.8 Series [1,270g for the frame] and the manufacturing started to get really refined,’ says Dodman. ‘Those frames had the first power pyramid, conical taper-butted down tube, meaning it had a bottom bracket diameter of about 50mm at 1mm wall thickness, and a 35mm diameter at 3mm wall thickness at the head tube. After realising how advanced our control of aluminium was becoming, some bright spark – probably Todd again – created an acronym tying the company and its material together: Cannondale Advanced Aluminium Design, or CAAD.’

Despite the ever-improving technology, convincing a traditional road bike market of CAAD’s qualities proved a difficult task.

‘Steve Berti, a colleague who has driven sales in Europe for us for over 32 years, tells it best,’ says Dodman.

‘I started visiting dealers in 1994 with our 2.8 frames,’ says Berti. ‘Most of them said thanks but no thanks. I was even shown the door by one guy who told me he sold professional racing machines, not rain gutters. In the autumn of 1996, at the World Championships Road Race in Lugano, we “unofficially” started telling dealers we would be sponsor of the Saeco-Estro team in 1997. They didn’t believe it.

‘It was a hard start to our sponsorship, but the Giro d’Italia that year changed everything – six stage wins [for Saeco], as well as Ivan Gotti taking the GC. We were called the “Dream Team” by the end of that race, and at the Milan trade show later in 1997 we had lines of dealers outside our booth just waiting to get in.’

A stellar 1998 and 1999 proved the CAAD bikes weren’t a flash in the pan, with more Grand Tour stage success for Mario Cipollini.

‘It was his four straight stage wins at the 1999 Tour de France – along with him going up to a TV camera and saying, “Cannondale makes the best bikes,” – that helped popularise CAAD bikes on the global stage,’ says Berti.

Onwards and upwards

By this point CAAD was up to version 4.

‘CAAD 4 introduced “S-bend” seatstays to encourage vertical compliance and lessen its reputation as a harsh ride,’ says Dodman. ‘The bottom bracket shell also had material removed between the threads, the dropouts had windows and the chainstays were butted, all to save weight.’

Cannondale’s production method allowed for rapid developments, so it could produce a new CAAD every year from 1996 to 2003, when CAAD 8 came out.

‘CAAD 5 was a big step, not just for us but for bringing road bikes to where they are today,’ says Dodman. ‘I think we might have been the first to switch to 11/8in steerers with integrated headsets on road. It paved the way to drop the quill stem and bring in carbon fork steerers, and most bikes still use that dimension on their steerers today.

‘CAAD 6 added an oversize bottom bracket shell, introducing the BB30 standard so we could fit our new HollowGram Si cranks – the first to use a 30mm aluminium spindle. They were 100g lighter than Dura-Ace at the time and 4% stiffer. We put Saeco through 20,000km of ride testing to validate the cranks. We later added an SRM power meter, making CAAD the first production bike with an SRM.’

Having apparently perfected the recipe, Cannondale then changed the ingredients for 2002’s CAAD 7.

‘We used a new alloy we call Optimo. It was 15% stronger than before, meaning we could make the CAAD 7 very light, but it ended up noticeably less stiff than CAAD 6,’ says Dodman.

CAAD 8 switched in a new seat tube to reintroduce some of that lost stiffness, but by the early 2000s carbon composite was showing its potential as the de facto race bike material. Metal bikes were dropping like flies in the pro peloton, but CAAD clung on longer than most, becoming the last metal bike to win the Giro d’Italia under Damiano Cunego in 2004. Cunego reportedly liked the CAAD 8 so much that the next year, when Saeco switched to Cannondale’s new carbon and aluminium Six13 frames, Cannondale just repainted his old CAAD 8 and let him carry on.

Staying power

In time, the Six13, along with the original SystemSix, did steal the spotlight from CAAD on the world stage, but Cannondale continued to invest in the platform. CAAD 9 added a bigger down tube and tapered top tube to underline its performance credentials. Despite maintaining its race bike label, CAAD recaptured its ‘first bike’ roots as cash-savvy racers began building up framesets in custom specs to suit needs and budgets. The ‘dream bike’ label came in 2009 when Dura-Ace builds were released.

‘To most other brands, dressing up an aluminium bike like that was silly, but we understood the desire for it. Besides, our aluminium could outshine early budget carbon frames significantly,’ says Dodman.

CAAD achieved a reputation as a high-performance, low-cost racer that few aluminium bikes could match in the past, and which remains today with the current CAAD 14, though the journey from 9 to 14 wasn’t exactly smooth.

‘Cannondale was bought by Dorel in 2009,’ says Dodman. ‘Frame production in Bedford [Pennsylvania] closed in September 2010. It had been running for 15 years non-stop but production was now moved overseas. We enlisted the help of outside consultants who had experience making high-end bikes in Asia and they developed CAAD 10 based on their manufacturing knowledge to our requirements. It was a complete departure from the US CAAD series that had each built on the prior model and evolved over 15 years.’

It goes to 12

To reinvigorate the platform in 2015 and emphasise a departure from CAAD 10, Cannondale skipped 11 and went straight to 12.

‘We went back to in-house design for 12 but changed the way we created the frame in the software,’ says Dodman. ‘It was the most digitally analysed frame we had ever done, with over 200 different simulations run. The top tube was tapered, not round or oval, and the seat tube was flared and very asymmetric. Every tube was pushed to the limits, helping to make it 200g lighter than CAAD 10, 10% stiffer and 50% more compliant.’

Perhaps uniquely, CAAD bikes could still compete with carbon, but that success might have been the reason 13 fell flat. Cannondale’s carbon race bike, the SuperSix Evo, had an aero makeover in 2019 and the CAAD 13, released a couple of months later, attempted to recreate the design. But carbon and aluminium have distinct material properties, and trying to copy composite in metal meant some of CAAD’s core features – smooth welds, stiffness-to-weight – were lost.

‘So CAAD 14 filtered out the too radical elements – 25.4mm seat tube, asymmetric BB30 shell, rim brake variant – and added modern features such as UDH, thru-axles and bigger tyre clearance,’ says Will Gleason, Cannondale’s road product manager and lead on the CAAD 14 project. ‘Crucially, by going back to oversized round tubes, clean welds and a double diamond frame shape, we refocused the 14 on the ride feel that has always made CAAD stand out – that balance of stiffness, comfort and razor-sharp handling.’

‘CAAD’s journey has been perfectly imperfect,’ says Dodman. ‘Without the highs and lows we might not be where we are today. Where CAAD goes in future we’re still working on, but one thing’s for sure: it will not be going away.’

Masters of metal

A brief history of the Cannondale CAAD

1983: The ST500 is Cannondale’s first bicycle, using oversized thin wall aluminum tubing fabricated with CAD software and lasers.

1997: CAAD 2 is the first road frame to use the moniker. It features weight-optimised tubing and racing geometry.

1998: CAAD 3 offers better stiffness-to-weight thanks to more aggressive machining and shaped tubing.

1999: CAAD 4 introduces ‘S-bend’ seatstays to promote compliance.

2000: CAAD 5 is the first frame to use integrated headset bearings and a 11/8in steerer tube.

2001: CAAD 6 introduces BB30 bottom bracket to incorporate Cannondale’s HollowGram Si chainset, refined with input from the Saeco pro team.

2002: A newer, stronger aluminium is used in CAAD 7. The frame gets lighter but isn’t as stiff.

2003: A revised, tapered seat tube reintroduces stiffness with CAAD 8. It becomes the last metal bike to win the Giro d’Italia under Damiano Cunego in.

2007: Cannondale continues developing CAAD while other brands drop aluminium in favour of carbon. CAAD 9 uses a bigger down tube to reaffirm its racing status.

2010: First non-US-made CAAD is introduced. CAAD 10 refines 9 and is well received, but Cannondale wants to recapture more control of the platform.

2015: CAAD skips 11 and jumps to 12, returning to US-designed blueprint. Asymmetrical tube shaping and a thin seatpost make it 200g lighter than CAAD 10, 10% stiffer and 50% more compliant.

2019: CAAD 13 attempts to copy aero makeover of the SuperSix race bike, but loses the essence of the CAAD platform and receives a lukewarm reception.

2026: CAAD 14 goes back to the design’s roots of oversize round tubes, clean welds and a classic frame shape to recapture the platform’s USP.

The post The complete history of the Cannondale CAAD appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Forever Fun: Forty Years of Marin Bikes
entry.content:
Forever Fun is the official film celebrating 40 years of Marin Bikes, the mountain bike brand born in Marin County, California. Made with the creative team at Misspent Summers, it tells the story of the riders, people and ideas behind four decades of building bikes Made For Fun. Forty years ago, a bright idea in Marin County kicked off something nobody saw coming, least of all us. We built bikes that more people could ride. Suddenly, a whole new generation of riders were grinning up climbs, whooping down descents, and reaching places they never dreamed of getting to under their own steam.

The post Forever Fun: Forty Years of Marin Bikes appeared first on The Radavist.

entry.title: In The Drops: 3T Racemax+ WPNT, Rapha jeans return, 2026 Pro Cycling Trumps, Stubble & Co sling bag and London gravel
entry.content:
Cyclist
In The Drops: 3T Racemax+ WPNT, Rapha jeans return, 2026 Pro Cycling Trumps, Stubble & Co sling bag and London gravel

I know what you’re thinking. An In The Drops on a Monday? What sacrilege. However, I hold my hand up. I blame a certain bike show in London over the course of last week, plus the fun and games caused by a certain company’s email outage. Regardless, we’ve still managed to keep ourselves busy over the past week.

The pro season is over, but last week, we caught up with Netcompany Ineos sprinter Dorian Godon, domestique Chris-Juul Jensen and Maninder Pal Singh, the man who’s bringing the UCI World Championships to India soon.

A few launches and reveals broke cover last week, but Van Rysel’s latest RCR-R is the biggest splash of the lot. Ridden by Paul Seixas at this year’s Tour, the weight-saving machine has been one of the worst-kept secrets in the WorldTour. The bike’s not on sale until January, so don’t expect it to be cropping up in any of our Black Friday deal round-ups any time soon.

Anyways, it’s time to talk dirty. Let’s unleash this week’s first selection of cycling goodies.

3T Racemax+ WPNT

We’re kicking things off big this week, with the launch of Italian brand 3T’s latest gravel machine: the Racemax+ WPNT.

The Racemax+ WPNT is an updated version of the brand’s aero-focused gravel bike, first launched in 2020. Since then, it’s undergone several iterations, Italia and Italia X, but the Racemax is the latest to receive a facelift, having been launched last week. It’s also the most budget-friendly option from the range, with the price lowered in this new generation. In fact, 3T claims an equivalent build of the new Racemax+ WPNT is around €1,000 cheaper.

The geometry has been updated from the previous Racemax WPNT model to include subtle 3mm increases to stack and reach, longer chainstays – now 425 mm – and a revised fork offset in order to balance high-speed stability with responsive handling. Now available in six sizes from XS to XXL, the new Racemax+ offers a broader fit range to suit more riders.

The bike is compatible with both 1x and 2x drivetrains, but 3T’s own builds come with options for a mechanical Shimano GRX groupset or the 13-speed SRAM Rival XPLR AXS electronic drivetrain.

The bike’s clearance is now 51 mm with a 1x drivetrain and 48mm on a 2x drivetrain, comfortable enough for gravel racing terrain. 45mm Vittoria Terreno T50s are supplied on every 3T build, which is much appreciated on tougher gravel terrain. Although, the bike’s aggressive geometry will have you wanting to hit the trails at full pelt.

If you’re stumped as to what WPNT means, it’s ‘We Paint’ without the vowels. The colours they paint – or THCLRSWPNT – are Foresta Green, Quarzo Grey and Vela Beige (as photographed above). All bikes are assembled in Italy, with prices starting from £2,908.

  • Learn more about the Racemax+ WPNT

Rapha + Hiut jeans

It’s no joke. The Rapha jeans are back!

Yes, the London-based brand has re-released some of its much-loved pieces as part of Rapha’s Icons collection. The range combines some of those cult classics alongside new limited-edition collaborations.

As part of this, Rapha has rekindled its collaboration with Welsh denim atelier Hiut, several years on from when the jeans first made a splash.

All the jeans are hand-cut and sewn in Aberteifi (Cardigan) in western Wales and are filled with nods to Rapha, not least the pink buckles and stitching around the fly. The inside of the leg is adorned with Rapha’s logo and each pair comes with a number penned by the last seamstress to craft your breeks.

There are three cuts to choose from in this collaboration: the Jerald (men’s), the Miles Selvedge (men’s) and the Edna Jean (women’s). I’ve gone for the classic Jerald – a high-rise, classic straight-leg cut in durable 12oz ISKO Organic denim.

Who said cycling fashion was all Lycra and Polartec, eh?

  • Available from Rapha (£260)

Pro Cycling Trumps: 2026 Edition

Without any road racing on at the moment, we have to find new ways to get our competitive fix. To chase that high, I present Pro Cycling Trumps.

The premise is simple: Top Trumps, but with cyclists. Not any old cyclists; this pack features the stars of the 2026 season, including Paul Seixas, Mathieu van der Poel, Tadej Pogačar, Tim Merlier and Britain’s Matthew Brennan.

Each card is decked out with a cartoon sketch alongside scores for time-trials, breakaways, one-day races, climbing, sprinting and GC. Choose your chosen stat wisely as you pit the cards head-to-head, with the highest stat coming out ‘trumps’.

The cast of 2026 can be played alongside other Pro Cycling Trumps packs, but let it be known that there are few riders quite as untrumpable as Pogačar.

  • Available from Pro Cycling Trumps (£19)

Stubble & Co Motion Sling bag

There’s nothing less nonchalant than carting a huge backpack around, looking like a Year 7 on their first day of school. Stubble & Co know this, and have a solution with their Motion Sling bag.

This magazine-sized bag is a bum bag on steroids, with a surprisingly spacious main compartment and a sleeve for a 14in laptop. It also features two side pockets for water bottles, can be thrown over your shoulder, and even has a handy loop for attaching a light.

The bag’s held in place by an adjustable crossbody strap, with a cross chest strap for extra stability. What’s more, the bag’s design is intended to spread weight equally, so there’s no awkward swinging about or bag interference when you are hanging over the bars.

In terms of material, the Motion Sling relies on a breathable 3D mesh back panel for consistent airflow and a PFC-free water-resistant coating. The bag is available in three colours: magma, ash and charcoal. Plus, there’s 20% off this bag online courtesy of Stubble & Co’s Black Friday sale.

  • Available from Stubble & Co (£85)

What we’re into this week: Going off-road

Between all the chaos of being in and around a certain three-day event in London this week, I’ve been enjoying riding the aforementioned 3T on some of the gravel trails of northeast London.

News flash: cycling journalist rides bike.

Embarrassingly, I’d never gone off-road in London before this month. In fairness, I only moved here six months ago and riding the Traka back in May led me to believe I’d never want to sling my leg over a gravel bike again. Alas, I’m all here for it and am loving the bump and grind of dodging dogwalkers and children in Epping Forest.

The post In The Drops: 3T Racemax+ WPNT, Rapha jeans return, 2026 Pro Cycling Trumps, Stubble & Co sling bag and London gravel appeared first on Cyclist.

entry.title: Garmin Sales Begin: Huge deals on Garmin Fenix, Edge, Forerunner Series and more!
entry.content:
Like clockwork, Garmin has put forth their sale plans for the Black Friday and Holiday season. Garmin is actually one of the most predictable companies in this space when it comes to sales and how they structure them (with Wahoo probably being *the* most predictable one). The sale prices Garmin puts forth now are essentially their deals for the holidays. They don’t tend to reduce prices on these specific products further, and don’t really add anything else. This is it, at least from a US perspective (European sales are the Wild West and field of dreams of pricing…anything is possible).

The exception to that rule in the US is Uncle Amazon. Uncle Amazon has a long history of throwing very random deals into the mix, especially over Black Friday weekend. These tend to fall into one of two buckets. The first is buckets where Garmin has basically worked with Amazon to offload huge chunks of older inventory, and you’ll see some crazy deals on that. The second is when Amazon doesn’t partner with Garmin at all, and simply decides to randomly cut the price yolo style. This is usually previous-generation stuff, but at least once or twice over each Black Friday it ends up being a newly released product.

Anyway, my advice here is simple: If you see something on sale you want, buy it now, and then if you find a better Amazon deal later, you can always return it or such. For Amazon, you can return items bought Nov 1-Dec 31st until Jan 31st 2027. As always, the random deals don’t tend to last. They’re flash in the pans. Got that?

With that, onto the deals! And thanks for supporting the site via the links below. As an Amazon Associate, I earn from qualifying purchases. Enjoy!

Watches & Wearables:

This covers anything you can wear that’s watch-like or activity band-like, including sensors.

entry.title: Suunto Mostly Leaving Finland, Wahoo Adds Oura/COROS/Apple Sleep Integrations
entry.content:
We’ve got two sports tech news items hitting today, both with a Finnish connection. First up is news about Suunto continuing to dismantle said Finnish connection, and then after that there’s news of Wahoo joining up with Finnish brand Oura, maker of Oura rings.

Suunto Announces Further Finnish Layoffs:

According to an article published this morning by the largest daily newspaper in Finland, Suunto plans to lay off the majority of remaining staff in Finland, and continue consolidating functions in China, via its owners since 2022 – Liesheng. HS (the newspaper) reports that Suunto had 160 people in Finland, and on Monday the company notified 118 of those that their jobs may be lost. Suunto (pre-acquisition) had moved most of its less expensive watch manufacturing to China, and then in 2024 that followed with moving all sports watch manufacturing to China.

Since then, Liesheng has shifted virtually all Suunto software development to China, as well as most other functions. That has resulted in Suunto actually delivering frequent software updates on a predictable quarterly-ish update schedule. While many of these features are mostly catch-up to their competitors, this was a massive change from the previous decade, which saw on-again/off-again progress in terms of making competitive products.

While 2024 and 2025 saw Suunto deliver a number of strong watch contenders at very good prices, since this summer Suunto has taken an oddly different tack – specifically around pricing. They launched the Suunto Run 2 at $349USD, substantially higher than the $249 the previous Suunto Run 1 was launched at (especially given it was originally billed as Suunto’s entry-level/budget watch). This price wasn’t completely a deal-killer given the more premium materials twist. But the real head-scratcher was the recent Suunto Race 3S, which was bafflingly priced at $599USD, a 70% price increase over the previous Suunto Race S unit (it also shifted to more premium materials). All while falling far short of the much less expensive COROS Pace 4 Pro that was launched a week prior. Point being, pricing shifts may be joining workforce shifts.

Having been around Suunto a long-long time, nearly all of the people I knew who had been there for decades are now gone. While Suunto the brand is still making good watches, it’ll soon be pretty hard to meaningfully call it a Finnish brand. Nonetheless, there’s plenty of non-Finnish sports brands still making great GPS watches. Only time will tell whether Suunto, as a brand/name, can stay the course of making good watches, country association aside.

(And as an aside, I was actually wrapping up my written review of the Suunto Run 2, after almost precisely a month of wearing it, when this news hit this morning, so expect that review tomorrow.)

Wahoo Partners with Oura/COROS/Apple Health For Readiness Insights:

Wahoo has joined Zwift in announcing recent integrations with Oura (Zwift did so a week or so ago). Apparently, whoever at Oura is responsible for partner integrations is going for the Christmas bonus this year. This new integration with Wahoo feeds your Oura ring data into their Training Insights feature, allowing you to combine that data with your Wahoo training data.

But Oura isn’t the only one. Both COROS and Apple Health are coming next week. However, Oura is here today, so I’ll show that. First, setting it up is relatively easy. You’ll see a notice at the top that you can connect Oura; simply tap that, and a few seconds later you’re done.

From there on the main dashboard, you’ll see the Recovery Response metric populated. This isn’t a direct metric from Oura, but rather a calculated score by Wahoo.

In this case, if I were to tap that, I’m brought to a different dashboard that shows a bit more of my sleep details, including last night’s sleep, last night’s HRV, and last night’s resting HR. It also shows temperature and respiration rate. For SpO2, I didn’t have that toggled on in the Oura app (it’s a manual toggle). Currently, when I tap on any of the metrics for more details, it shows that a historical chart is coming soon.

For the mental capacity bit, that’s a short game/test you take over 90 seconds, typing when a color square shows up, how many milliseconds it takes you to respond to it. Since I just started that fun today, it takes 3 days of anxiety-inducing tapping to light up that scorecard.

For the specifics, here are some extra tidbits from Wahoo:

Data imported from Oura: HRV (rMSSD), resting heart rate and sleep (time asleep), plus blood oxygen (SpO2), respiratory rate and body temperature as illness markers. Readiness and sleep need are calculated by Wahoo, not imported from Oura. When Recovery Response is elevated, My Readiness flags the anomaly to the athlete.
Integration: One-way, with data flowing from Oura to Wahoo.
Compatibility: All generations of the Oura ring. An active Oura membership is required.
Historical data: When connecting, athletes can import up to 90 days of Oura data, so My Readiness has a personal baseline from day one.
Training history: My Readiness uses every workout in the athlete’s Wahoo App history, whichever device or platform recorded it.

In any case, as for COROS & Apple Health, those are again slated to light up on Tuesday the 17th (November). So I’ll give those a poke then.

With that – thanks for reading!

entry.title: Trainer Apps Roundup Coming: Which Apps to Include?
entry.content:
It’s been a hot minute since I’ve done an indoor trainer app roundup, and in some ways the landscape has changed, and in others it’s kinda still same-same. The same major players are still all here, though consolidated a bit by who owns them. Still, the biggies remain – and include the likes of Zwift, TrainerRoad, MyWhoosh, Rouvy, FulGaz, Peloton, Tacx Training App, and TrainingPeaks Virtual.

But then beyond that there are basically three buckets of smaller apps, which I’d probably divide into the following categories (note I use ’smaller’ here in the context compared to the ones above):

Group A) Smaller-ish apps that have been around the block a long time but have a following: e.g., Kinomap, BigRingVR, Wahoo SYSTEM, Xert, etc…

Group B) Newer-ish smaller apps that have gained popularity or notoriety in the last little while: e.g., BikeTerra, Vieta, etc…

Group C) The gazillions of mostly AI-created trainer apps that vary wildly in concept/support/etc…

Now, with that said, one of the reasons I’ve fallen behind on keeping my trainer apps list up to date is that it’s mostly nightmare fuel to do properly. Sure, I could create a quick list of all the apps out there, pretend I rode them as most publications do, and then call it a review. Or, they just ask some AI platform to quickly make a list with some screenshots. But that’s not my style. I actually want to ride these apps, and there’s no AI-written garbage here. Many of them I’ve ridden already for years, either frequently or infrequently. So I’m familiar with some of them.

But there’s a whole lot of ones in Group C above that I’ve never heard of (and frankly, might disappear next week after someone stops paying a hosting fee). Some of these are totally wild (in a good way), and many of them are free. But tracking them all in my inbox is mostly impossible. Meaning, even if you’ve e-mailed me about them, I’d strongly recommend dropping it below in the comments too. :)

So, here’s the deal: To make this semi-manageable, I’ve already started on a number of apps to be included in an updated guide, and I’m gonna keep chugging over the next 7-10 days on riding a bunch of the newer apps. But, knowing there’s a lot of interesting apps out there, consider this open season for posting the app below in the comments section.

Anyone is welcome to post an app name and/or link. If you’ve created the app – cool, go forth! If you’ve ridden the app, I’m game too (and to hear your thoughts, good and/or bad). Deal?

(Note: Due to spam reduction bits, for non-DCR Supporters, I have to manually approve links, so it may take a few hours for your link-inclusive comment to show up).

entry.title: Garmin Bringing Edge 1060 Features to Older Units: Full Details!
entry.content:
﻿

When Garmin announced the Edge 1060, they noted that the majority of features would come to existing Edge x50 series devices (Edge 550/850/1050), as well as a handful of features going to older x40 series devices (Edge 540/840/1040/1040 Solar). Heck, even the Edge MTB gets new tricks too.

The good news is that we don’t have to wait long, at least for some of the new features. Garmin has already started rolling out a portion of the new features in public beta, and I’ve got an outline for all the remaining features and which devices are getting what.

Which Features Go To Which Units:

Now, in my Edge 1060 post I explain all the new features in a bit more detail, but in short, these are the key software features that can be ported back (voice features like voice control and voice messaging require a microphone, which simply isn’t in older Garmin Edge hardware). Here’s what we’re looking at:

Strava Live Segment Updates: This essentially has three components to it. The first is allowing for collapsible portions within the Strava Live Segment page (e.g., resizing the different chunks, or getting rid of certain ones). Next, you can now see competitor icons on the map & elevation profiles (e.g. KOM position). And finally – the biggie, you can now do Strava Live Segments on *any* route (previously it was just Strava Routes). [Coming to Edge x50 & Edge MTB in Q1 2027]
